v_city_first_night.title: First night in the line
v_city_first_night.text:
Up the communication trench in the dark, single file. Then the firestep, and your rifle, and
the dark.

You've never seen dark like it. In Leyton there's always a lamp somewhere, a gas mantle in a
window, the glow of the town on the clouds. Here there's nothing, and then a flare, white,
hanging, and everything stands still like a photograph, wire and posts and a tree with no top,
and then it goes out and you're blind again.

The trench stinks of chloride of lime and something sweet under it.

[if war.mate1]Beside you Webb has his little black notebook out, the one he kept the petty cash in, and a stub of pencil, and every time a shell comes over he makes a mark. "Fourteen," he whispers. "Since stand-to. I'll want the totals." He's writing down everything. Time, weather, the names of the trenches.[else]Down the bay a clerk from the Prudential has a notebook out, and every time a shell comes over he makes a mark. "Fourteen," he whispers. "I'll want the totals."[/if]

choices.text: Tell Webb diaries are forbidden. If he's taken, they read it.
choices.text_after:
"I know," Webb says. "I know what the order says." He closes the notebook and holds it. "But
somebody ought to keep the books. Properly. Or afterwards nobody will know what happened."
He puts it in his inside pocket, over his heart, where the pay book goes.

choices.text: Let him count. It's keeping his hands steady.
choices.text_after:
You let him. His pencil goes all night. By stand-to his hand's stopped shaking and yours
hasn't, and you think he may have the right idea.

v_city_letter.title: A letter from home
v_city_letter.text:
A parcel, done up properly in brown paper and sealing wax the way your father does the gas
company's, and inside: socks, a tin of Huntley and Palmers biscuits, a bar of Pears soap, and
the smell of the scullery in Leyton coming off all of it.

"Dear Son, I hope this finds you well. You will have read in the papers about the Zeppelin.
It came over on Monday night, and we stood in the street and watched it, everybody did, like a
great silver cigar up in the searchlights, and it was beautiful, God forgive me. It dropped its
bombs on Stoke Newington and Hoxton, and they say children were killed. Your father has
put the shutters up.

[if war.mate1]Mrs Webb says Arthur writes every day, and they are like an accountant's report. Can you not get him to say how he is.[else]Mrs Webb has had the letter about Arthur. She has stopped going to church.[/if]

Keep your feet dry. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back tonight, two sides, in ink.
choices.text_after:
You tell her the French have Pears soap too, which isn't true. You tell her to stay in the
house when the Zeppelins come. You don't tell her that half the men in the section have
stood in the street at home and watched one, and all of them say it was beautiful.

choices.text: Send the field postcard. Cross out what doesn't apply.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. Strike out the rest. The biscuits go round the bay, and the soap goes in your
pack, and you take it out at night and smell it.

v_city_desk.title: The office
v_city_desk.text:
A long envelope with the firm's crest: the Gresham and Lombard Assurance, Cornhill. The manager
writes to all the men from the office on active service, every quarter, a typed letter. The
firm is proud of you. Your salary is being made up and paid to your mother. There is a Roll of
Honour in the front hall, in gilt, and four names on it already in a separate column.

And a second sheet, folded inside, handwritten.

"Dear Sir, You will not know me. I am Miss Holland and I have been given your desk while you
are away. I am learning the ledgers and I hope I am not making a mess of them. I have kept your
pen rest and your blotter, I did not like to throw them out. If there is anything you would like
sent, the office is happy to send it. Yours sincerely, F. Holland."

choices.text: Write back to Miss Holland.
choices.text_after:
You tell her where the key to the bottom drawer is, and which of the old ledgers lie, and that
Mr Gedge in Marine likes his tea without sugar but won't say so. You tell her to keep the pen
rest. You don't know why you tell her about the fog on the river from the third-floor window,
but you do.

choices.text: Put it away. You don't know what to say to a girl at your desk.
choices.text_after:
You put it in your pay book. Every so often you take it out and read it, F. Holland, and try
to think what the F stands for.

v_city_match.title: The match
v_city_match.text:
At rest, and Fenton's got a football. Of course he has. He carried it up from the boat in his
pack, deflated, with the bladder wrapped in his spare shirt, and now it's blown up hard and he's
challenged the pitmen in B Company to a match.

It's in a stubble field with a goal at each end made of rifles. The pitmen are short and wide and
don't run, they barge, and they've a man in goal who's built like a coal tub. Half the battalion
is round the edge of the field, shouting.

Fenton played centre-forward for the office eleven on Saturday afternoons at Walthamstow. He's
better than anybody on the field and everybody knows it.

choices.text: Play. Right half, behind Fenton.
choices.text_after:
You lose four goals to two. One of their half-backs puts you on your back in the stubble so
hard you see stars, then picks you up and dusts you off and says "Howay, man, you're all
right," and you are. Fenton scores both. He's grinning for a week. For an hour and a half
nobody thinks about anything else at all.

choices.text: Watch from the edge with a mug of tea.
choices.text_after:
You stand on the edge with the others and shout yourself hoarse. The pitmen win four goals
to two. Fenton scores both and walks off the field with his arm round their goalkeeper, and
the two of them are talking about Newcastle United like old friends.

v_city_spectacles.title: Spectacles
v_city_spectacles.text:
Marsh has broken his spectacles. A rifle butt in a crowded trench, an accident. One lens is gone
altogether and the other's starred across.

He can't see. You didn't know how badly. He learned the eye chart by heart at the recruiting
office, the whole thing, top to bottom, the night before, so they'd pass him. He tells you this
in a whisper in the dugout, holding the broken frames in his hand.

"If the MO knows, they'll send me back," he says. "Base, or home. Unfit. And everybody at
chapel will know why." He looks at you without his glasses, naked-faced. "I can't see the wire,
out there. I can see that there is wire."

choices.text: Write to his mother for his spare pair. Stay by him till they come.
choices.text_after:
Ten days, and you're his eyes. On sentry you stand next to him and tell him what you see. On
the carrying party you walk in front and he holds your pack strap. The spare pair come in a
parcel with a cake and a Bible, and he puts them on and looks at you, and says, "Oh. That's
what you look like."

choices.text: Tell the MO. He'll be killed out there blind.
choices.text_after:
The MO tests him with a card held at the end of the dugout, and Marsh gets it wrong, and the
MO looks at him and sighs and writes something. He's sent to the base for a fortnight, and
comes back with army spectacles, steel, ugly, that pinch, and he doesn't speak to you for a
week. Then he does.

v_city_eve_loos.title: Moving up
v_city_eve_loos.text:
Three nights of marching in the rain, and on the third morning you come up into the assembly
trenches and look over at a mining village, rows of houses, slag heaps, and over the middle of
it two great iron towers side by side, joined at the top.

"Tower Bridge," somebody says, and it's what everybody's calling it by dinner time. It's the
shape. It's the first thing that's looked like home since the boat.

Along the parapet, under sacking, the gas cylinders.

[if war.mate2]Fenton's got his football out of his pack. He's pumping it up with the bicycle pump he brought for the purpose. "When we go over," he says, "I'm kicking this across. First man to put it in their trench gets a quid." Nobody tells him he's daft. Somebody asks if it's a real quid.[/if][if war.mate1] Webb's writing in the notebook. Everything. The towers, the cylinders, the weather.[/if]

The company sergeant major comes round with pay books. If you want to write anything, now's
the time.

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
You write it in your office hand, properly, as if it were going to the manager. Then you tear
it up and write it again the way you'd say it. That you love them. That the firm will see her
right. That your bat and pads are to go to the boys' club. You fold it small.

choices.text: Leave it. Writing one is asking for it.
choices.text_after:
You leave it. You eat the last of the biscuits, and look at Tower Bridge, and think of the
real one in the fog, and the tram going over it.

v_city_roll.title: The ledger
v_city_roll.text:
At the end of the year at the office, the senior clerk closes the accounts that are closed. A
double line ruled under the last entry, in red ink, with a ruler, and the word Closed, and the
date. You did it a hundred times without thinking.

They form what's left of the battalion up in a field behind the line, in the rain, and the
sergeant major reads the roll, and you stand there and watch him rule the lines.

[if war.mate1]"Webb." "Here, sir." Precisely, as if he were answering at the office.[else]"Webb." Nothing. "Webb, A." The rain on the caps.[/if]
[if war.mate2]"Fenton." "Here, sir!" Too loud. He's been too loud since Saturday.[else]"Fenton." Nothing. Somewhere out by the German wire there's a football.[/if]
[if war.mate3]"Marsh." "Here." Through the rain, and you can see him wipe his spectacles.[else]"Marsh." Nothing. You think of the eye chart, learned by heart.[/if]

choices.text: Answer for the men you saw fall, when their names come.
choices.text_after: "Killed, sir. I saw him." The sergeant major makes his mark. A double line, in red. Closed.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let somebody else tell it.
choices.text_after:
Somebody else does, or nobody does, and the names go down as missing: an account left open,
that nobody will ever balance.

v_city_raid.title: Wood Street
v_city_raid.text:
The London papers come up a week late, and they're full of it. In September the Zeppelin came
over the City itself. Not the suburbs this time. Wood Street, Bartholomew Close, the warehouses by
Aldersgate. Bombs in the City, among the warehouses and the offices, fires all night, and a bus hit in the street
with the people still on it.

And a letter from the office. The windows on the Cornhill side are out. Nobody was hurt; the
building was empty, it being night. The Roll of Honour in the front hall came off the wall and
the glass broke, and Miss Holland swept it up herself and saved the names.

[if war.mate1]Webb reads the paper and goes white. "Wood Street," he says. "My father's warehouse is in Wood Street."[/if]

choices.text: Help Webb find out. Ask everybody who's had a letter.
choices.text_after:
It takes four days. A man in D Company has a brother in the Fire Brigade, and a letter from
him says the warehouse is standing, scorched, the next one gone. Webb writes it in his
notebook, carefully, the date and the source, and then puts his head down on his knees.

choices.text: Read the paper through and pass it on.
choices.text_after:
You read it twice, every street name, and every one is a place you've walked at dinner time
with a sandwich. Then you pass it down the bay, and watch it go from hand to hand, Londoners
reading about London as if it were somewhere abroad.

b_loos_city_advance.title: Loos
b_loos_city_advance.text:
Rum at five, from a stone jar, a tot in the lid of your mess tin. It goes down burning, like the
brandy your mother keeps for shocks.

At ten to six the gas goes over. A hiss all down the line, like every gas main in Leyton opened
at once, and the cloud comes up white and greenish and leans out towards their wire. Some of it
hangs. Some of it comes back. Pepper and pineapple and a bite under it. You pull the hood down.
Wet flannel, the stink, your own breath hot against the little window.

Through the eyepiece, through the smoke, Tower Bridge.

Half past six. The guns stop.

[if war.mate2]Fenton's on the ladder above you with the football under his arm. He goes over, and drops it on the far side of the parapet, and kicks it, a long low punt into the smoke, and goes after it at a jog, the way he'd go after a ball at Walthamstow.[else]Somebody along the line goes over with a football and kicks it into the smoke, and goes after it at a jog.[/if] Beside you on the ladder is {mate}.

[if war.stalled]You get your head over the top. The first wave is lying down in the grass in rows, too straight, like the clerks' desks in the long room at the office, and in front of them their wire is standing whole.[else]You get your head over the top. The first wave is walking into the smoke with their rifles at the port, after the ball, and nobody's falling yet.[/if]

choices.text: Over the top. Walk with the wave. ({risk_push})
Go up with {mate}. Stay at his shoulder. ({risk_help})
Over, and straight down into the first shell hole. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_city_trench.title: Loos
b_loos_city_trench.text:
Their trench, and then the village. Loos, under the iron towers: streets of little brick
houses, a church with no roof, a cemetery where the Germans have dug in among the graves. You go
through it street by street, house by house, and every cellar has to be bombed, and the noise in
the narrow streets is like the Underground when the train comes in, only it doesn't stop.

In the cemetery a German machine gun behind a family vault. Marble angels with their faces
shot off.

[if war.stalled]The machine gun in the cemetery has the street, and men lie down in it and don't get up, and the bombers can't get near.[else]"Through the cemetery! Bombers! Go on, go on!"[/if]

choices.text: Into the cemetery after the bombers. ({risk_push})
Stay with {mate}. Watch his back at the doorways. ({risk_help})
Get down behind a gravestone and fire from there. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_city_hold.title: Loos
b_loos_city_hold.text:
By the afternoon you're dug in at the edge of the village, by a slag heap two heaps long that
the maps call the Double Crassier, and the rain's come in. Nobody's brought water. The gas has
left a taste like licking a penny.

Somewhere behind you in the village a piano is playing. Somebody's found a piano in a house with
no front wall, and is playing it, a music-hall song, badly, and men are singing along in the rain.

Then shouting on the left, and rifle fire, picking up the way rain does on the glass roof at
Liverpool Street.

"Stand to! They're coming back!"

choices.text: Up on the parapet. Fire till they stop coming. ({risk_push})
Keep {mate} fed with clips. Stay low beside him. ({risk_help})
Stay under the parapet. Fire blind over the top. ({risk_ground})

l_city_1915.title: Home on leave
l_city_1915.text:
The leave train comes in to Victoria at night, and you get off it in your mud, as you are, with
your rifle and your tin hat and France on your boots, and the women on the platform with their
furs step out of your way. A lady gives you a cup of tea from an urn and calls you a brave boy.
The station smells of steam and soot and wet umbrellas, and of a thousand men off the boat.

The streets are darker than you left them, the lamps half painted over for the Zeppelins. You
take the Underground and a tram and walk the last bit, and the street's the same, every house,
and you have to stand at the gate a minute.

Your mother opens the door before you knock. She doesn't say anything. She holds your face in
both hands. Then she smells you, and sends you to the scullery.

[if flag.city_wrote_home]Your letter's on the mantelpiece, behind the clock, with the rent book.[/if][if flag.city_postcard]The field postcard is on the mantelpiece. "Quite well," your father reads, in his gas-company voice, and puts it back.[/if][if !flag.city_letter]"You might have written," she says to the copper.[/if]

On the Monday you go up to the office, because you can't not. The Roll of Honour's back in the front hall in a new frame. The manager shakes your hand and calls you a credit to the firm. [if flag.city_wrote_holland]Miss Holland is at your desk. She stands up. She's smaller than you thought, with ink on her middle finger, and she shows you your pen rest, still there, and you stand by your own desk like a visitor, and neither of you can think of a thing to say, and it doesn't matter.[/if][if !flag.city_wrote_holland]There's a girl at your desk, typing, who looks up at you and doesn't know who you are.[/if]

[if war.mate1]Mrs Webb asks if Arthur is well. You tell her he keeps the books. She doesn't understand, and you don't explain.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.city_helped_webb] Mr Webb shakes your hand for a long minute in the scorched doorway in Wood Street.[/if][if !war.mate1]The Webbs' front-room curtains are drawn in the middle of the day.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.city_wrote_webb] Mrs Webb has your letter, and Arthur's notebook, which came back with his things. She hasn't been able to open it. She asks you to.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.city_played]Fenton's father, who never missed a Saturday, wants to hear about the match with the pitmen, every kick of it, in the front parlour, and laughs till he cries.[/if][if war.mate2 && !flag.city_played]Mr Fenton wants to know about the football at Loos. He's read about it in the papers. You tell him it was Percy's ball.[/if][if !war.mate2]The office eleven are playing on, short a man. They kept Percy Fenton's shirt in the pavilion, and nobody will wear it.[/if][if !war.mate2 && flag.city_wrote_fenton] Mr Fenton has your letter framed beside the photograph of the eleven.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.city_kept_marsh]Mrs Marsh gives you a cake and a Bible to take back, and asks you to keep looking after Leonard's eyes. "He wrote that you were his eyes," she says.[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.city_told_mo]Mrs Marsh says Leonard wrote that he has army spectacles now, and that you saw to it. She doesn't know whether to thank you.[/if][if !war.mate3]At the chapel the Sunday school class has a new teacher. The children made a card for Mr Marsh, and nobody knew where to send it.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.city_wrote_marsh] Mrs Marsh has your letter in her Bible.[/if]

[if flag.city_spoke_at_roll]At church a woman stops you in the porch. "You were the one who told them about our Ronald," she says. "In C Company. They said it was quick." You tell her it was.[/if][if flag.city_silent_at_roll]On the tram a woman is telling the conductor that her son is only missing, that missing means a prisoner. You saw. You get off a stop early and walk.[/if]

At night the quiet keeps waking you. Then a tram, far off, and you sleep.

Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v_farm_first_night.title: First night in the line
v_farm_first_night.text:
Up the communication trench in the dark, single file, each man holding the scabbard of the
man in front. Then the firestep, and your rifle, and the dark.

You've been out on the moor at night after a lost ewe, with no moon and the fog down. You know
dark. This dark is wrong. It smells wrong, of lime and something sweet under it, and it's never
quiet the way a field's quiet. A flare goes up and everything stands still, wire and posts and
a tree with no top, like rabbits in a lamp.

And then, behind the line somewhere, in what's left of a wood, a nightingale starts.

[if war.mate2]Pearce has his head up over the parapet, which you're not to do, sniffing the air like a dog. "There's a hare out there," he says. "In the wire. I can see her ears." He's got a bit of brass wire in his pocket. Of course he has. "Back in ten minutes."[else]Down the bay a lad from Brendon has his head up over the parapet, which you're not to do. "There's a hare out there," he says. "In the wire."[/if]

choices.text: Go over with Pearce. Somebody has to watch his back.
choices.text_after:
Over the parapet on your belly, through our wire by the gap the wiring party left, out into
the long grass, and Pearce moving through it like water, not a sound. He sets his wire in
the dark by feel. A flare goes up and you both lie with your faces in the dirt and the
nightingale still going. Back in twenty minutes. In the morning there's a hare in the wire,
his wire, and the sergeant wants to know whose it is, and nobody knows.

choices.text: Pull him down. You'll both be shot.
choices.text_after: [if war.mate2]You get him by the belt and haul him down off the step. He swears at you, low. Then he grins. "You'm right," he says. "Not tonight. They don't know me yet." The nightingale goes on.[else]Somebody pulls the lad down. The nightingale goes on, and you stand and listen to it till stand-to.[/if]

v_farm_letter.title: A letter from home
v_farm_letter.text:
A parcel, brown paper and binder twine, and the smell of the kitchen when you open it: a
saffron cake, socks, a twist of tea, a pot of cream with a bit of muslin over it gone sour on
the way.

"Dear Son, I hope this finds you as it leaves us. Your father is ploughing the Long Field with
old Blossom on her own since they took Prince and Duke for the army, and it takes him the week.
He says the mare is too old for it and so is he. The squire has taken on two maids from the
town for the dairy and they do not know one end of a cow from the other.

[if war.mate1]Mr Cottle says to tell Will that Fly is off her food and lies by the gate in the evenings looking up the lane.[else]Mr Cottle has not been to market since the letter came about Will. Fly lies by the gate in the evenings looking up the lane.[/if]

Keep your feet dry. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back tonight, two sides, by a candle end.
choices.text_after:
You tell her the French farm the same as us, only worse, with oxen and their women at the
plough. You tell your father to rest the mare. You tell her the cream came sour and you ate
it anyway, with a spoon, in the bottom of the trench, and it tasted of home.

choices.text: Send the field postcard. Cross out what doesn't apply.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. You strike out the rest. The saffron cake goes round the bay in a quarter
of an hour, and the lads from the town have never had it before, and want to know what makes
it yellow.

v_farm_venn.title: Mr Venn
v_farm_venn.text:
The platoon officer is young Mr Venn from the big house. You were a beater on his father's
shoots from when you were ten: sixpence and a pasty to walk through the wet bracken with a stick,
driving the birds over the guns. He was one of the guns.

He stops you in the support line. "Good to see a Dunsworthy face," he says, and calls you by
your Christian name, and then remembers, and goes red, and calls you by your surname.

He wants a servant. Somebody to keep his kit, bring his water, make his tea, look after him. A
soldier-servant. You'd be excused fatigues. You'd be with him in the line, always.

choices.text: Say yes. He's from home.
choices.text_after:
You clean his boots in the dugout by candlelight, and he sits writing to his mother, and
sometimes reads you a line, about the dogs, about the house, as if you were at home together
in the gunroom. You find you don't mind. You find you like him.

choices.text: Say no, sir. You'd sooner stop with the lads.
choices.text_after:
"Of course," he says. "Of course." He takes a lad from Taunton instead. When he passes you in
the trench after, he nods, and it's as if you'd both been caught at something.

v_farm_bell.title: The bell
v_farm_bell.text:
At rest, in a village with half a church. The tower's still up, though the roof of the nave
is gone, and there's a bell rope hanging down in the dust inside the tower door.

Bert Yeo stands and looks at it the way other men look at a girl. He rang the tenor at
Dunsworthy from the age of twelve. Every Sunday, every wedding, every funeral. He takes hold of
the rope and tests the pull of it, and you can see his whole body wants to pull.

But in the line, any bell is the gas alarm. A bell rung here, this close, and the whole village
will be in its masks.

choices.text: Let him ring it once. Say it was you, if anybody asks.
choices.text_after:
He pulls, once, the way you'd ring a tenor down, and the bell speaks, one deep note that goes
out over the broken roofs and the orchards. Somewhere a dog starts barking. Men come out of
barns with their masks half on. The sergeant major wants to know who. You say it was you.
Bert stands behind you with his face shining like a lad at his first wedding.

choices.text: Take his hand off the rope. Not here.
choices.text_after:
He lets go. He stands there a minute longer with his hand still curled the way it held the
sally. "After," he says. "I'll ring the whole peal, after. When we get home." You walk him
back to the billet.

v_farm_hare.title: Pearce
v_farm_hare.text:
The military police have got Pearce. Behind the lines, at rest, with two hares and a brace of
French partridges in the bottom of his pack and a set of wires in his pocket. The farmer's
complained. The French farmers complain about everything, and this time they've a case.

It's Field Punishment Number One. Tied to a limber wheel for two hours a day, in the open, by
the road, where everybody going past can see. Twenty-eight days of it.

[if flag.farm_went_out]Since the hare the first night he's been out every night at rest, and you've known, and said nothing.[/if][if flag.farm_stopped_pearce]You pulled him down off the parapet the first night. You couldn't pull him down for ever.[/if]

Pearce isn't saying anything. He's looking at the ground. The partridges are on the table at
the orderly room, and the corporal asks if he was alone.

choices.text: Say one of the hares was for you. Share it.
choices.text_after:
You both get fourteen days. Two hours a day on the wheel by the Béthune road, side by side,
arms out, in the August sun, with the columns going past and the lads from home calling out.
Pearce talks to you the whole two hours, every day, about rabbits and ferrets and which
keeper on Exmoor was the worst. It's the most you've ever liked anybody.

choices.text: Say nothing. He knew the risk.
choices.text_after:
Twenty-eight days on the wheel. You walk past him on the road going up, and he's tied there
in the sun with his arms spread, and he catches your eye and winks, and you can't tell if
it's forgiveness or a joke.

v_farm_harvest.title: Harvest
v_farm_harvest.text:
August, at rest, and the French women are getting the harvest in by hand, the ones whose men are
away, with the old men and the children. They're cutting a field of oats with sickles behind the
billet, slow, in a line, bent double in the heat.

You stand at the gate and watch them, and your hands ache for a scythe the way a drinking man's
ache for a glass. You can smell it: cut oats, dust, sweat, the hot green smell of the stubble.
[if war.mate1]Cottle's beside you at the gate. He's not said a word. He's got his sleeves rolled up already.[/if]

choices.text: Go in and help. Find a scythe.
choices.text_after:
The farmer's wife finds you two scythes in the barn, rusty, and you stone them up, and go
into the oats in a line, swinging. You haven't forgotten. The body never does. By evening
the field's down and stooked, the way your father taught you, and the old woman brings you
cider in a jug and won't take any money, and kisses you on both cheeks. Your back aches like
home.

choices.text: Rest. You'll need your strength in the line.
choices.text_after:
You lie in the shade of the hedge and watch them work. It's the hardest thing you've done in
France, lying there. You can hear the sickles all afternoon.

v_farm_eve_loos.title: Moving up
v_farm_eve_loos.text:
Three nights of marching in the rain, and on the third morning you come up into the assembly
trenches and look over, and it's open country, flat, with slag heaps on the skyline and pit
towers, and halfway across no man's land, on its own, a tree. A cherry tree, the lads say, a
little one, all on its own between the lines, with its leaves still on. Everybody's calling it
the Lone Tree. It's where you're to go.

Along the parapet, under sacking, the gas cylinders.

[if war.mate1]Cottle's looking at the tree. "Like the one beech on Dunsworthy Down," he says. "You can see that from every farm in the parish."[/if][if flag.farm_servant] Mr Venn has you lay out his things on the firestep: a clean collar, a letter for his mother, a hunting flask. "In case," he says, and laughs, and doesn't finish it.[/if]

The company sergeant major comes round with pay books. If you want to write anything, now's
the time.

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
You don't know what to put. In the end you put that your father's to rest the mare, and that
your mother's to have your best boots for whoever needs them, and that you love them. You've
never said that in that kitchen. You fold it small.

choices.text: Leave it. Writing one is asking for it.
choices.text_after:
You leave it. You eat the last of the saffron cake from your mother's parcel, slow, a crumb at
a time, and look at the tree.

v_farm_count.title: The count
v_farm_count.text:
After the big snow of the winter you were fourteen, you went up on the moor with Will Cottle's
father to count the flock, and dug them out of the drifts one at a time, and counted. And at the
end of the day the old man stood at the gate and counted again, and said the number, and went
quiet, and that was how you knew how many were still under the snow.

They form what's left of the battalion up in a field behind the line, in the rain, and the
sergeant major reads the roll.

[if war.mate1]"Cottle." "Here, sir." Slow, the way he says everything.[else]"Cottle." Nothing. "Cottle, W." The rain on the caps.[/if]
[if war.mate2]"Pearce." "Here, sir," and you can hear he's grinning, and you don't know how.[else]"Pearce." Nothing. Pearce, who could cross a field in the dark without a sound.[/if]
[if war.mate3]"Yeo." "Here." Like the first note of a peal.[else]"Yeo." Nothing. You think of the tenor bell at home, with nobody to ring it.[/if]

And then the officers. Second Lieutenant Venn is read out with the dead.[if flag.farm_servant] You laid out his clean collar on the firestep that morning.[/if]

choices.text: Answer for the men you saw fall, when their names come.
choices.text_after:
"Killed, sir. I saw him." The sergeant major makes his mark. You think of old Cottle at the
gate, counting, and the number he didn't say.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let somebody else tell it.
choices.text_after:
Somebody else does, or nobody does, and the names go down as missing. You stand in the rain
and keep what you saw, like a ewe under the snow nobody's found.

v_farm_venn_letter.title: Mrs Venn
v_farm_venn_letter.text:
A letter for you, in a hand you don't know, on thick cream paper with a crest. From the big
house. From Mrs Venn.

"I am told that you were near my son. I would be so grateful for anything you could tell me. The
War Office says so little. I know you will not want to write it. I would rather know."

You've never had a letter from the big house in your life.

choices.text: Write and tell her the truth, as gently as you can.
choices.text_after: It takes you three nights. [if flag.farm_servant]You were his servant. You ask the men who were near him at the end, and tell her he was in front, and that he was laughing at something just before, which is true, and that it was quick, which you don't know. You tell her about the hunting flask, and the letter he had on the firestep for her.[else]You weren't near him, but you ask the men who were, and you put down what they tell you, and leave out what they don't say.[/if] You sign it with your full name, the way she wrote hers.

choices.text: Leave it. You don't know how to write to the big house.
choices.text_after:
You carry the letter about in your tunic for a month, meaning to. You never do. The paper goes
soft at the folds, and the crest wears off.

b_loos_farm_advance.title: Loos
b_loos_farm_advance.text:
Rum at five, from a stone jar. It goes down like the first cider at harvest home and sits there.

At ten to six the gas goes over. A hiss all down the line, like the threshing engine letting off
steam at the end of a day, and the cloud comes up, white and greenish, and leans out over no
man's land. Then the wind drops, and some of it comes back. Pepper and pineapple and a sting
under it. You pull the hood down. Wet flannel, the stink, your own breath hot against the
window.

Through the eyepiece, the tree, in the smoke, on its own.

Half past six. The guns stop.

Beside you on the ladder is {mate}. [if flag.farm_servant]Mr Venn's at the foot of it with his whistle in his teeth, white as a sheet, and he looks at you, and nods, as if you were both back at the big house waiting for the first drive.[/if]

[if war.stalled]You get your head over the top. The first wave is lying down in the grass by the Lone Tree in rows, too straight, the way the corn lies after the binder, and in front of them their wire is standing whole.[else]You get your head over the top. The first wave is walking towards the tree with their rifles at the port, through the long grass, and nobody's falling yet.[/if]

choices.text: Over the top. Walk with the wave. ({risk_push})
Go up with {mate}. Stay at his shoulder. ({risk_help})
Over, and straight down into the first shell hole. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_farm_trench.title: Loos
b_loos_farm_trench.text:
The tree. You go past it close enough to touch. A little cherry, the bark ripped, the leaves
still on, and men lying all round its foot, the way sheep lie up under the one tree in a field
in the heat. Some of them are ours from the first wave. None of them move.

Their wire beyond it is cut in places, in places not. You go through a gap with a crowd of men
and the machine gun that knows about the gap, and then you're down in their trench in the
white chalk, deafened, and the bombs are going off round the traverse a bay at a time.

[if war.stalled]A machine gun opens up from the second line straight down the trench, and the bombing stops dead, and men come back round the traverse fast, and one of them hasn't a face.[else]"Up the trench!" Somebody's shouting. "Bombers first! Go on, go on!"[/if]

choices.text: Round the traverse after the bombers. ({risk_push})
Stay with {mate}. Watch his back round the corner. ({risk_help})
Get down in the bottom of the trench and stay there. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_farm_hold.title: Loos
b_loos_farm_hold.text:
By the afternoon the rain's come in, thin and cold, off a sky like the moor in November. You're
holding a length of their trench that faces the wrong way. Nobody's brought water. The gas has
left a taste like a mouthful of copper.

Back across no man's land you can see the tree, small now, with the rain on it.

Shouting on the left. Then the rifles, picking up the way the rain does on the barn roof, a few
drops and then all of it.

"Stand to! They're coming back!"

choices.text: Up on the parapet. Fire till they stop coming. ({risk_push})
Keep {mate} fed with clips. Stay low beside him. ({risk_help})
Stay under the parapet. Fire blind over the top. ({risk_ground})

l_farm_1915.title: Home on leave
l_farm_1915.text:
The train to South Molton, and the carrier's cart the rest of the way, and then you walk the
last two miles up the lane in the dark because you can't sit still. The smell comes to you
before the farm does: woodsmoke, and the muck heap, and wet sheep, and you stand in the lane and
breathe it like a man come up out of water.

The dogs know you before your mother does. Then the door opens and the light comes out across the
yard, and she's there. She doesn't say anything. She puts her hand flat on your chest as if to
make sure. Then she smells you, and sends you to the wash-house.

[if flag.farm_wrote_home]Your letter's on the dresser, behind the willow-pattern plate, gone soft at the folds.[/if][if flag.farm_postcard]The field postcard's on the dresser. "Quite well," your father says from his chair, and puts his pipe back in his mouth. "Quite well."[/if][if !flag.farm_letter]"You might have written," she says, to the kettle.[/if]

Your father's thinner. The stable's half empty. Old Blossom puts her head over the door and
whickers at you, and there's nobody in Prince's stall or Duke's.[if flag.farm_harvested] You tell him about the French oats, and the scythes, and he laughs, and says you never stooked that well at home.[/if]

[if war.mate1]On the Sunday old Mr Cottle takes you up on the moor to see the ewes, with Fly at his heel, and asks after Will. Fly runs to you, and then runs on up the track, and stops, and looks back for somebody else.[/if][if !war.mate1]Up at Cottle's the blinds are down. Fly still lies by the gate in the evenings. Old Mr Cottle has stopped calling her in.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.farm_wrote_cottle] He has your letter in his coat pocket. He doesn't speak of it. He gives you a ewe lamb's fleece for your mother, which is what he has.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.farm_shared_pearce]Mrs Pearce has heard about the limber wheel, from Dan's letter, and is furious, with Dan and with you and with the army, and gives you a rabbit pie to take back for the both of you.[/if][if war.mate2 && !flag.farm_shared_pearce]Mrs Pearce asks if Dan's behaving. You tell her he is, near enough.[/if][if !war.mate2]The keeper at the big house stops you in the lane. He spent fifteen years trying to catch Dan Pearce. "I'll miss him," he says, and means it.[/if][if !war.mate2 && flag.farm_wrote_pearce] Mrs Pearce has your letter. She reads you the bit about the hare in the wire, and laughs, and then can't stop.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.farm_bert_rang]On the Sunday the ringers are short, with Bert away, and they ask you to take a rope. You can't ring. You stand in the tower and listen to them, and think of one note going out over a French village, and the dogs barking.[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.farm_bert_stopped]The ringers ask after Bert. You tell them he means to ring the whole peal when he's home. They say they'll keep the tenor for him.[/if][if !war.mate3]The bells don't ring at Dunsworthy now. They rang Bert Yeo's half-muffled the Sunday after the letter came, and not since.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.farm_wrote_yeo] Mrs Yeo has your letter in her Bible.[/if]

The big house has its blinds down for Mr Venn.[if flag.farm_wrote_venn] Mrs Venn sends the groom down for you. You sit in her drawing room in your uniform on a chair too good to sit on, and she asks you everything, and you tell her, and she holds her teacup without drinking it the whole time.[/if][if !flag.farm_wrote_venn] You walk past the lodge gates and don't go in.[/if]

[if flag.farm_spoke_at_roll]At church a woman from Brendon takes your hand at the lych-gate. "You were the one who told them about our Sid," she says. "They wrote it was quick." You tell her it was.[/if][if flag.farm_silent_at_roll]At market a woman is telling everybody her lad's only missing, missing means taken, he'll turn up. You saw. You buy your father's tobacco and go without your change.[/if]

At night the quiet keeps waking you. Then an owl, and you sleep.

v_first_night.title: First night in the line
v_first_night.text:
You came up the communication trench in the dark, single file, each man holding the scabbard
of the man in front. The boards rocked under your boots. There was water under them. You
could hear it slopping and couldn't see it.

Now you're on the firestep with your rifle and the dark is full of noises. Somewhere to the
left a machine gun is traversing, and the bullets come over in a long crack-crack-crack like a
lad running a stick along the park railings. A flare goes up, white, and hangs. Everything
stops. Wire, posts, a tree with no top, a boot in the wire with something still in it. Then
the flare dies and it all moves again.

The trench stinks of chloride of lime, and under the lime there's something sweet you don't
want to think about.

"Got a fag?" Duckworth's on the step next to you, whispering. "I've lost mine. I've lost me
nerve and all, but I'll settle for the fag."

choices.text: Give him one of your last two Woodbines.
choices.text_after:
He cups the match in both hands under the parapet. In the glow his face is grey and
about twelve years old. "You're a pal," he says, and coughs, and laughs at himself for
coughing.

choices.text: Tell him you've none left.
choices.text_after:
"Liar," he says, without any heat in it. You smoke one later, alone, cupped low, and it
doesn't taste of much.

v_lice.title: Chatting
v_lice.text:
Out at rest, in a barn that used to have cows in it and still has one at the far end. The
straw is warm and damp and smells of her. Everybody's chatting: shirts off, candle stubs on
upturned buckets, running thumbnails down the seams. The lice crack. [if war.mate2]Duckworth keeps count
out loud like the tally at the end of a shift.[/if]

Walter Pilling sits apart with his back to the wall. There's not a hair on his chest. When he
sees you looking he pulls his shirt back on with the lice still in it.

"I'm nineteen," he says, before you've opened your mouth.

He'll be seventeen in March. You know because his mam made the cake for his birthday and your
sister's the same week, and you ate half of both.

"Don't tell Sarge." He's whispering. "They'll send me home. Me mam'll have written already, I
know she has. Don't you tell him."

choices.text: Keep it to yourself.
choices.text_after:
You throw him your candle stub. He catches it and doesn't say thank you, and then he
starts on his seams, and after a while he's counting under his breath.

choices.text: Tell the sergeant. He's a child.
choices.text_after:
Sarge hears you out with his pipe in his teeth. "Pilling is nineteen," he says. "It says so
on his attestation, and I'm not paid to read minds." He looks at you a bit longer. "Nor
are you."

Pilling doesn't speak to you for a week. Somebody has told him.

v_letter_mill.title: A letter from home
v_letter_mill.text:
The post comes up after dark with the rations, the mailbags slung in among the bread and the
tins of bully and the jars of plum and apple. There's a parcel for you, brown paper and string
knotted three times, which is how your mother knots everything.

Socks. A tin of toffee from the Co-op. A bar of carbolic, and the smell of it in the dugout is
so like the scullery at home that you have to sit down on the ammunition box.

And a letter, two sides in pencil, pressed so hard you can read it backwards through the paper.

"Dear Son, just a few lines hoping this finds you as it leaves us at present. They have took
girls on in the card room and your father says it will be the ruin of the trade but he says
that about everything. [if war.mate1]Mrs Shaw says {mate1_first} never writes, so you tell him
from me he wants a clip round the ear.[else]Mrs Shaw has had the letter about {mate1_first}. She
has not been to chapel since and I don't blame her.[/if] Keep your feet dry. Are you eating.
Don't do anything daft. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back tonight, two sides, by a candle end.
choices.text_after:
You tell her the food is good. You tell her about the farm woman at the billet who
laughs at the way you say eggs. You don't tell her about the boot in the wire. By the time
the candle goes your hand has cramped, and you sleep better than you have since you came
out.

choices.text: Send the field postcard. Cross out what doesn't apply.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. You leave that line and strike out the rest with the stub of pencil. You
mean to do a proper letter at rest. You put the toffee in your pack and the carbolic under
your pillow, if you can call it a pillow.

v_billet.title: Eggs and chips
v_billet.text:
Behind the lines, in the village with half a church. The estaminet is somebody's front room
with a counter put in, a stove going, and a woman who knows exactly enough English: egg, chip,
beer, no, finish. You eat egg and chips off a cracked plate, the yolk running into the chips,
and the beer is thin and sour and you'd fight a man for the next one. For a quarter of an
hour the war is somewhere else.

Shaw has a letter-card on the table and a stub of pencil, and he's been looking at them both
since the eggs came.

"Will you do it for me?" Low, so nobody else will hear. "I can read all right. It's the
putting it down. I'll tell you what to say. She'll think I've gone soft, else, never writing."

choices.text: Write it for him. Every word he says.
choices.text_after:
He tells it to you slowly, looking at the stove. That he is well. That the French have
funny bread. That she's to tell his dad the allotment wants turning before the frost. Then
he stops, and you wait with the pencil, and he says, "Put that I think about her," and
goes red to his ears.

choices.text: Make him write it. Help him with the spelling.
choices.text_after:
It takes the whole evening. He holds the pencil like a shuttle he's afraid of dropping.
Allotment has two Ls; frost has one T. When it's done it's six lines and a blot, and he
reads it back to himself three times with his lips moving, pleased as a lad with a
sixpence.

v_sniper.title: The crater
v_sniper.text:
There's a place in the bay by the old mine crater where the sandbags have settled, a hand's
width lower than the rest. This morning a man from C Company straightened up in it to ease his
back. One shot. You heard it after. It went in just under his cap badge, and he sat down on
the firestep as if somebody had called his name.

They've hung a sack over the low place since. Somewhere out there, in the grey mess of stumps
and chalk behind their wire, a man with a telescopic sight is looking at that sack. He knew
where the low place was before you did.

The lads have started calling him Fritz-at-the-crater. [if war.mate2]Duckworth says it like a music-hall
turn. Nobody laughs.[/if]

choices.text: Build the low place up tonight, under the flares.
choices.text_after:
Three hours of it, filling sandbags on your knees, passing them up, the chalk cold and
wet under your nails. Every time a flare goes up you freeze with a bag in your arms like a
baby. By stand-to it's level. Your back aches all the next day and you don't mind it.

choices.text: Leave it. Duck as you pass, and tell the new men.
choices.text_after:
You duck there every time, the way you'd duck the low beam in the shed. You stop thinking
about it. That's the part that frightens you, when you notice it.

v_eve_loos.title: Moving up
v_eve_loos.text:
Three nights of marching in the rain, never in daylight. The roads are so full of men and
guns and limbers that you go ten yards and stop, ten yards and stop, and sleep standing up
against the man in front.

Now you're in the assembly trenches. Along the parapet, under sacking, are the cylinders. Big
grey iron things, rows of them. Nobody's to say the word. The officers call it the accessory.
The men from the Special Companies who look after them have their own armbands and won't talk
to you.

[if flag.gave_fags && war.mate2]Duckworth finds you in the dark and pushes a Woodbine into your hand. "I owed
you," he says. "Don't say I never pay up."[/if][if !flag.gave_fags && war.mate2]Duckworth's further down, telling the same joke
over and over to anybody who'll listen. You can hear his voice going higher.[/if] [if war.mate3]Pilling
is asleep sitting up with his mouth open, his rifle across his knees like a toy.[/if]

The company sergeant major comes round with pay books. If you want to write anything, now's
the time.

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
You don't know what to put. In the end you put that you love them, which you have never
said out loud in that house, and that your mother is to have your Sunday boots mended and
give them to our Jack. You fold it small. It sits against your chest like a hot hand.

choices.text: Leave it. Writing one is asking for it.
choices.text_after:
Half the company thinks the same. Half the company is writing anyway, licking the pencils,
hiding the pages with their arms like boys in a schoolroom. You watch them and say nothing.

v_roll_call.title: Roll call
v_roll_call.text:
They form what's left of the battalion up in a field behind the old line, in the rain. The
sergeant major has the roll. He reads it in the same voice he reads everything.

A name, and somebody says "Here." A name, and nobody does, and he says it again, and then
somebody says, "Killed, sir, I saw him," or "Wounded, sir," or just nothing, and he puts a mark
and goes on.

[if war.mate1]"Shaw." "Here, sir." Albert's voice is a croak.[else]"Shaw." Nothing. He says it again. "Shaw, A." The rain on the caps.[/if]
[if war.mate2]"Duckworth." "Present and correct, sir," and somebody near him nearly laughs.[else]"Duckworth." Nothing. You stare at the back of the neck in front of you till it blurs.[/if]
[if war.mate3]"Pilling." "Here." High, like a lad answering the register.[else]"Pilling." Nothing. Nobody says he was sixteen.[/if]

It takes most of the afternoon. The field smells of trodden grass and wet wool and the cookers
going behind the hedge, and nobody eats when the stew comes.

choices.text: Answer for the men you saw fall, when their names come.
choices.text_after:
"Killed, sir. I saw him." Your own voice sounds like somebody else's. The sergeant major
nods and makes his mark, and that's the man written down, and you think: his mother will
get a letter with my words in it.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let somebody else tell it.
choices.text_after:
Somebody else does. Or nobody does, and the names go down as missing, and you stand there
with what you saw and keep it.

v_crater_again.title: Back to the crater
v_crater_again.text:
They put you back in the old line in October, by the crater, as if Loos was something that
happened to somebody else. Same sandbags. Same smell. New faces in the bays, half of them
from the drafts, lads who don't know where to put their feet.

[if flag.built_up_crater]Your bit of parapet is still level, a bit slumped, holding. You put your hand flat on it going past, the way you'd pat a horse.[else]The sack is still over the low place. It's rotted through at one corner and nobody's mended it.[/if]

On the second morning a draft lad from Rochdale stands up two bays along to look at the
sunrise. You hear the shot after.

Fritz-at-the-crater is still there. He's had the whole of Loos and he's still there.

choices.text: Show the new lads where the low places are.

b_loos_advance.title: Loos
b_loos_advance.text:
Rum at five, from a stone jar, a tot in the lid of your mess tin. It burns all the way down
and sits in your stomach like a lump of coal from the grate.

At ten to six the gas goes over. You hear it before you see it, a long hiss all down the line,
like every steam pipe in the shed letting go at once. Then the cloud comes up, white and
greenish, and leans towards their wire. Not all of it. A drift of it comes back along the
trench, smelling of pepper and pineapple and something under both that bites the back of your
throat. You pull the hood down. Wet flannel, the chemical stink of it, your own breath going
hot against the little window.

Half past six. The guns stop. In the gap a man down the bay is saying the Lord's Prayer too
fast to get to the end of it.

"Walk," says the sergeant through his hood. "Keep your dressing. Nobody runs till I say."

Beside you on the ladder is {mate}. His hands are shaking so hard the rung is ticking against
the sandbags. [if flag.told_on_pilling && war.mate3]Further along, Pilling is looking at you. He looks away.[/if]

[if war.stalled]You get your head over the top. The first wave went fifty yards. They're lying down in the chalk in rows, too straight, the way lads lie down for a photograph on the moor, and in front of them their wire is standing whole.[else]You get your head over the top. The first wave is walking into the smoke with their rifles at the port, and nobody's falling yet.[/if]

choices.text: Over the top. Walk with the wave. ({risk_push})
Go up with {mate}. Stay at his shoulder. ({risk_help})
Over, and straight down into the first shell hole. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_trench.title: Loos
b_loos_trench.text:
Their front line is a ditch of white chalk and grey men. Some of the grey men are dead. Some
have their hands up. One of them, a lad with spectacles, keeps saying the same word over and
over, and you don't know what it means, and you will never know.

Your ears have gone. Everything comes through cotton wool, like the shed when you've done a
double shift: the bombs going off along the trench to the right, a crump and a scream and a
crump, a bay at a time.

[if war.stalled]Then a machine gun opens up from the second line, straight down the communication trench, and the bombing stops dead. Men come back round the traverse fast with their heads down. One of them hasn't got a rifle any more. One of them hasn't got a face.[else]The sergeant has lost his hood and his cap and half his ear, and he's pointing. "Up the communication trench. Bombers first. Clear it. Go on, go on!"[/if]

choices.text: Round the traverse after the bombers. ({risk_push})
Stay with {mate}. Watch his back round the corner. ({risk_help})
Get down in the bottom of the trench and stay there. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_hold.title: Loos
b_loos_hold.text:
By the afternoon the rain's come in, thin and cold, and the chalk goes to paste. You're holding
a length of their trench that faces the wrong way. The firestep is on the other side, so you
stand on dead men's packs to see over.

Nobody has brought water. Your tongue sticks to the roof of your mouth. The gas has left a
taste like sucking a penny.

Shouting on the left. Then rifle fire, picking up the way rain does on the shed roof, a few
drops and then all of it.

"Stand to! They're coming back! Stand to!"

choices.text: Up on the packs. Fire till they stop coming. ({risk_push})
Keep {mate} fed with clips. Stay low beside him. ({risk_help})
Stay under the parapet. Fire blind over the top. ({risk_ground})

l_mill_1915.title: Home on leave
l_mill_1915.text:
The train's three hours late and so cold the window has frosted on the inside. When it pulls
in, the station smells of coal smoke and fish from the market platform and the wet wool of
your own greatcoat, and under all of it, home. You have to stand still on the platform a
minute before your legs will go.

Your mother has the door open before you knock. She doesn't say anything. She puts her hand
flat on your cheek, the way she did when you had the measles. Then she smells you, and takes
you straight through to the scullery.

"Get them off," she says. "All of it. They're walking."

She boils your shirt in the copper. You sit in the tin bath in front of the fire in your
father's old coat, and listen to the clock on the mantel. You'd forgotten the clock.
[if flag.wrote_home]Your letter is behind it with the rent book, gone soft at the folds.[/if][if flag.sent_postcard]The field postcard is propped against it. "I am quite well," she reads out, not looking at you. "Quite well." She doesn't say anything else about it, and it would be better if she did.[/if][if !flag.letter_mill]"You might have written," she says to the copper.[/if]

[if war.mate1]In the morning Mrs Shaw is on her step two doors up, in her shawl, waiting for you. "Is he eating?" she says. "Is our {mate1_first} eating?" You tell her yes. You tell her he's grown a moustache. [if flag.taught_shaw]"He wrote me himself," she says. "Six lines. Spelt allotment right and all." [/if][if flag.wrote_for_shaw]"He wrote," she says, and looks at you. "It were your hand." She doesn't mind. [/if]She laughs, and then puts her apron up to her face.[else]In the morning the blinds are down at the Shaws'. They've been down since the buff envelope came. [if flag.wrote_to_mrs_shaw]On the second day Mrs Shaw sends their girl round for you. She has your letter in her apron pocket, creased to rags already. She wants it all again, every bit, and you tell her, and leave out what she can't have.[else]Mrs Shaw doesn't come out, and you don't knock, and you hate yourself for it all the way to the end of the street.[/if][/if]

[if !war.mate2]The Duckworths have a black ribbon on the knocker.[/if][if !war.mate2 && flag.wrote_to_mrs_duckworth] His dad stops you at the corner, a tackler, hands like shovels. "That joke," he says. "The parson's wife." He laughs till he has to hold the wall.[/if]

[if flag.told_on_pilling && war.mate3]Mrs Pilling stops you outside the Co-op. "They told me you tried," she says. "With the sergeant. I wrote to the War Office twice." She grips your sleeve. "Thank you for trying, love."[/if][if flag.kept_pilling_secret && war.mate3]Mrs Pilling stops you outside the Co-op. "Is our Walter behaving himself?" she says. You tell her he is. You don't tell her anything else.[/if][if !war.mate3]The Pillings' blinds are down as well. Walter was sixteen.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.wrote_to_mrs_pilling] Mrs Pilling has your letter. She doesn't come out, but on your last morning there's a cake on your mother's step in a tin, and no note.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.kept_pilling_secret] You knew how old he was and you kept it for him. You'd keep it again. It doesn't help.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.told_on_pilling] Mrs Pilling sees you from her window and lets the curtain drop.[/if]

[if flag.spoke_at_roll]On Sunday after chapel a woman you don't know takes hold of your hand in both of hers. "You were the one who told them," she says. "About our Ernest, in B Company. They wrote that it were quick." You don't remember whether it was quick. You tell her it was.[/if][if flag.silent_at_roll]In the Co-op a woman is telling the girl behind the counter that her lad is only missing, that missing means a German hospital, he'll turn up, you'll see. You saw. You pay for your father's tobacco and go out without your change.[/if]

At night the quiet keeps waking you up.

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v_pit_first_night.title: First night in the line
v_pit_first_night.text:
Up the communication trench in the dark, single file, the boards rocking under your boots and
water slopping under the boards. Then the firestep, and your rifle, and the dark.

You've been in darker places. Two hundred fathoms down with your lamp out, that's dark. This is
different. Underground the dark keeps still. This dark moves. A flare goes up and hangs, white,
and everything stops, the wire and the posts and a tree with no top, and then the flare dies and
it all moves again.

The trench stinks of chloride of lime, and under the lime of something sweet.

[if war.mate1]Robson's not looking over the parapet. He's down on his knees on the duckboards with his ear flat to the trench wall, the way he'd listen to the roof at the face. He stays like that a long time. Then he looks up at you.

"They're working," he says. "Under us. Can you not hear it?"

You put your ear where his was. Wet clay, cold on your cheek. And then, so faint you think it's your own blood, a tap. A wait. A tap.[else]Somebody along the bay is down on his knees with his ear to the trench wall, the way a man listens to the roof at the face. "They're working," he says. "Under us." You put your ear to the clay. Wet, cold. A tap. A wait. A tap.[/if]

choices.text: Go and tell the officer. Now, tonight.
choices.text_after:
The officer is twenty, with a moustache he's still growing, and he hears you out in the
dugout by a candle. He doesn't laugh. He writes it down, the bay number and the time, and
says he'll pass it up. "You're colliers," he says. "You'd know." You don't know whether he
believes it or just wants you out of his dugout.

choices.text: Leave it. Who's going to listen to a private?
choices.text_after:
You stand your sentry and try not to listen, and listen anyway, all night, the way you'd
listen to a bad roof, waiting for the crack that comes before it goes.

v_pit_letter.title: A letter from home
v_pit_letter.text:
The post comes up with the rations after dark. A parcel for you in brown paper, smelling of the
kitchen when you open it: a cake wrapped in a bit of cloth, socks, a quarter of black bullets
from the Store, and a tin of the ointment your father uses on his hands.

And a letter, in pencil, two sides.

"Dear Son, I hope this finds you well as it leaves us at present. Your father is on fore shift
and his chest is no better but he will not go to the doctor. The manager has been round the
rows asking the lads not to go for soldiers, he says coal is war work and they are short at
the face, and your father says it is a bit late for that. [if war.mate1]Old Mr Robson says to tell Tommy the young birds are flying well and he took first at Bedlington with the blue hen.[else]Old Mr Robson has not been out to his birds since the telegram. Mrs Robson lets them out of a morning and stands and watches them go round.[/if] Keep your feet dry. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back tonight, two sides, by a candle end.
choices.text_after:
You tell her the cake came whole. You tell her the French have pits too, with the winding
towers just like at home, and you can see them on a clear day from the support line. You
tell your father to go to the doctor, which he won't, and you know it.

choices.text: Send the field postcard. Cross out what doesn't apply.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. Letter follows at first opportunity. You strike out the rest. The black
bullets you share round the bay, and the lads suck them on sentry, and the whole trench
smells of aniseed for a night.

v_pit_pigeons.title: The loft
v_pit_pigeons.text:
Behind the lines there's an army pigeon loft on the back of a lorry, painted grey, and a
sapper corporal who looks after the birds and talks to them the way men talk to dogs.

Robson finds it the first afternoon at rest. You find him there, stood at the wire mesh with his
hands in his pockets, watching the birds walk up and down. He doesn't say anything for a long
while. The loft smells of corn and droppings and warm feathers, of Saturday afternoons in his
da's cree at the end of the rows.

"They're nowt special," he says at last. "Me da's got better at home." Then: "He'll
be out to them now. Clocking them in."

choices.text: Stay with him and talk birds with the corporal.
choices.text_after:
The corporal lets Robson hold one, a blue chequer cock, and Robson turns it over in his big
hands, gentle, opening a wing with one finger, and tells the corporal what's wrong with it,
and the corporal agrees. Walking back, Robson says more words in a row than you've had out
of him since the cage.

choices.text: Leave him to it. He'll want it to himself.
choices.text_after:
You go back to the barn. He comes in after dark and lies down on the straw without a word,
and smells of the loft, and goes straight to sleep, the first time you've seen him sleep
easy since the boat.

v_pit_baths.title: The baths
v_pit_baths.text:
Baths, at a brewery behind the lines: the big vats filled with hot water, ten men to a
vat, steam up to the rafters and the whole place smelling of old beer and carbolic and men.
You get your uniform back from the fumigator still warm, and the lice in the seams are
sleeping, not dead.

Bell's in the vat with you, up to his chest, a newspaper held up out of the water. The Herald,
a week old.

"The Welsh lads came out," he says. "Two hundred thousand of them, in July. They called them
traitors in the Commons." He folds the paper so you can see. "The owners are making more out of
coal than they ever made, and the Welsh lads asked for their share, and they're traitors." His
voice is getting louder. "First bath the army's given us. You know what? It's the first bath
I've had at work in my life. The owners never gave us one."

A sergeant from another company, in the next vat, tells him to shut his mouth or he'll shut it
for him.

choices.text: Stand by Bell. He's not wrong.
choices.text_after:
You say it, loud enough. The sergeant looks at the pair of you, two pitmen up to your necks
in a beer vat, and laughs, and says, "Geordie agitators," and turns his back. Bell grins at
you through the steam like a lad who's just won at quoits.

choices.text: Tell Bell to give it a rest. Not here.
choices.text_after:
"Not here," you say. "Not now." Bell looks at you a long time with the water dripping off
his nose. Then he folds the paper away. "When, then?" he says. You haven't an answer for
him, and he knows it.

v_pit_mine.title: The mine
v_pit_mine.text:
It goes up at stand-to, in the grey, four bays along. You feel it before you hear it: the
firestep lifts under your boots like the cage when it takes the weight, and then the noise,
and then the earth comes down, clods of it, stones, sandbags, a boot, rattling on your helmet
like hail on a tin roof. Where the bay was there's a crater you could put the chapel in, still
smoking, stinking like the shot-firer's smoke after a round at the face, a hundred times over.

[if flag.pit_reported]They'd listened. Two sappers came up a week back with a thing like a doctor's stethoscope and lay on the floor of that bay for a whole night, and the next day the bay was thinned out to two sentries.[else]Nobody listened, because nobody told them. The bay was full. Eight men.[/if]

Men are buried in it. You can hear one of them.

And across the way, their whistles. They'll be coming for the crater lip.

choices.text: Get in the crater with a shovel. Dig for the buried men.
choices.text_after:
It's a fall. That's all it is, a fall, and you know what to do in a fall: you dig with your
hands near the face so you don't take a man's head off with the shovel, and you listen,
and you shout to him to keep shouting. [if war.mate1]Robson's beside you, digging like a machine. [/if]You get one out alive, grey with earth, his mouth full of it, and you clear it with your finger like you would at the pit. The rest you get out later.

choices.text: Get up on the crater lip with your rifle. Hold it.
choices.text_after:
You lie on the loose earth of the lip, warm from the blast, and fire into the grey till
your shoulder's numb. They don't get the crater. Behind you, under you, the diggers work,
and you can hear the man still shouting, and then you can't.

v_pit_eve_loos.title: Moving up
v_pit_eve_loos.text:
Three nights of marching in the rain, never in daylight, and on the third morning you come up
into the assembly trenches and look over, and it's home.

It's a coalfield. Pit heads, winding gear, the big black slag heaps, rows of little brick
houses with their backs to the pits. Over the village they're to take stand two great winding
towers side by side, iron, joined at the top. The lads are calling it Tower Bridge. [if war.mate1]Robson
stares at it a long time. "Like gannin' to work," he says.[/if][if !war.mate1]Somebody says it's like going to work, and nobody laughs.[/if]

Along the parapet, under sacking, the gas cylinders. Nobody's to say the word.

[if war.mate3]Charlton has been on a mule party all night, bringing the cylinders up, and he comes in with his hands stinking of mule and his eyes shining, because they were good mules, he says, they never once played up, and one of them leaned on him in the dark like old Captain used to in the stables.[/if]

The company sergeant major comes round with pay books. If you want to write anything, now's
the time.

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
You don't know what to put. In the end you put that your father is to go to the doctor about
his chest, and that your pit boots are to go to whoever needs them, and that you love them.
You've never said that in that house. You fold it small.

choices.text: Leave it. Writing one is asking for it.
choices.text_after:
You leave it. You eat your bait instead, bully and a biscuit, and save the last bit of
your mother's cake for after, because there has to be an after if there's cake waiting for it.

v_pit_roll.title: The tokens
v_pit_roll.text:
At the pit, going down, you hand your token in at the lamp cabin, a little brass disc with
your number on, and it goes on the board. Coming up, you take it back. At the end of a shift,
any token still on the board is a man still down. Every bairn in the rows knows what it means
when the women go and stand at the lamp cabin and look at the board.

They form what's left of the battalion up in a field behind the old line, in the rain, and the
sergeant major reads the roll, and you stand there and watch the tokens left on the board.

[if war.mate1]"Robson." "Here, sir." Low and flat, the way he says everything.[else]"Robson." Nothing. "Robson, T." The rain on the caps.[/if]
[if war.mate2]"Bell." "Here, sir," and you can hear in it that he's got something to say after, and will.[else]"Bell." Nothing. For once in his life Jim Bell has nothing to say.[/if]
[if war.mate3]"Charlton." "Here." He's shaking. He's been shaking since Saturday.[else]"Charlton." Nothing. You think of the pony stables, and the ponies, and who'll tell them.[/if]

choices.text: Answer for the men you saw fall, when their names come.
choices.text_after:
"Killed, sir. I saw him." The sergeant major makes his mark. You think of the women at the
lamp cabin, and that this is the same, only the board is in France and the women don't
know yet.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let somebody else tell it.
choices.text_after:
Somebody else does, or nobody does, and the names go down as missing. You keep what you
saw. It sits in you like stone dust.

v_pit_horses.title: The transport lines
v_pit_horses.text:
Charlton's taken to going down to the transport lines when you're at rest. The horses and
mules stand in a field of mud in long rows, steaming, with their rugs on, and Charlton walks
up and down the rows with his hands in their manes and talks to them. The transport sergeant's
noticed. He's short of drivers.

"I could do it," Charlton says. "I could. I was the best driver at the pit, everybody says.
Captain would go for nobody else." He's looking at you as if it's yours to give. "Only it's
leaving the section. It's leaving you lot."

choices.text: Tell him to go. Put a word in with the sergeant.
choices.text_after:
The transport sergeant looks Charlton over and says he'll ask. Charlton walks back up the
road beside you with his hands in his pockets, whistling, and stops twice to look back at
the horse lines, as if they might not be there.

choices.text: Tell him the section needs him. It does.
choices.text_after:
"Aye," he says. "Aye, I know." He goes on going down to the horse lines at rest, every
time, with his pockets full of crusts saved off his own bread.

b_loos_pit_advance.title: Loos
b_loos_pit_advance.text:
Rum at five, from a stone jar, a tot in the lid of your mess tin. It goes down like hot
coals and sits there.

At ten to six the gas goes over. A hiss all down the line, like the compressed air when they
open the valve on the haulage, and then the cloud, white and greenish, leaning towards their
wire. Some of it comes back along the trench. Pepper and pineapple and a bite under it that
gets in your throat like bad air in an old working. You pull the hood down. Wet flannel, the
stink of the chemical, your own breath going hot against the little window.

Through the eyepiece, through the smoke, the winding towers.

Half past six. The guns stop.

Beside you on the ladder is {mate}. In the hood his breath goes in and out, in and out, and
you think of the cage at the top of the shaft, the gate going across, the drop.

[if war.stalled]You get your head over the top. The first wave is lying down in rows in the grass, too straight, and in front of them their wire is standing whole.[else]You get your head over the top. The first wave is walking into the smoke towards the pit heaps with their rifles at the port, and nobody's falling yet.[/if]

choices.text: Over the top. Walk with the wave. ({risk_push})
Go up with {mate}. Stay at his shoulder. ({risk_help})
Over, and straight down into the first shell hole. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_pit_trench.title: Loos
b_loos_pit_trench.text:
Their front line, chalk and grey men, and then the village beyond it, and it's a pit village.
Rows of little brick houses, back to back, with their yards and their wash-houses and their
netties at the bottom, the same as Blackhaugh, only smashed. A woman's apron on a line. A
birdcage in a window with no glass.

The Germans are in the cellars. You go along the rows, house by house, and the bombs go down the
cellar steps, and the cellars cough smoke and plaster dust, and sometimes men.

[if war.stalled]A machine gun in the end house opens up straight down the row, and the bombers go flat in the yards, and don't get up, and the row is theirs again.[else]The sergeant's lost his hood and half his ear. "Down the row! Clear the cellars! Go on, go on!"[/if]

choices.text: Down the row after the bombers. ({risk_push})
Stay with {mate}. Watch his back at the doors. ({risk_help})
Get down in a yard behind the wash-house wall. ({risk_ground})

b_loos_pit_hold.title: Loos
b_loos_pit_hold.text:
By the afternoon you're dug in at the foot of a slag heap, and the rain's come on. The heap's
been burning inside for years, the way they do, and where the shells have opened it the smoke
comes out yellow and stinking of sulphur, the smell of the pit heap at home on a wet night, so
strong you could cry.

Nobody's brought water. The gas has left a taste like sucking a penny.

They're on the top of the heap. They've been there all along. And now they're coming down it.

choices.text: Stand up and fire up the heap at them. ({risk_push})
Keep {mate} fed with clips. Stay low beside him. ({risk_help})
Get down in the slag and fire from cover. ({risk_ground})

l_pit_1915.title: Home on leave
l_pit_1915.text:
The last train up the branch line, and the dark, and the pit heap glowing red on the skyline
where it's been burning since your grandfather's time, and then the smell of it through the
carriage window, sulphur and smoke, and you have to put your face against the glass.

The rows are dark. The buzzer goes for the night shift while you're walking up from the station,
and you stop dead in the street, because you haven't heard it in seven months, and it sounds
like a shell coming.

Your mother has the set-pot boiling before you're through the door. She doesn't say anything.
She puts the tin bath in front of the fire, the way she has for your father every day of his
life, and you get in it, and she washes your back, which she's not done since you were small,
and the water goes grey with France. [if flag.pit_wrote_home]Your letter's on the mantel behind the tea caddy, with your father's pay notes.[/if][if flag.pit_postcard]The field postcard is on the mantel. "Quite well," your father says, from his chair, and coughs, and says it again. "Quite well."[/if][if !flag.pit_letter]"You might have written," she says, to the set-pot.[/if]

Your father coughs half the night through the wall. He's still on the fore shift.

[if war.mate1]On the Saturday old Mr Robson takes you down to his cree at the end of the rows and shows you the young birds, one at a time, and asks after Tommy. You tell him Tommy's well.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.pit_saw_loft] You tell him what Tommy said about the army's birds. The old man laughs out loud, the first time anybody can remember. "Nowt special," he says. "Nowt special. That's my lad."[/if][if !war.mate1]The Robsons' blinds are down. Old Mr Robson's birds are still flying. He lets them out every morning and stands in the yard and watches them go round, and doesn't clock them in.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.pit_wrote_robson] He's had your letter. He doesn't say anything about it. He gives you a bird to take back, a blue hen, in a basket, and you can't tell him they'd never let you.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.stood_with_bell]At the Miners' Hall on the Sunday, Bell's father, who's on the lodge committee, shakes your hand in front of everybody. "Our Jim says you stood up for him," he says. "In a beer vat." The whole hall laughs.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.told_bell_shut]At the Miners' Hall, Bell's father asks after Jim, and you tell him Jim's well, still talking. "Aye," he says. "He would be. Somebody has to."[/if][if !war.mate2]Bell's father is on the lodge committee. He gets up at the Miners' Hall on the Sunday and starts to say something about his lad, and can't, and sits down.[/if][if !war.mate2 && flag.pit_wrote_bell] He keeps your letter in his jacket. He reads bits of it to men in the club who never asked.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.pit_helped_charlton]Mrs Charlton has had a letter from George. He's with the horses. She reads it to you on the step, all of it, and it's all horses, a page and a half about a mule called Jerusalem, and nothing at all about the war, and she's never been so happy.[/if][if war.mate3 && !flag.pit_helped_charlton]Mrs Charlton asks if George is eating. You tell her he gives his crusts to the mules. She laughs, and says that's him, that's him.[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.pit_kept_charlton] You told him the section needed him more than the horses did. You don't tell her that.[/if][if !war.mate3]Down at the pit stables, the old horse-keeper tells you Captain's not been right since George went. He doesn't know about George yet. You don't tell him.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.pit_wrote_charlton] Mrs Charlton has your letter. She's put it in the Bible.[/if]

[if flag.pit_dug_out]At the club a man from the next row stands you a pint and won't say why. Later somebody tells you: his cousin was the one you dug out of the crater, and wrote home about it.[/if][if flag.pit_held_lip]In the club they've heard about the mine. Everybody wants to know about the mine, and they're pitmen, and they all know what a fall is, so you don't have to tell them much.[/if]

[if flag.pit_spoke_at_roll]On the Sunday a woman from the far end of the rows stops you on the chapel steps. "You were the one who said about our Ned," she says. "They wrote that he never knew." She holds your hand in both of hers. You don't remember if he knew. You say he didn't.[/if][if flag.pit_silent_at_roll]In the Store a woman is saying that her lad's only missing, that missing means taken, he'll turn up. You saw. You buy your father's baccy and go out without your change.[/if]

At night you lie in your own bed and listen for the roof.

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

w_tunnel_pit.title: The tunnellers
w_tunnel_pit.text:
A Royal Engineers officer comes to the billet in the new year with a list. He's not like the
infantry officers. He's got clay on his boots up to the ankle and he talks like a mining
engineer, because that's what he was, and he wants colliers.

Six shillings a day, against your shilling. Work you know: picks, timber, pumps, air,
