listening. The tunnellers don't go over the top. They go under it.

[if flag.pit_reported]"Somebody in this company heard them digging last summer," he says, "and told his officer, and we had that bay down to two sentries before it went." He looks round the barn. You keep quiet.[/if][if flag.pit_mine && !flag.pit_reported]"You'll have seen what a mine does," he says. "Last summer, four bays along. Eight men. That's what we're for."[/if]

[if war.mate1]Robson listens to all of it with his arms folded. "It's the face," he says to you after. "Only the face, with Germans at the far end of it." He doesn't put his name down. "I'm stopping with the lads," he says. "Somebody has to."[/if][if war.mate2] Bell says he came out to fight Germans, not to dig for them, and he's not leaving the section.[/if]

choices.text: Go to the tunnellers. You'll leave the section.
Stay with the men from home.

v16_tin_hats.title: Tin hats
v16_tin_hats.text:
February, and the ground's iron. Your breath freezes on the blanket round your face and in the
morning you crack it off like the skin on cold gravy.

The tin hats come up with the rations, a whole limber of them. They're heavier than they look
and they sit on your head like a basin, and the leather lining smells of somebody else's sweat
already. The sergeant says they'll stop shrapnel but not a bullet, so don't go getting ideas.

[if war.mate2]Duckworth wears his on the back of his head and calls it his Sunday best.[/if] A draft comes up the same week: Derby men, attested
last autumn, some of them older than your father, one with a cough you can hear three bays off.
They look at the old hands the way you looked at the old hands, last May.

choices.text: Show the new men how to stand on a firestep.

v16_edith.title: Edith
v16_edith.text:
Shaw has a photograph in his pay book now, between the pages where he keeps his next-of-kin.
A girl in a white blouse in front of a painted garden at the studio on Market Street, trying
not to laugh.

"Edith," he says. "Edith Holt. From the card room." He keeps it out of the wet in an oilskin
tobacco pouch. "We're getting wed. Next leave, if they give me one before Whitsun."

He's red to the ears. He keeps turning the pouch over in his fingers like a shuttle.

"Will you stand up with me? Best man. You're the one who wrote her the letters, near enough."

choices.text: Say yes. Shake his hand on it.
choices.text_after:
His grip's like a vice. "Right," he says. "Right, then." And then, because he can't think
of anything else: "She does a lovely meat-and-potato pie." It's the most words in a row
you've had out of him since France.

choices.text: Tell him to ask you after the war, when it's done.
choices.text_after:
"After the war," he says, as if he's trying the words for size. He puts the photograph back
in the pouch, and the pouch back in the pay book, carefully, and buttons the pocket.

v16_pilling_papers.title: Papers
v16_pilling_papers.text:
March, and it's Pilling's birthday, and his mam's sent a cake in a tin with SEVENTEEN TODAY
piped on it in white. Everybody in the bay reads it. Nobody says owt.

By the next morning there's a paper for him at the orderly room. His mother's written to the
War Office, and to the MP, and the War Office has finally written to the battalion. He's to go
down the line to the base, until he's old enough.

He comes and finds you behind the cook-house with the paper folded small in his fist.

"I'm not going," he says. "I'm not leaving you lot. They'll put me in a bloody bakery, and
you'll all be up here." His voice cracks on bloody, and he's furious about it.

choices.text: Tell him to go. Get on the lorry and don't look back.
choices.text_after:
He goes to the orderly room. He comes back an hour later without the paper. "They've lost
it," he says. He doesn't look sorry. He doesn't look at you either.

choices.text: Tell him it's his choice to make, not yours.
choices.text_after:
He tears the paper up small and puts the bits in the brazier, one at a time, and
watches each one catch. Then he cuts the cake with his bayonet, eight ways.

v16_eve_somme.title: The bombardment
v16_eve_somme.text:
A week of it. Seven days and nights of our guns, so many of them that the noise stops being
noise and turns into the ground you stand on. You feel it in your back teeth. You feel it in
your water. They say nothing can live under it. They say the wire will be cut.

At night the sky over their line flickers like the cinema on Bury Road with the reel slipping.
You can't sleep and then you sleep standing up.

The colonel comes round. Walking pace, he says. Keep your dressing. The guns will have done
it for you; you'll be in their third line by dinner.

[if flag.last_letter]Your letter from Loos is still in your pay book, gone soft as cloth.[/if] The company sergeant major is round with the pay books again.

choices.text: Write a letter for the pay book. A new one.
choices.text_after:
It comes out different this time. Shorter. You tell them you're not frightened, which they
won't believe, and that if it comes to it, it'll have been quick, which nobody can promise.
You tell your father he was right about the trade.

choices.text: Leave the pay book as it is.
choices.text_after:
You lie on the firestep with your eyes shut and count the guns till you lose count, and
then you start again.

v16_after.title: July
v16_after.text:
For weeks after, the men who were caught on the wire are still on it. Nobody can get out to
them in daylight and at night their snipers watch the wire. July is hot. When the wind comes
from no man's land you breathe through your mouth and it doesn't help, because then you can
taste it.

The battalion that walked out on the first of July was eight hundred men and some. The one that
answered the roll the next day you could have got in the chapel.

One night they ask for men to go out and bring in identity discs. Just the discs. So the
mothers will know.

choices.text: Go out for the discs.
choices.text_after:
Two hours on your belly in the dark, with a pair of scissors and a sandbag. You cut the
cords by feel. Some of the faces you know by feel too. You bring back nineteen. Your hands
stink for a week however you scrub them, and you scrub them till they bleed.

choices.text: Stay in. You haven't got it in you tonight.
choices.text_after:
You lie in the dugout and listen to the others go out, and come in, one at a time, quiet.
Nobody says anything to you about it, then or after.

v16_tank.title: The tank
v16_tank.text:
September. Behind the lines one evening there's a noise like the engine house at the mill when
the big flywheel's going, and something comes down the road at walking pace that you have no
word for. An iron box the size of a tram, with a gun sticking out of each side and a tail of
two wheels dragging behind it, and it stinks of hot oil and petrol and men.

The crew climb out at the end of the road, and they're grey in the face and being sick in the
ditch, and one of them's got blood running out of his ear.

[if war.mate2]"It's a loom," says Duckworth, staring. "It's a bloody loom on legs. Me dad'd have it running in a week."[else]Somebody says it's a water carrier. Somebody says it'll end the war by Christmas. The crew don't say anything at all.[/if]

choices.text: Walk round it once. Put your hand on the iron.

v16_word_from_crater.title: A letter from the old line
v16_word_from_crater.text:
A letter comes from a man you knew at the depot, who went to the other battalion. They're in
your old line now, by the crater. He writes that it's quiet. He writes that they've had three
men killed in a month, all in the same bay, all through the head, all in the morning.

"The lads call him Fritz-at-the-crater," he writes, as if you wouldn't know. "Somebody says he
was there before your lot came. Somebody says he's been there since 1914."

You fold the letter up and put it with the others. You can see the bay. You can see the sack
over the low place.

choices.text: Write back. Tell him where the low places are.

b_somme_1.title: The first of July
b_somme_1.text:
The first of July comes up hot. Mist in the valley, burning off, and by seven the sun's on your
neck. You're carrying sixty-odd pounds: rifle, two hundred rounds, a pick, rations, two
sandbags, a groundsheet, a tin triangle sewn to your pack so the gunners can see how far you've
got. It's like a sack of flour on your shoulders, and the sack has to walk.

At twenty past seven, away to the south, a mine goes up under their line. The ground lifts
under your boots like the shed floor when the engine starts. Then our guns stop, all of them,
and in the quiet you can hear a man three bays down being sick, and a bird, and your heart.

Half past seven. Whistles.

[if war.path == rifleman]You go up the ladder behind your corporal with {mate} on the next rung down.[/if][if war.path == nco]The section's yours now. Seven men on the ladder behind you, looking at your back to see when to go.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You go in the second line with the gun on your shoulder and your No. 2 behind you with the drums. Twenty-eight pounds of gun on top of the sixty.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer, a reel of cable paying out behind you and the telephone banging on your hip. Battalion will want to know where the company is. The line has to get there with you.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You're with the bombers, a bucket of Mills bombs in each hand. Their trench is your job, if anybody gets there.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the second line with the scoped rifle wrapped in sacking. Their machine gunners are your job, if you can find them.[/if]

[if war.stalled]By the time you're up, the first line is lying down in rows forty yards out, and the noise from the ridge has started: their machine guns, the whole length of the ridge at once, like every loom in the shed starting together. Their wire is standing. Nobody cut it. It's thick as a hedge, and there are men hung up on it like washing.[else]The first line is walking, rifles at the port, and the noise from the ridge has started: their machine guns, the whole length of the ridge at once, like every loom in the shed starting together. Men go down in rows, neatly, the way washing comes off the line in a wind. Some get up again.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Get the gun into a shell hole and fire on their guns.[/if][if war.path == signals]Keep going, paying out the wire.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Run for their wire with the buckets.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Find a fire position and hunt their gunners.[/if][if war.path == nco]Take the section on at a walk.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Walk on into it.[/if] ({risk_push})

[if war.path == nco]Get your wounded into cover first.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Get the drums forward to the men who need them.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Drag {mate} into a shell hole. He's hit in the leg.[/if][if war.path == signals]Stay with the officer. He's down.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Get a wounded bomber back to the sap.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Spot for the Lewis gun beside you.[/if] ({risk_help})
Get down. Wait for the fire to slacken. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_2.title: The first of July
b_somme_2.text:
You don't remember crossing. You remember the wire: a gap a shell had blown, men crowding to it,
and the machine gun that knew about the gap. Then you're down in their trench, and it's quiet,
and it's deep, deeper than ours, with steps cut down into the chalk. At the bottom of the steps
there's electric light. Wooden walls. Bunks with blankets. A picture postcard of a woman pinned
over a bunk, and a coffee pot, and the coffee's still warm.

Then the bombs start coming over the traverse from the next bay.

[if war.path == lewis]The gun's choked with chalk. You strip the cocking handle with your fingers shaking and it goes on the parapet, facing the wrong way, and your No. 2 is gone and you don't know when.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your men. Four. You don't know where the others are and there isn't time to know.[/if][if war.path == signals]The wire's cut somewhere behind you. You've two pigeons in a wicker basket on your back, and one of them is dead.[/if][if war.path == bomb]This is your work. A bay at a time: pin, throw, count, round the traverse after it.[/if][if war.path == snipe]In a trench the scoped rifle's a club. You leave it in the dugout and pick up a dead man's rifle with a bayonet on.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]You've lost your corporal. {mate} is with you, white as paper, his rifle shaking.[/if]

[if war.stalled]There are eleven of you. You can't see anyone else from the battalion, left or right. Behind you no man's land is a field of men lying down.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == bomb]Round the traverse with the bombs.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Clear the gun and hose the next bay.[/if][if war.path == nco]Lead the four of them round the traverse.[/if][if war.path == rifleman || war.path == signals || war.path == snipe]Round the traverse after the bombers.[/if] ({risk_push})
Keep the wounded together at the dugout steps. ({risk_help})
Get down into the dugout entrance and stay there. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_3.title: The first of July
b_somme_3.text:
The afternoon goes on and on. The sun comes round and the trench fills with heat and flies.
You've drunk your water. You've drunk the water of the dead man by the steps. Your lips have
split and your tongue's a strip of leather.

Nobody's coming. Every time anyone puts his head over the back, towards our line, the machine
guns open up on no man's land again, and no man's land is full of men who aren't moving, and
some who are.

[if war.path == lewis]You're on your last drum. You've been counting rounds in your head the way you'd count picks on a loom.[/if][if war.path == nco]You've four men, and a lance corporal who won't stop talking about his allotment.[/if][if war.path == signals]You let the live pigeon go with a message on its leg: cut off, need bombs and water. It goes round twice and then off the right way, and you watch it till it's gone.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You've six bombs left, and their bombers have the whole of their own trench to fetch more from.[/if][if war.path == snipe || war.path == rifleman]You've ninety rounds and a bayonet and your own two hands.[/if]

They come at you from both ends of the trench at once, about four o'clock. Bombs first.

choices.text: Up on the firestep. Meet them. ({risk_push})
Pass up bombs and clips. Keep the others fighting. ({risk_help})
Stay under the parapet. Throw blind. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_4.title: The first of July
b_somme_4.text:
Dark at last. Somebody says go, and you go, back over the parapet into no man's land.

It isn't empty. It's full. Men lying everywhere in the long grass, and the ones who are alive are
calling out. Water. Stretcher-bearer. Mother. A name, over and over, a girl's name. One of them
gets hold of your ankle as you go past and doesn't let go.

A flare goes up and everybody freezes and the machine guns sweep the field low, just over the
grass, and stop. The calling starts again.

choices.text: Get up and run for our wire. ({risk_push})
Bring in the man who has your ankle. ({risk_help})
Crawl, shell hole to shell hole, as slow as it takes. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_autumn_1.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_1.text:
It's rained for a week. The ground between here and the next ridge isn't ground any more, it's
porridge with things in it. Your puttees are clay to the knee and the clay weighs more than
your boots.

On the right one of the new tanks is going forward, slow as a cart, rocking like a boat. It
noses down into a shell hole, and stops, and sits there tilted with its tail in the air,
smoking. Nobody climbs out.

[if war.path == lewis]The gun's wrapped in a groundsheet against the wet and it'll jam the moment it comes out.[/if][if war.path == signals]Nobody has even tried to run a wire across this. It's runners or nothing.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section is three old hands and four lads from the last draft, who've never been over.[/if][if war.path == bomb]The bombs are wet. Half of them won't go.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You can't see fifty yards in this rain.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} goes in to the waist in the first ten yards and you haul him out by his webbing.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The first wave's stuck in the mud forty yards out, going nowhere, and they're being shot where they stand.[else]Whistles. Up and over, and the mud takes your boot off on the first step.[/if]

choices.text: Keep going. Get across before you sink. ({risk_push})
Haul out the men who are stuck. ({risk_help})
Get down in a shell hole, water or not. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_autumn_2.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_2.text:
Their trench, when you get to it, is mostly water, with duckboards floating in it and a dead man
floating face down among the duckboards. The Germans in it are as wet and as filthy as you are.
Some of them want to surrender and some of them don't, and you can't tell which from their faces.

Somebody's bombing up the trench towards you, steady, a bay at a time.

choices.text: Go to meet them round the traverse. ({risk_push})
Get the prisoners down and the wounded out of the water. ({risk_help})
Get down behind the traverse and hold it. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_autumn_3.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_3.text:
Night, and the rain again, and they come back at you out of it. You only see them by the flashes:
a helmet, a face, a man with his mouth open, gone. You fire at where the last flash was. Your
hands are so cold you can't feel the bolt.

choices.text: Stand up in the water and fire. ({risk_push})
Keep the new lads firing. Load for them. ({risk_help})
Stay down in the water and fire over the top. ({risk_ground})

l_mill_1916.title: Home on leave
l_mill_1916.text:
December again, the second one. The town's quieter than you remember, and it takes you till the
end of the station road to work out why. There are women everywhere: on the trams, in the
railway yard in men's caps, coming off shift at the mill with their hair tied up in scarves.
And every third house has its blinds down.

July came here too. It came in August, mostly, in buff envelopes, a street at a time. Your
mother says Mrs Ormerod had two in one week.

[if war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Shaw and Edith were wed in October on his leave. You weren't there. He had his cousin stand up with him instead. Edith shows you the photograph and says, "He kept your place," and you don't know what to say to that.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.after_the_war]Edith Holt stops you on Market Street. "Has he said anything?" she says. "About after?" You tell her he has. You don't tell her he's waiting till it's over.[/if][if !war.mate1]Edith Holt is in black, though they weren't wed. Nobody tells her she can't be.[/if]

[if war.mate3]Mrs Pilling has a new hat. [if flag.urged_pilling_go]"They lost the papers," she says, "can you credit it," and looks at you as if she knows exactly who didn't lose them.[/if][if flag.let_pilling_stay]"He wrote me," she says. "He says he's needed." She says it with her mouth tight, proud and furious at once.[/if][/if][if !war.mate3]The Pillings have taken in a lodger, a Belgian. Mrs Pilling doesn't go out.[/if]

[if flag.brought_discs]Somewhere in this town a mother has a disc on a cord that you cut by feel in the dark. You'll never know which one. You look at every woman in black at chapel and wonder.[/if]

Your mother took your father to see the Somme film at the Hippodrome in the summer. She tells you
about it at tea: the guns, the men going over, the wounded smiling at the camera. She wants to
know if it's like that. You say yes.

In September a Zeppelin came over in the night and bombed Bolton. Your father went up on the
roof to watch. You can hear the pride in his voice, telling it.

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v16p_gone_under.title: The ones who went under
v16p_gone_under.text:
February, and eleven men from the company have gone to the tunnellers. Six shillings a day.
You see them sometimes, coming up out of a hole behind the support line at the end of a shift,
grey-white with chalk from head to foot, blinking at the daylight the way you used to at bank.
They walk different already. They walk like men going home.

The infantry don't like them. The infantry say they're paid six times as much to stay out of
the rain. Then one night a camouflet goes up under the next company's sap, and in the morning
the tunnellers carry out four of their own, wrapped in groundsheets, and nobody says it again.

[if war.mate1]Robson watches them go down every evening. "I could have," he says.[/if]

choices.text: Stand with Robson and watch the shift go down.
choices.text_after:
Neither of you says anything. The last man down turns on the ladder, a pitman from the
next row at home, and lifts a hand to you, the way you would at the shaft top.

choices.text: Go back to the dugout. You made your choice.
choices.text_after:
You made it. You stay with it. That night, on sentry, you listen to the ground under your
boots, and it's the tunnellers you hear now, and you can't
tell if that's worse or better.

v16p_bell_brother.title: Matty Bell
v16p_bell_brother.text:
Bell's had a letter, and he's not said a word about it for two days, which is the longest
he's been quiet since the Miners' Hall.

It comes out on sentry. His brother Matty, the young one, who's not down the pit because he
was bad with his chest as a bairn and works in the Store. He's had his papers under the new Act,
and he's gone before the tribunal and said he won't. Won't fight, won't wear the uniform, won't
carry a stretcher. Conscience. The tribunal gave him nothing. He's in the guardroom at Newcastle,
and they say he'll go to prison.

"Our Matty," Bell says. "Wouldn't hurt a fly. Used to cry at the killing of the pig." He's
looking out at the wire. "Half the company'd shoot him. I don't know if I would."

[if war.mate1]Robson, on the next step, says nothing at all.[/if]

choices.text: Tell Bell his brother has more nerve than most of the company.
choices.text_after:
Bell looks at you a long time in the dark. "Aye," he says. "Aye. He has." And then, because
he's Bell: "Daft little beggar." He laughs, and it cracks in the middle.

choices.text: Say nowt. It's not a thing you can say anything to.
choices.text_after:
You stand the rest of the watch together and don't talk. Near dawn he hands you his tin of
tobacco without being asked, which is Bell's way of saying he knows.

v16p_birds.title: The basket
v16p_birds.text:
For the big push every company is to carry pigeons, two birds in a wicker basket, with little
aluminium tubes for messages, because the telephone wires won't last. The company officer
asks who knows birds.

Twenty men look at Robson.

He takes the basket like it's a bairn somebody's handed him. That night in the dugout he has
the lid open and the birds out, one in each hand, turning them over, looking at their eyes and
their feathers, talking to them low. "This one's a good 'un," he says. "This one wants feeding
up." He saves bits of his biscuit for them, soaked in his tea.

choices.text: Help him look after them. Learn the message tubes.
choices.text_after:
He shows you how to roll the flimsy and slide it into the tube, and how to hold a bird so
it doesn't panic: firm round the wings, its feet between your fingers. It's warm, and its
heart goes like a watch. "If I'm down," Robson says, "you take the basket." It's the most
he's said about the first of July.

choices.text: Leave him to it. They're his.
choices.text_after:
He doesn't mind. He sits up with them by the candle long after the dugout's asleep, and in
the morning the basket smells of tea.

v16p_bombardment.title: The bombardment
v16p_bombardment.text:
A week of it. Our guns, all of them, day and night, and the noise goes on so long you stop
hearing it, the way you stop hearing the screens at bank, and then you only hear it when it
stops for a minute and the quiet hits you like cold water.

The lads are cheerful. Nothing can live under that. We'll walk over, the officers say. Take a
walking stick.

In front of you, across the valley, the German line goes up past the village on a little rise,
and just to the right of the village is the place they call the Glory Hole, where the lines
are so close you can hear them cough. Everybody knows by now. Under the Glory Hole the
tunnellers have put a mine. The biggest ever, they say. It goes up two minutes before zero.

[if war.mate3]Charlton's been taking mules up with ammunition every night. He says there are more guns behind you than there are lamps in the lamp cabin, wheel to wheel, all down the valley.[/if]

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
It's shorter than the one before Loos. Look after Father. Make him go to the doctor. The
pit boots to whoever needs them. Love to all. You fold it small and it sits against your
chest.

choices.text: Try to sleep. You'll need it.
choices.text_after:
You lie on the firestep with your helmet over your face and the guns going and you
sleep, an hour, two, and dream you're at the face with your father, and the roof's talking,
and he says it's all right, it's only the roof.

v16p_july.title: July
v16p_july.text:
For days after, they're still coming in from no man's land, the ones who can crawl. Then the
ones who can't are brought in by the burial parties.

The crater's a mark on everything. You can see it from anywhere: a white hole in the chalk a
hundred yards across, deep as a shaft, and men from both sides still in the bottom of it. The
smell of it comes over on the wind in the evenings, chalk and lime and the other thing.

The battalion's a third of what it was. They bring the company out to a field and sort out who's
left into new sections, and the sergeant major reads names off a list, and men from Blackhaugh
are put with men from places they've never heard of, and stand there not looking at each other.

The papers from home come up a week late. The whole of the North East is in them. Column after
column. Every village.

choices.text: Read the lists. Every name.
choices.text_after:
It takes you an hour, in small print, by the light from the dugout door. Men you went to
school with. Men you stood beside at the face. Two from your own row. You read every name
and you put the paper down, and then you pick it up and read them again.

choices.text: Don't. You were there.
choices.text_after:
You use the paper to light the brazier. It catches slowly, the lists curling and going
brown and then black, and you hold your hands over it till the warmth comes.

v16p_mule.title: The mule
v16p_mule.text:
September, and the rain's come, and the tracks behind the line have gone to porridge. You're on
a carrying party, coming back empty, and you come on Charlton's limber stuck to the axles, and
one of his mules gone off the track into a shell hole full of water. It's in up to the neck. Its
eyes are rolling. It's making a noise you didn't know a mule could make.

Charlton's in the water with it, holding its head up, talking to it, the way he used to talk
to the ponies when the roof was working. A corporal from the transport is standing on the edge
with his rifle.

"Can't get her out," the corporal says. "I've seen 'em go like this. She's finished."

"She's not," Charlton says. "She's not. Give us a rope."

choices.text: Get the party on a rope. Pull.
choices.text_after:
Eight of you on the rope, up to your knees in the porridge, heaving, and Charlton in the
water pushing from behind, and she comes out of it at last with a great sucking noise,
shaking and steaming, and stands on the track with her legs spread. Charlton puts his face
against her neck. Nobody says anything about the time.

choices.text: Tell Charlton the corporal's right. Get him out of the water.
choices.text_after:
You get him out. He comes, in the end, because he knows. He turns his back while the
corporal does it, and you stand with him on the track, and he's shaking, and it isn't the
cold. "I'll not forget her," he says. "Her name was Bella."

v16p_first_shift.title: Under
v16p_first_shift.text:
The shaft goes down from a dugout behind the support line, forty feet on a ladder, and at the
bottom it's chalk. Not coal. White chalk, wet, that glows in the candlelight and takes the print
of your hand.

You work it with a bayonet, not a pick. A pick rings. You work in your socks, on sandbags laid
along the floor, and nobody talks above a whisper, because somewhere the other side of the
chalk the Germans are working too, and listening. You prise out a lump, catch it before it
falls, pass it back hand to hand to the man with the sandbags. Hour after hour. The air's thick
and warm and stinks of candle smoke and sweat and wet chalk, and after an hour your head aches
with it, the way it does when the air's going in an old working.

There's a canary in a cage at the face. You know what it's for. Every man here knows what it's
for. You look at it more than you look at anything.

It's the face. It's only the face. You'd forgotten how much you'd missed it, and how much you
hated it.

choices.text: Get your head down and work.

v16p_crew.title: The crew
v16p_crew.text:
There are four of you on a shift, and you live together, eat together, sleep in the same hole
in the chalk, and you know them by their breathing in the dark.

Evans is from the Rhondda, a hewer, short and wide, with a voice that fills a gallery when he
forgets to whisper. He came out with the rest of South Wales last July. "They called us
traitors," he says, "and then they sent for us to dig." Pascoe's a tin miner from Camborne, old,
forty if he's a day, who's dug in Cornwall and South Africa and Montana and never once raised his
voice. And Mott, the kicker, a little Londoner who dug the tunnels for the Underground railway
lying on his back on a wooden cross, kicking out the clay with a spade on his feet. He talks
about the Tube as if it's a cathedral.

Four trades, four ways of talking. Underground none of it matters. You can all hear the same
thing.

choices.text: Tell Evans about Jim Bell in the beer vat.
choices.text_after:
Evans laughs so loud Pascoe has to put a hand over his mouth. "Your Bell," he says, in a
whisper, delighted. "I'd buy your Bell a pint. I'd buy him a barrel."

choices.text: Listen to them. Say little.
choices.text_after:
You say little. It's a pitman's way, and they're all pitmen of some sort, and they don't
mind. By the end of the month Pascoe calls you "my 'andsome" and Mott calls you "Geordie"
and Evans calls you "boyo", and you answer to all three.

v16p_charge.title: The charge
v16p_charge.text:
June, and the guns going day and night overhead so the chalk trembles, and down here it's
quiet as chapel. You're carrying the charge in.

Ammonal, in tins like syrup tins, fifty pound a time, passed hand to hand along the gallery,
man to man, in silence, from the shaft to the chamber at the end, a thousand feet away under
their line. Then sandbags to tamp it, hundreds of them, packed tight behind the charge so the
blast goes up and not back. Then the leads, paid out carefully all the way back.

It takes days. When it's done, the chamber at the end of the gallery has more explosive in it
than you thought was in the world. The men in the trench above it are Germans. You've heard
them, through the chalk, through the geophone, talking, coughing, a gramophone once.

The last tin goes in. Somebody's chalked something on it.

choices.text: Chalk your own name on a tin, and the date.
choices.text_after:
Your name, and BLACKHAUGH, and 28.6.16, in chalk on the lid, by the light of a candle. Evans
writes CYMRU on the next one. You don't know why you did it. It's like signing your name
to something before you know what it is.

choices.text: Leave it. Just get it done.
choices.text_after:
You pass the last tin on and wipe your hands on your trousers and don't look back down the
gallery. Mott, behind you, whistles under his breath, low, a music-hall tune, the
same three bars over and over, until Pascoe tells him to stop.

v16p_listening.title: The geophone
v16p_listening.text:
A listening post at the end of a gallery, alone, on your stomach in the chalk, with the two
discs of the geophone pressed to the floor and the earpieces in your ears like a doctor's. It's
so quiet you can hear your own blood.

Then you hear them. Picks, faint as a clock in the next house. A pause. Voices. Germans, talking, not whispering, the
way men talk at the face when they think nobody's near. Somebody laughs. Somebody starts singing,
a slow song, a hymn maybe, and the others join in, and it comes through the chalk thin and
far away, like the chapel choir heard from the end of the rows on a summer night.

They're close. Ten feet. Less. If they're laying a charge, it'll be under the gallery Evans and
Pascoe are working in.

The rule's simple. You report it, and the officer decides, and he'll blow a camouflet, and
the singing will stop.

choices.text: Go back and report it. Now.
choices.text_after:
The officer listens himself, then nods. The charge goes in that night, a small one, tamped
hard, meant to crush their gallery without breaking the surface. When it goes, the ground
thumps under you like a door slamming in an empty house. Next shift you listen at the same
place, a long time. Nothing. Only the chalk.

choices.text: Wait. Let them finish their song.
choices.text_after:
You lie there till they finish. It's a long song. Then you go back and report it, and the
officer blows a camouflet that night, and it's the same in the end, and it isn't. You find
yourself humming the tune for weeks, and you never learn what it was.

v16p_visit.title: The battalion
v16p_visit.text:
The battalion's out at rest in a village four miles back, and you walk over on your afternoon
off to find the lads. It takes you an hour to find anybody you know.

It's a third of what it was. There are new faces everywhere, lads from Sunderland and Hull and
places you've never heard of, in Blackhaugh's company.

[if war.mate1]Robson's there, sat on an upturned bucket cleaning his rifle. He looks up, and nods, as if you'd been gone ten minutes. "All right," he says. "All right, Tommy," you say.[/if][if !war.mate1]Robson's not there. Somebody tells you, as if you knew.[/if][if war.mate2] Bell's there, and talks for an hour without stopping, about July, about the generals, about the wire that was never cut, and his voice goes on and on and you let it.[/if][if !war.mate2] Bell's not there either.[/if][if war.mate3] Charlton's down at the horse lines. He walks you back to the road with his hand on a mule's neck.[/if][if !war.mate3] Nobody's at the horse lines that you know.[/if]

choices.text: Stay till dark. Share what you've got.
choices.text_after:
You've a tin of pineapple chunks and twenty cigarettes, six shillings a day buys a lot,
and they go round. When you leave in the dark, walking back to your hole in the chalk, you
feel like a man who's been to a funeral and a wedding on the same day.

choices.text: Go back early. You're not one of them now.
choices.text_after:
You go before the light goes. On the road back you meet a sapper from your own company and
walk with him, and talk about timbering, and it's easier.

v16p_letter.title: A letter from home
v16p_letter.text:
"Dear Son, I hope this finds you well as it leaves us at present. Your father has had to come
off the face. His chest got too bad. They have put him on at bank on the screens with the old
men and the lads, picking stone out of the coal, and he comes home and sits in the chair and
does not say anything. He says it is like being a bairn again.

They have took boys on underground at thirteen now, they are that short. Mrs Armstrong's
youngest went down Monday. [if war.transferred]Your money came. I have bought a new mangle and put the rest in the Store, and your father says six shillings a day is more than he ever made and he does not know whether to be proud or ashamed.[/if][if !war.transferred]The whole village had the blinds down in July. There is not a row without one.[/if]

Keep your feet dry. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write to your father. Just to him.
choices.text_after:
It's the first letter you've ever written him. You don't know what to say, so you tell him
about the face, [if war.transferred]the chalk and the socks and the canary, the timbering,[/if][if !war.transferred]the timbering in the German dugouts, the depth of them,[/if] the things he'd want to know.
At the end you put: I wish you were here to see it. You don't know if that's true, but it's
what you'd say to him at the face.

choices.text: Keep it with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket. You read the bit about the screens again, by the brazier, and
you can see him, bent over the belt with the old men, picking stone, coughing.

b_somme_pit_1.title: The first of July
b_somme_pit_1.text:
The first of July comes up hot, mist in the valley burning off, and by seven the sun's on your
neck.

[if war.path == tunnel]You're at the firing point, a dugout at the head of the gallery, with the leads coming up out of the dark and the exploder on a ration box. The officer looks at his watch every half a minute. Down there, at the end of a thousand feet of chalk, is every tin you carried.[else]You're in the assembly trench at the head of the valley, sixty pounds on your back, and to your right, on the rise, is the Glory Hole. Under it is the mine. Everybody's watching it. Nobody's watching anything else.[/if]

Twenty-eight minutes past seven.[if war.path == tunnel] The officer pushes the handle down.[/if]

The ground doesn't shake. It lifts, like the floor of the cage when the brake comes off. Then
the noise, and a column of earth and chalk goes up out of the German line, higher than the pit
heap, higher than the church, higher than anything, and hangs there, and comes down. For two
minutes it rains chalk: lumps the size of a man's head, then stones, then dust, white over
everything, in your mouth, tasting of chalk and burnt ammonal.

Half past seven. Whistles. Somewhere on the left, pipes.

[if war.path == rifleman]You go up the ladder with {mate} on the next rung, chalk dust coming down on you both like flour.[/if][if war.path == nco]Seven men on the ladder behind you, watching your back to see when to go.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You go in the second line with the gun on your shoulder and your No. 2 behind you with the drums.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer, a reel of wire paying out behind you.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You go with the bombers, a bucket of Mills bombs in each hand, for the crater.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the second line with the scoped rifle wrapped in sacking, looking for their machine guns.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You go over in the second wave with a party of sappers, for the crater, to blow in any dugout that still has Germans in it.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The mine didn't touch the village. The machine guns in it open up straight down the valley, all of them at once, like the coal-cutter starting at the face, only it doesn't stop. The first line goes down before it's twenty yards out, in rows.[else]The first line goes forward into the white dust. The machine guns in the village open up, and men go down in rows, and some get up, and the rest go on.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Get the gun into a shell hole and fire on the village.[/if][if war.path == signals]Keep going, paying out the wire.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Run for the crater with the buckets.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Find a fire position and hunt the guns in the village.[/if][if war.path == nco]Take the section on at a walk.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Walk on into it.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Go for the crater with the sappers.[/if] ({risk_push})

[if war.path == nco]Get your wounded into cover first.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Get the drums forward to the men who need them.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Drag {mate} into a shell hole. He's hit in the leg.[/if][if war.path == signals]Stay with the officer. He's down.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Get a wounded bomber back to the sap.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Spot for the Lewis gun beside you.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Carry a wounded sapper back to the trench.[/if] ({risk_help})
Get down. Wait for the fire to slacken. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_pit_2.title: The crater
b_somme_pit_2.text:
The crater. You've never seen a hole like it, not at any pit, not anywhere. A hundred yards
across and deep as a shaft, white chalk sides still smoking, and men sliding down into it for
cover, ours and theirs, and at the bottom water and broken timber and things you don't look at.
[if war.path == tunnel]You made it. You carried it in, tin by tin.[/if][if war.path == tunnel && flag.p16_chalked_tin] Somewhere down in the bottom of it, in a thousand pieces, is your name.[/if]

On the far lip, what's left of their trench. Their dugouts go down thirty feet into the chalk,
timbered better than any pit you ever worked, and there are Germans in them still, and the
bombs start coming over the lip at you.

[if war.path == bomb]This is your work. Pin, throw, count, along the lip.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]A dugout entrance, smoke coming out of it. You've a charge in your haversack and a fuse.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your men. Four.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's choked with chalk. You strip it with your fingers shaking.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} is beside you on the lip, white with chalk, like a man come up from the screens.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == tunnel]Blow the dugout entrance.[/if][if war.path != tunnel]Go round the lip for their trench.[/if] ({risk_push})
Get the wounded down into the crater out of the fire. ({risk_help})
Get down on the crater's inside slope and stay there. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_pit_3.title: The crater
b_somme_pit_3.text:
The afternoon in the crater. Hot. No water. The chalk throws the sun back at you so your eyes
run, and the flies come, thousands of them, and the shells come in on the lip and every one
brings the sides down in a slide of chalk and stones.

Nobody knows where anybody is. Battalion doesn't know where you are. The wire's long gone.

[if war.mate1 && flag.p16_birds]Robson has the basket. He writes the message out on his knee, the officer's words, slow and careful, and rolls it and slides it into the tube on the bird's leg, and holds her up in both his big hands, and lets her go. She goes up out of the crater, round once, round twice over the chalk, the way his da's birds go round over the rows, and then straight west, and Robson watches her till she's gone.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.p16_birds]You have the basket. Robson said you'd take it if he was down. You write the message, and roll it, and hold the bird the way he showed you, firm round the wings, and let her go. She goes round once over the crater and then west, and you watch her all the way.[/if]

Late in the afternoon they come out of the village to take the crater back.

choices.text: Up on the lip and fire into them. ({risk_push})
Pass up ammunition from the dead. ({risk_help})
Keep down inside the crater. ({risk_ground})

b_somme_pit_4.title: Night
b_somme_pit_4.text:
Night, and quiet, or nearly. Out in the valley, all across it, the wounded are calling. Hundreds
of them. Water, and stretcher-bearer, and names, and mam. Some of them in Blackhaugh voices. You
know some of the voices.

You know what you'd do if a man was trapped at the face. Everybody would go. Nobody would wait to
be asked.

But this isn't the face, and the flares are going up, and their machine guns traverse the valley
every few minutes, slow, like a man sweeping a yard.

choices.text: Go back across for water and bring it out. ({risk_push})
Crawl out to the nearest voice and bring him in. ({risk_help})
Stay in the crater till you're relieved. ({risk_ground})

b_butte_1.title: The Butte
b_butte_1.text:
October. The rain hasn't stopped in a fortnight and the ground's gone to a paste that takes your
boots off. In front of you, across a mile of it, there's a hill, if you can call it a hill: a
great white mound of chalk, bare, with nothing growing on it, like the pit heap at home if the
pit heap were made of bone. They call it the Butte. The Germans have tunnelled it through and
through, and it's full of machine guns.

[if war.path == tunnel]You're up with the infantry to dig them in on whatever they take, and to find the tunnels in the Butte if anybody gets there.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} goes over the bag beside you and sinks to his knees in the first yard.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section goes over the bags behind you, slow, the mud holding every step.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's caked. The drums are caked. You've wrapped the gun in a sandbag and you'll unwrap it when you get there.[/if][if war.path == signals]No wire across this. Runners. You're the runner.[/if][if war.path == bomb]The bombs are in a sandbag on your back, wrapped against the wet.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Your rifle's wrapped in sacking. You're looking for the slits in the chalk.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The barrage gets away from you in five minutes. Nobody can walk fast in this. The Butte opens up, and men stand stuck in the mud and are shot standing.[else]The barrage goes over, and you go after it, slow, a yard at a time, like wading the burn in flood.[/if]

choices.text: Keep up with the barrage, whatever the mud does. ({risk_push})
Pull men out of the mud as you go. ({risk_help})
Get into a shell hole and wait for the fire to slacken. ({risk_ground})

b_butte_2.title: The Butte
b_butte_2.text:
A trench at the foot of the Butte, or what was one, half full of water, and Germans in it with
their hands up, and Germans in it fighting, and you can't tell which from ten yards in the
rain.

Above you, in the white side of the Butte, the slits. Every one of them a gun.

choices.text: Bomb up the slope at the nearest slit. ({risk_push})
Get the prisoners and the wounded down into the trench. ({risk_help})
Get down in the water and fire at the slits. ({risk_ground})

b_butte_3.title: The Butte
b_butte_3.text:
Night, and rain, and the Butte still theirs above you, and the trench you've got is a ditch with
the dead in the water. Your hands are so cold you can't feel the bolt. Somebody passes along a
tin of rum and it's the only warm thing in France.

Before dawn they come down the Butte at you, out of the tunnels, out of the chalk, like men
coming up out of a drift.

choices.text: Stand up in the ditch and fire into them. ({risk_push})
Keep the next man's rifle working. ({risk_help})
Keep down below the lip of the ditch. ({risk_ground})

l_pit_1916.title: Home on leave
l_pit_1916.text:
December, and the village is quiet the way it's never quiet. The buzzer still goes, the cage
still winds, the heap still burns red on the skyline, but the rows are full of drawn blinds and
black armbands, and the women stand in their doorways in the cold and watch you come up the
street, and you know every one of them is looking at your face to see if it's somebody else's.

Your father's in his chair by the fire. He's thinner. He doesn't get up. He holds his hand out
and you take it, and it's an old man's hand, soft from the screens, the calluses gone.[if flag.p16_wrote_father] "I got your letter," he says. He's got it in his waistcoat pocket. He doesn't say anything else about it. He doesn't need to.[/if]

[if war.transferred]Your mother's got a new mangle in the wash-house, and she shows it to you twice. "Six shillings a day," your father says, and coughs. "Down a hole. In France." He laughs till the coughing stops him. "I could have told you that was where you'd end."[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_chalked_tin] You don't tell anybody about the tins, and your name on the last one.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_blew_camouflet] Some nights in your own bed you feel the ground thump under you, like a door slamming in an empty house, and you're awake before you know why.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_visited] You carry the lads' messages round the rows, from the afternoon you walked over to the battalion, and the mothers make you say them twice.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_heard_the_song] At chapel on Sunday they sing a hymn you don't know, and for a moment, in the second verse, you think it's the one. It isn't.[/if]

[if !war.transferred && flag.p16_read_lists]You know every house with the blinds down. You read them all, in France, in small print. You go round them, one a day, and sit in their kitchens, and tell the mothers what you can.[/if][if !war.transferred && !flag.p16_read_lists]You didn't read the lists. You learn them now, walking up the rows, a blind at a time.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.p16_backed_matty]Mrs Bell takes you aside at the Store. Matty's in prison, in Durham. Jim wrote that you stuck up for him. She doesn't say thank you. She gives you a quarter of black bullets and goes.[/if][if !war.mate2]Bell's father doesn't come to the Miners' Hall any more. Matty's in prison. Jim's in France, under it.[/if]

[if war.mate1]Old Mr Robson's out at the cree. [if flag.p16_birds]Tommy wrote him about the basket on the first of July. He wants to know everything: which way she went, how long she circled, whether she came in. You tell him she came in. You don't know. He nods as if he knew she would.[/if][if !flag.p16_birds]He asks after Tommy, and you tell him Tommy's well, still saying nothing.[/if][/if][if !war.mate1]Old Mr Robson's given up the birds. The cree's empty, the door open, banging in the wind.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.p16_saved_mule]Mrs Charlton has a letter from George, all about a mule called Bella who fell in a shell hole and came out again. "You were there," she says. "He says you were on the rope."[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.p16_shot_mule]Mrs Charlton says George's letters have gone short. She doesn't know why. You do, and don't tell her.[/if][if !war.mate3]In the pit stables, the old horse-keeper has put George's photograph up on a nail by Captain's stall.[/if]

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v17_pilling_eighteen.title: Eighteen
v17_pilling_eighteen.text:
In March Pilling turned eighteen, and nobody sent a cake. He's old enough now, in the eyes of the
War Office. He's been old enough in everybody else's for a year.

He's not the lad who cried for his mam on the boat. He volunteers for everything, raids,
patrols, wiring, as if he's owed something and means to collect it. He's got a German officer's
watch on his wrist that he won't talk about. When the new draft comes up he looks at them the
way the old sweats looked at you.

"Eighteen," he says, and laughs, and it isn't his laugh. "Me mam said I could join up at
eighteen."

choices.text: Tell him to ease off. Nobody's counting.
choices.text_after:
"Somebody is," he says. He doesn't say who. That night he's out with the wiring party,
and he comes back with his hands cut to ribbons, singing.

choices.text: Leave him be. He's a man now; it's his war.
choices.text_after:
You share your rum with him, without saying it's a birthday present, and he knows, and
doesn't say thank you, and drinks it.

v17_caves.title: The caves
v17_caves.text:
Under Arras there are caves, old chalk quarries from hundreds of years back, and the tunnellers
have joined them up into a town under the town. Thousands of you are down here, waiting. There's
electric light strung along the walls, and a light railway, and water dripping everywhere, and
the air is thick with the breath of a whole brigade and the smell of wet chalk and paraffin and
feet.

Somebody's carved his name in the chalk, and a date, and a girl's name. Somebody else has
carved a picture of a woman that the sergeant major makes them chip off.

The attack's tomorrow. Up the steps and out into the morning. You can't sleep. Nobody can.

choices.text: Write a letter for the pay book.
choices.text_after:
You write it on your knee by the electric light. It's the third one now. They get shorter
each time. This one says: Look after Mother. Tell Jack he's not to join up, whatever they
say at the drill hall.

choices.text: Carve your own name in the chalk.
choices.text_after:
You do it with your bayonet, slowly, in capitals, and the town after it, and the date. The
chalk comes away soft as cheese. It'll be there, you think, after.

v17_airman.title: Aeroplanes
v17_airman.text:
Since Arras the sky has been full of aeroplanes, theirs and ours, and every afternoon there's a
fight up there that you watch with your neck cricked back, like a football crowd. Ours keep
falling. The lads called April Bloody April, and they meant the Flying Corps.

One comes down near your bay in the evening, on fire, slowly, turning over and over, and you
can see a man in it. It hits beyond the support line with a sound like a dropped tray.

choices.text: Run to the wreck with the others.
choices.text_after:
There's nothing to do when you get there. The smell of the burning dope on the wings is
sweet and chemical, like pear drops, and under it the other smell. One of the lads takes
the pilot's goggles, which are lying in the grass without a mark on them. You don't stop him.

choices.text: Stay where you are. Turn away.
choices.text_after: You turn your back on it and clean your rifle, every part of it, twice, until it's dark.

v17_crater_hunt.title: The crater again
v17_crater_hunt.text:
After Arras they send the battalion north, to rest, they say, and it turns out to mean the old
line. The crater. The same bay, the same low place, the sandbags rotted and patched and rotted
again.

He's still there. Two men from the battalion you relieved were shot through the head in that bay
last month, both in the morning, both looking at the sunrise.

The sniping officer, a long thin man from Fleetwood who used to shoot rabbits for a living, is
going to have him. He wants a man who knows the ground. [if war.path == snipe]He wants you. It's your work, now.[else]He looks at you.[/if]

choices.text: Go with him. Find the man at the crater.
choices.text_after:
Three days in a hide in the old crater lip, lying in the stink of it, watching a heap of
bricks through a telescope until your eye waters. On the third morning, the flash. The
officer fires once. Nothing more comes from the bricks, that day or any day after.

Nobody ever sees him. Nobody ever knows for sure. But after that week no one is shot in that
bay again, and the men stand up in it to stretch, and after a while they forget they ever
didn't.

choices.text: Let somebody else go. You've had enough of that bay.
choices.text_after:
The officer goes with somebody else. Three days later there's a single shot from the old
crater lip, early, and then nothing, and nobody tells you anything, and you never find out
whose shot it was.

v17_shaw_father.title: A letter for Shaw
v17_shaw_father.text:
Shaw gets a letter and reads it standing up, by the ration dump, and then sits down on a box
of bombs, which you're not supposed to do, and reads it again.

"A lad," he says. "Seven pound four. Born Tuesday." He looks up at you and his face is wet and
he doesn't seem to know it. "She's calling him Albert. I told her not to. She's calling him
Albert anyway."

choices.text: Wet the baby's head with the section's rum.
choices.text_after:
The corporal looks the other way. The rum goes round the section in a mess tin lid, each man
saying something, to the lad, to Albert, to Edith, to home. Somebody sings. Shaw keeps the
letter inside his shirt against his skin.

choices.text: Take his turn on sentry so he can write back.
choices.text_after:
You stand his two hours on the firestep in the cold. Behind you in the dugout you can hear
him writing, the pencil going slow and careful, the way you taught him or the way he taught
himself.

v17_shaw_edith_writes.title: A letter for Shaw
v17_shaw_edith_writes.text:
Shaw gets a letter and reads it once and folds it small and puts it in his pocket and
goes back to cleaning his rifle.

It's two days before he says anything, and then it's in the dark, on sentry. "She's walking
out with a lad from the gasworks," he says. "Exempt. Reserved occupation." He says it as if he's
reading it off a notice. "Said she couldn't wait for after. Said after might not come."

He's quiet a long while. "She's not wrong," he says.

choices.text: Stay on the firestep with him till his turn's done.
choices.text_after:
Neither of you says anything else. Towards dawn he gives you half his cigarette without
being asked, and you smoke it, and the sky gets light over the German wire.

choices.text: Leave him be. He'll want to be on his own.
choices.text_after:
You leave him be. In the morning he's the same as always, and nobody mentions Edith Holt
again, ever.

v17_mustard.title: Mustard
v17_mustard.text:
A new gas, in Flanders. The shells come over with a soft plop, not a bang, and you think
they're duds. It doesn't smell of much: mustard, some say, or garlic, or horseradish. It hangs
in the shell holes and the low places and soaks into everything.

Hours later the men who were in it start to blister, under the arms, between the legs, wherever
they were sweating. Then their eyes go. They come down the communication trench in a line, each
man with his hand on the shoulder of the man in front, bandages over their eyes, shuffling, like
a Sunday school treat going home.

choices.text: Lead the line of blinded men down to the aid post.
choices.text_after:
The first man's hand is on your shoulder all the way, light, trusting, and he keeps asking
whether it's dark yet, because he can't tell.

choices.text: Stay at your post. Somebody has to.
choices.text_after:
You watch them go past you, one hand on each shoulder, and the line goes round the traverse,
and the last man's hand is reaching for a shoulder that's already gone round the corner.

v17_mother_letter.title: A letter from home
v17_mother_letter.text:
"Dear Son, just a few lines. We are all right but the queues are something cruel, I stood two
hours for margarine Saturday and they run out before me. Sugar is a scandal. Your father says
the Germans are trying to starve us out with their submarines and they will not manage it
because Lancashire folk can live on fresh air and spite.

You will have heard about the explosion at Ashton in June. We heard it here, it rattled every
window in the street. Forty-odd killed, they say, women and children some of them.

[if !war.mate1]Mrs Shaw asked after you. She asks every week.[/if][if war.mate1]Mrs Shaw says to tell Albert his dad's chest is bad again.[/if] Look after yourself. Do not volunteer for anything. I know you. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Keep it in your breast pocket with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in with the rest, a fat damp wad of them now, held with a bootlace. You've never
thrown one away.

b_arras_1.title: Arras
b_arras_1.text:
Up the steps out of the caves at half past five, into sleet. After a night underground the cold
takes your breath. The guns open all at once behind you, more guns than you knew there were in
the world, and the barrage starts walking, a wall of bursts a hundred yards in front, moving
forward a bit at a time like a man pacing out an allotment.

"Lean on it," the officers keep saying. "Keep close to the barrage. Lean on it."

[if war.path == rifleman]{mate} is beside you, snow on his helmet.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section's behind you in a line, and the new men are watching the old ones to see what to do.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's on your shoulder, wet, the drums in their panniers clanking behind you.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer and the wire goes out behind you, and for once, the first hour, it holds.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Their first trench is yours if it's still got men in it.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the first wave, looking for the machine guns the barrage missed.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You were at the end of an exit gallery with the charge set and the leads in your hand. At zero you blew the last few feet, and the daylight came down on you with the chalk, and the infantry came up past you out of the ground.[if flag.p17_exits] Your props held, every one.[/if] Now you go up after them, with a bag of charges, for their dugouts.[/if][if flag.p17_kiwi && war.path != tunnel] Keep your head down coming out the top, the New Zealander said. You keep it down.[/if]

[if war.stalled]On the left the barrage has got away from the men. It's two hundred yards ahead and their machine guns are up and firing into the gap.[else]Their front line comes up out of the sleet, smashed flat, the wire in heaps, and grey figures climbing out of it with their hands up.[/if]

choices.text: Lean on the barrage. Keep right up to it. ({risk_push})
Keep the line together. Bring up the stragglers. ({risk_help})
Get down and let the barrage go on ahead. ({risk_ground})

b_arras_2.title: Arras
b_arras_2.text:
It's working. For the first time in two years, it's working. You're through their first line
and their second and there are prisoners going back past you in dozens, some of them carrying
our wounded without being asked.

Then, unbelievably, cavalry. A whole squadron of them, coming up behind you at a trot through
the snow, lances up, the horses steaming. The lads cheer them. Ten minutes later you see some of
the horses coming back with no riders.

Then a pocket of them in a sunken road that the barrage missed, firing.

choices.text: Go for the sunken road. ({risk_push})
Get the wounded and the prisoners down into cover. ({risk_help})
Get down in their trench and fire on the road. ({risk_ground})

b_arras_3.title: Arras
b_arras_3.text:
By evening it's snowing properly, big wet flakes that settle on the dead. The guns can't get
forward over the broken ground and you're out on your own on the far slope, in shell holes, with
no wire, no water and no hot food. Your feet have gone.

In the dusk they come back at you, out of the village on the hill, in long grey lines.

choices.text: Stand up and fire. Stop them coming. ({risk_push})
Go along the shell holes, keep the men firing. ({risk_help})
Keep down in the shell hole. Fire from cover. ({risk_ground})

b_pass_1.title: Flanders
b_pass_1.text:
It hasn't stopped raining since the end of July. The ground here was always low and wet, and
the shelling has smashed the ditches that used to drain it, and now it's not ground. It's a sea
of mud and water with shell holes in it, rim to rim, each one full to the brim with green water
and some of them with men in.

You go up to the start line in the dark on the duckboard track, single file, a pace apart. Step
off the boards and the mud takes you to the thigh. A man two ahead slips off and goes in to his
chest and they can't get him out, and the column can't stop, and you go past him.

[if war.path == lewis]The gun's twenty-eight pounds and the mud's on it like porridge.[/if][if war.path == signals]No wire across this. Runners and pigeons, and the pigeons won't fly in the rain.[/if][if war.path == nco]You've counted your men onto the duckboards and you count them off.[/if][if war.path == bomb]The bombs are in a sandbag on your back, wrapped in your groundsheet against the wet.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Your rifle's wrapped in sacking, and so is the sight.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You're with the tunnellers, sent up behind the infantry to turn whatever pillboxes they take into shelters, with a bag of tools and no idea where the line will be.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} has his hand on your pack strap so as not to lose you in the dark.[/if]

[if war.stalled]At zero the barrage goes over and the first wave goes out after it, and the barrage gets away from them in ten minutes because nobody can walk fast in this.[else]At zero the barrage goes over, and you go out after it, slow, from shell-hole rim to shell-hole rim, like walking on a pudding.[/if]

choices.text: Keep up with the barrage, whatever the mud does. ({risk_push})
Pull men out of the shell holes as you go. ({risk_help})
Go to ground on the nearest rim. ({risk_ground})

b_pass_2.title: Flanders
b_pass_2.text:
A pillbox. You've heard about them: concrete, three feet thick, half sunk in the mud, with a
machine gun firing out of a slit at the level of your knees. Our shells bounce off them. This one
sits on a little rise and fires across everything.

The bombers are working round it from the side, in the mud, a yard at a time. Somebody has to
keep its slit busy while they do.

choices.text: Work round to the back of it and bomb the door. ({risk_push})
Fire at the slit to keep their heads down. ({risk_help})
Get down behind the rim and wait for it to be over. ({risk_ground})

b_pass_3.title: Flanders
b_pass_3.text:
There's no trench to hold. There's a line of shell holes with men in them, up to their waists in
water, a few yards apart, and that's the new front line. The rain keeps coming. Your rifle's so
caked with mud the bolt won't move, and you open it with the heel of your hand, and it jams again.

Their counter-attack comes in the afternoon, through the rain.

choices.text: Climb out of the water and fire standing. ({risk_push})
Keep the next hole's men supplied and firing. ({risk_help})
Stay down in the water. Fire over the rim. ({risk_ground})

b_pass_4.title: Flanders
b_pass_4.text:
Night, and the relief. Getting out is worse than getting in. It takes six men to carry one
stretcher across this, and they have to put it down every fifty yards, and there are more
stretchers than there are men.

Around you in the dark, in the shell holes, the wounded who can't be got to are calling. Some of
them are sliding down, slowly, into the water, and calling all the way.

choices.text: Get yourself out. Keep to the boards. ({risk_push})
Take a corner of a stretcher. ({risk_help})
Wait in the hole for the shelling to stop. ({risk_ground})

l_mill_1917.title: Home on leave
l_mill_1917.text:
The third December. Your mother looks smaller. She's had her hair cut short, for the mill, and
she touches the back of her neck all the time as if she's forgotten.

There's no sugar in the tea and the bread's grey, war bread, with potato in it. She's saved
the butter ration for a week so you can have it on your first morning, and she watches you eat
it and won't have any.

[if war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Edith brings the baby round. He grabs your finger and won't let go, and Edith laughs and says he's got his father's grip, and you look at the little fist and think of Shaw's hand on the rung of the ladder at Loos.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.best_man && flag.wet_babys_head] "Albert wrote that the whole section drank his health," she says. "In rum. I hope you all had headaches."[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.best_man && flag.stood_shaws_watch] "His long letter came," she says. "Six pages. He said a pal stood his watch for him." She looks at you.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.after_the_war]Edith Holt is married, to the lad from the gasworks. You see her in the Co-op queue. She looks at you and away.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.after_the_war && flag.sat_with_shaw] You think of the firestep, and the half cigarette, and you look away first.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Edith brings the baby round. She's in black. The baby grabs your finger and won't let go. "He's got his dad's grip," she says, and then she has to go outside.[/if]

[if war.mate3]Mrs Pilling asks if he's eating. He's eighteen and he's killed men, and he's still not eating, and you tell her he is.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.wrote_to_mrs_pilling]Mrs Pilling has your letter in a frame, next to his photograph.[/if]

[if flag.went_to_airman]Your mother's bought pear drops for you from the Co-op, a quarter in a paper twist, as a treat. You can't eat them. You can't say why.[/if][if flag.led_the_gassed] At chapel on Sunday the minister reads about the blind leading the blind, and you get up in the middle of it and go out.[/if]

[if flag.left_fritz]Some nights you wake to a single shot from a crater lip, and lie there not knowing whose it was.[/if]

[if flag.hunted_fritz]You don't tell anyone about the crater. There's nothing to tell, and too much.[/if][if flag.carved_name]Somewhere under Arras your name's carved in the chalk, and the town, and the date. Nobody here will ever see it.[/if]

[if war.commission]A letter has come for you, buff, official: you're to go before a board for a commission. An officer. You. Your mother reads it four times and puts it behind the clock with the rent book, and then she takes it out and reads it again.[/if]

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board. Come back an officer, a temporary gentleman.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v17p_frost.title: Frost
v17p_frost.text:
The hardest winter anybody can remember. The ground's iron a foot down, and the bread comes up
frozen, and the tea freezes in the dixie between the cookhouse and the line. Men lose toes.
The latrine buckets freeze solid and have to be chipped.

And the battalion wants a new trench dug. In this.

The officers look at the ground and then they look at the Blackhaugh company, because
everybody knows pitmen can dig anything.

[if war.mate2]Bell's on his feet before the sergeant's finished. "Rum first," he says. "Before, not after. That's the rate for hard ground at any pit in the county." The sergeant stares at him. The officer, who's from Gateshead, starts to laugh.[else]Somebody from the back says rum first, before, not after, that's the rate for hard ground at any pit in the county. The officer, who's from Gateshead, starts to laugh.[/if]

choices.text: Get stuck in. Show them how it's done.
choices.text_after:
You get the rum first. Then you dig, all night, in shifts, the way you'd work a hard seam,
short and steady, nobody racing, the picks ringing on the frozen clay like on stone. By
dawn there's a trench where there wasn't, and the company from Hull that was meant to help
is stood watching with their hands in their armpits.

choices.text: Dig at the pit's pace. No faster than you're paid for.
choices.text_after:
Steady, and not a stroke more. The officer comes by at two in the morning and watches you
a while and says nothing, because it's the right pace, and he can see it is.

v17p_caves.title: Under Arras
v17p_caves.text:
Under Arras there are old chalk quarries, hundreds of years old, and somebody's joined them up
with tunnels into a town under the town. Thousands of you are down here waiting, under electric
light, with water dripping and the air thick with the breath of a brigade.

You can't stop looking at the workings. Galleries cut square, timbered right, the props set
true, drainage in the floor. Whoever did this knew the job. The tunnels have names painted up
at the junctions: Wellington, Auckland, Christchurch. New Zealanders, a sapper tells you. Gold
miners and navvies from the other side of the world.

The attack's in the morning. Up the steps and out.

choices.text: Find a New Zealander and ask about the timbering.
choices.text_after:
He's a big quiet man from a place called Waihi, a gold miner, and he talks timber with you
for an hour in the electric light like two men at the pit gates on a Sunday. When you go
he shakes your hand. "Good luck in the morning, mate," he says. "Keep your head down when
you come out the top. That's where they'll be looking."

choices.text: Write a letter for the pay book.
choices.text_after:
The third one now. They get shorter. This one says: Look after Father. Make him rest. Tell
him the timbering here is the best I ever saw, he'd like it.

v17p_russia.title: News
v17p_russia.text:
The news comes up the line in old newspapers, and it comes all at once. The Tsar of Russia's
gone. Thrown out, by his own soldiers and his own workmen. And the Americans have come in.

Bell reads it out in the dugout by a candle, every word, twice, and then he puts the paper down
and he's grinning like a lad.

"Soldiers and workmen," he says. "Did you hear that? His own soldiers and his own workmen. Ten
million men, and they just said no more." He looks round at all of you. "Imagine that."

A corporal from another company tells him to watch his mouth. Bell doesn't hear him.

choices.text: Drink to it with him, in tea.
choices.text_after:
Two mess tins of cold tea, clinked. "To the soldiers and the workmen," Bell says, and drinks.
You drink. You don't know what you're drinking to, quite. Neither does he.

choices.text: Tell him to be careful who hears him.
choices.text_after:
"I know," he says. "I know." He folds the paper small and puts it in his breast pocket,
over his heart, and pats it. "But it happened. They can't make it not have happened."

v17p_blue_hen.title: The blue hen
v17p_blue_hen.text:
Robson has a letter from his da, and he reads it standing up, and then he sits on the firestep
with it on his knee.

The army's asking the fanciers at home for birds. His da's given them his best. The blue hen
that took first at Bedlington, and the two cocks he's been breeding off her for four years.
They've gone in a basket on the train to the army loft.

"Me da," Robson says. "He'd not sell her for ten pound. He turned down ten pound." He looks at
the letter. "He's given her to the army."

choices.text: Tell him his da's done a fine thing.
choices.text_after:
"Aye," Robson says. "Aye, he has." After a while: "Might be her carries the next one out of
a crater. Might be she knows the way better than the army's birds." He nearly smiles.

choices.text: Say nothing. Sit with him.
choices.text_after:
You sit with him. He folds the letter up small, and smaller. Then he unfolds it and reads it again,
and you know he's reading the bit about the hen.

v17p_horses.title: The horse lines
v17p_horses.text:
Flanders, and the shells come down on the horse lines at night the way they come down on
everything. In the morning there are horses dead in their rows, still tied, and mules lying
in the mud with their legs out stiff, and a smell of singed hair and blood and dung.

[if flag.pit_helped_charlton]Charlton's been up all night with them. He's sat in the mud with a horse's head in his lap, a big grey that can't get up, and he's stroking its face and talking to it, and he won't let the farrier near it yet.[else]Charlton went down to the horse lines as soon as he heard. He's sat in the mud with a big grey's head in his lap, a horse that can't get up, stroking its face, talking to it, and won't let the farrier near.[/if]

choices.text: Sit in the mud with him till the farrier comes.
choices.text_after:
You sit with him. The grey's breath comes slower, warm on your hands. When the farrier
comes Charlton nods, and stands, and turns his back, and you turn with him.

choices.text: Get the farrier. It's kinder.
choices.text_after:
You fetch the farrier and Charlton lets him. He doesn't look at you for two days. On the
third he gives you half his bread without a word, and that's that.

v17p_subways.title: The subways
v17p_subways.text:
They've sent the company to Arras, to help join up the old quarries under the town with
subways out to the front line, so a whole army can wait underground and come up at the
moment. New Zealanders did most of it: gold miners, navvies, men from the other side of the
world, who name their galleries after home. Wellington. Auckland. Christchurch.

Your job's the exits. Short galleries running up from the subways to just under the front-line
trench, stopped a few feet short of the air. On the morning, you'll blow the last few feet, and
the infantry will come up out of the ground.

[if war.mate1 || war.mate2 || war.mate3]Somewhere in these galleries, on the night, the Blackhaugh company will be waiting with the rest. You think of them coming up past you into the daylight.[/if]

choices.text: Do the job right. Every exit true.
choices.text_after:
You set the props in your exit as if your father were coming up through it. Evans laughs at
you for it. Then he goes back and redoes his own.

choices.text: Get it done. There's no time for the fine work.
choices.text_after:
You get it done. It's a good enough job. Pascoe goes along after you, without a word, and
knocks in two more wedges you'd missed.

v17p_gas.title: The canary
v17p_gas.text:
After a blow, the gallery fills with the fumes, and the fumes don't smell of anything, and that's
what kills you. You know that. Every pitman knows that. It's afterdamp. It's the thing that
killed the men at every disaster your father ever told you about.

Pascoe went in too soon to look at the face. Now he's not answering. The canary in the cage at
the gallery mouth is on its back on the floor of the cage.

There's a Proto set hanging in the shaft dugout, the breathing apparatus, the same as the rescue
brigade's at Blackhaugh, that you trained on once on a Sunday in the welfare hall. The rescue
men are coming. They're ten minutes away.

choices.text: Get the Proto on and go in for him.
choices.text_after:
The mask, the nose clip, the bag on your chest, oxygen hissing, and the gallery in the light
of your lamp, quiet, and Pascoe on his face at the end of it like a man asleep. You get him
under the arms and drag him the whole way. He comes round on the shaft floor, grey and
sick, and spends a week coughing, and lives. "My 'andsome," he says, when he can talk. It's
all he says about it.

choices.text: Wait for the rescue men. That's the rule.
choices.text_after:
That's the rule, because men who go in without the training die beside the men they went
for. You know it. You wait the ten minutes. They bring him out on a stretcher, and the
officer kneels by him, and shakes his head. Pascoe, from Camborne, who dug in Cornwall and
Africa and Montana and never once raised his voice.

v17p_clay.title: Blue clay
v17p_clay.text:
After Arras they send the company north, to Flanders, to the galleries under the Messines
ridge. These galleries are older than your time in France. Some were started in 1915. A
hundred feet down, under the wet sand, there's a blue clay, smooth and stiff as cold suet,
and it holds without timber, and it makes no noise when you work it.

It's Mott's clay. London clay, he says, it's the same as the Tube. He lies on his back on his
cross, a plank set at a slant against the face, with a spade on his feet, and kicks out the
clay, a lump at a time, silent, and passes it back, all shift, without a word, as happy as
you've ever seen a man.

The galleries run out under the German ridge. At the ends of them, the charges have been in
place a long time, waiting. Your work is keeping the water out, and listening.

choices.text: Get Mott to teach you to kick.
choices.text_after:
It takes a week, and your back aches in places it never ached at the face. "Like riding a
bike," Mott says. "Backwards. Lying down. Underground." By the end of the week you can do
it, slow. Mott's as proud of you as if he'd taught you to read.
