choices.text: Stay on the pumps. You know pumps.
choices.text_after:
The pumps go day and night, and you nurse them like the engine-man at Blackhaugh nursed his,
by the sound. When one starts to labour you hear it before anyone, and that's worth
something here, where water will drown a gallery in a night.

v17p_messines.title: Messines
v17p_messines.text:
Ten past three in the morning, the seventh of June. You're in a dugout at the top of a shaft,
with the crew, waiting. Nobody's talking. Evans has his hand flat on the timber of the dugout
wall, the way you'd feel a roof.

Nineteen of them. Nineteen mines, under the whole length of the ridge, some of them two years
in the making. Every gallery you've kept dry since May is under that ridge, full to the end.

Then they go.

It isn't a noise. It's the ground being taken out from under you and given back. The dugout
lifts and drops and lifts. Dust comes out of every crack in the timber. Up above, through the
shaft, a light, red, then white, all along the ridge, as if the sun's come up wrong. And then
the noise arrives, after, rolling, like every pit heap in Northumberland falling at once.

They'll say later that they heard it in England.

choices.text: Go up the shaft and look.
choices.text_after:
You climb out into the dawn. The ridge is gone, and where it was there's smoke and dust going
up into the sky, and the guns have started behind you, all of them. Evans comes up beside you
and stands there with his mouth open, and says something in Welsh, and you'll never know
what, and you don't need to.

choices.text: Stay below. You don't want to see it.
choices.text_after:
You stay in the dugout with your back against the timber, feeling it shake as the guns open
up, and you think of the Germans in their galleries, the ones you've heard through the clay
for a month, laughing, coughing, singing. You don't go up. Mott brings you down a tin of tea.

v17p_evans.title: Singing
v17p_evans.text:
Autumn, and the rain, and the company building deep dugouts behind the line in Flanders, forty
feet down in the clay, for headquarters that will move in when they're done and never say thank
you.

At the end of a shift, in the dugout, Evans starts to sing. Not loud. In Welsh, a hymn, slow,
and the dugout goes quiet. His voice fills the timbered dark the way it fills a gallery when he
forgets to whisper, and the drips from the roof keep time.

[if flag.p17_lost_pascoe]Pascoe used to hum along. Nobody does now.[/if][if flag.p17_saved_pascoe]Pascoe, on his bunk, still coughing, hums along under his breath.[/if]

choices.text: Join in. You know the tune from chapel, if not the words.
choices.text_after:
You know the tune. Half of Blackhaugh chapel sings it in English. You come in on the second
verse in English, and Evans doesn't stop, and the two languages go on together in the dark
and it sounds right.

choices.text: Lie on your bunk and listen.
choices.text_after:
You lie and listen with your eyes shut. When he stops, nobody says anything, and Mott, who
has never been to chapel in his life, says "Again," and Evans sings it again.

v17p_father.title: A letter from home
v17p_father.text:
It's in your mother's hand, but the pencil's gone soft and wandering, as if she wrote it on her
knee.

"Dear Son, I do not know how to put this so I will just put it. Your father passed away on
Thursday night. It was his chest. He was in his chair and he said he was tired and he would go
up, and I went up after and he had gone. He did not suffer the doctor says.

The lodge sent the banner and the band and they walked him up to the chapel, the whole row came
out. The manager sent a wreath. Your father would have had something to say about that.

I am all right. Mary is with me. Do not worry about me. Keep yourself safe, that is all I want
now. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Ask for compassionate leave.
choices.text_after: [if war.transferred]Your officer hears you out, and he's sorry, and he means it. There's no leave. There's no leave for anybody this summer.[else]The company officer hears you out in his dugout, and he's sorry, and he means it. There's no leave. Not this summer. Not for anybody.[/if] You knew. You had to ask.

choices.text: Write to your mother tonight.
choices.text_after:
You write it three times. In the end you put that you're proud of him, and that he was the
best man at the face in Blackhaugh, and that you'll be home at Christmas, and you'll go up
to the chapel with her. You don't know if that last part is true. You put it anyway.

l_pit_1917.title: Home on leave
l_pit_1917.text:
[if flag.p17_father_letter]The chair's still by the fire. Nobody sits in it. Your mother's put his pipe on the mantel and his cap on the hook by the door, where they always were, and she doesn't move them.[else]Nobody wrote it to you. Your mother couldn't, and the letter she tried went somewhere in France and never found you. She tells you on the step, before you've put your kit down. Your father's dead since the summer. His chest. The chair's still by the fire.[/if]

You go up to the chapel on the Sunday, the way you said you would[if !flag.p17_father_letter], though you never said it[/if], and stand at the grave with her. It's raw yet. The lodge has put a stone, plain, with his name and the pit and the years. Your mother holds your arm and doesn't cry, and you know she's done her crying, and that she's done it alone.

[if flag.p17_asked_leave]The company officer wrote to her himself, in the summer, to say he was sorry he couldn't send you home. She's kept it with your father's papers.[/if]

The heap's still burning on the skyline. The buzzer still goes. Your sister Mary's at the munitions works in Newcastle now, and comes home yellow, from the powder, and laughs about it.

[if !war.transferred && flag.p17_dug_frost]At the club they've heard, from somebody's letter, that the Blackhaugh lads dug a trench through frozen ground in one night that the Hull company couldn't have dug in a week. By the time it reaches you it's a mile long.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_learned_kick] Some nights you're on Mott's cross again, kicking the clay, and you wake with your legs going.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_saw_messines]You tell nobody about Messines. Then in the club an old pitman says they heard a bang in the night in June, the windows rattled, they thought it was the pit, and you have to go outside.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_saved_pascoe] A letter's come for you from Camborne, from Pascoe's wife. You don't open it till you're on the train.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_lost_pascoe] You write to Camborne, to Pascoe's wife, from your mother's kitchen table. It takes all evening.[/if]

[if war.mate1 && flag.p17_blue_hen]Old Mr Robson's had a letter from the army loft. The blue hen's been flying messages. He keeps the letter in the cree, pinned up over the nesting boxes.[/if][if !war.mate1]The Robsons' cree is empty and the door's off. Somebody's had it for firewood.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.p17_toasted_russia]Bell's father asks if Jim's still talking about Russia. You tell him he's never stopped. "Good," the old man says. "Good lad."[/if][if !war.mate2]On the board for the lodge's dead at the Miners' Hall, Jim Bell's name is spelt right and his age is wrong, and nobody's put it straight. He'd have had something to say.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.p17_sat_with_charlton]Mrs Charlton says George wrote about a grey horse. Just that, a page about a grey horse. She doesn't understand why he'd write a whole page about a horse, and you don't explain.[/if][if !war.mate3]Down at the pit stables somebody's tied a black ribbon on Captain's stall, and nobody's taken it off.[/if]

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v18_french_line.title: The French line
v18_french_line.text:
January, and they've moved you south, a long way south, to take over a stretch of line from
the French. The French have left it the way the French leave things: a stove in every dugout,
empty wine bottles in the sump, a cat that won't come out from under the duckboards, and a
picture of a woman in stockings pasted on the dugout wall. Nobody chips her off this time.

It's quiet. The old hands say it's too quiet, and then laugh at themselves for saying it. On a
still night you can hear a cart on the German side, miles off, with a wheel that wants grease.

And there's no line, not as you'd know it. The new idea is posts: little islands of men in the
chalk, a hundred yards apart, with wire round them, and the big redoubts further back. Between
the posts there's nothing but frost.

The ground's frozen a foot down. The pick rings on it like on a flagstone and jars you to the
teeth.

choices.text: Dig the post deeper while there's time.
choices.text_after:
Three weeks of it, in shifts, through the frost and then the thaw. Chalk under your nails,
chalk in your tea, chalk in the cracks of your hands till they look like your gran's. By
February there's a dugout under the post, twenty steps down, timbered with planks you
stole from the French.

choices.text: Get the French stove going. Make the post fit to live in.
choices.text_after:
It roars like the boiler house and you sit round it in your shirtsleeves for the first time
since October, toasting bread on bayonets, the cat on somebody's knee.[if war.mate2]
Duckworth teaches the cat to sit up for bacon rind and calls it Joffre.[/if]

v18_waiting.title: Waiting
v18_waiting.text:
February. They're coming. Everybody knows it. The prisoners say it, the airmen say it, the
deserters who come over in the night with their hands up say it, and give dates, and the dates
are all different.

You can hear them getting ready. Every night there are carts and lorries on roads you can't
see, and the clink of harness, more of it every week. Their guns register one at a time, a
single shell here, a single shell there, careful, like a man tapping the walls of a house he
means to buy.

At stand-to you look at the grey wire and the grey sky and think about the shed at half past
five on a winter morning, the gas mantles popping on one after another down the long room and
the first looms starting up. You'd give your back teeth for that noise.

[if war.mate2]Duckworth has a sweep going on the date. A franc a go. He's written the days up on a bit of ration box, and men keep coming to look at it as if it'll tell them.[else]A lance-corporal in B Company has a sweep going on the date. A franc a go, the days written up on a bit of ration box, and men keep coming to look at it as if it'll tell them.[/if]

choices.text: Put a franc on the twenty-first.
choices.text_after: [if war.mate2]"The twenty-first," Duckworth says, licking the pencil. "That's a Thursday. Nowt ever happens of a Thursday."[else]He writes your name against the twenty-first. "Thursday," he says. "Nowt ever happens of a Thursday."[/if]

choices.text: Keep your franc. It's asking for it.
choices.text_after:
You keep it. It's a dirty little paper note with a corner torn off, and you fold it into your
pay book, and it's still there months after, gone soft as cloth.

v18_boys.title: Backs to the wall
v18_boys.text:
April. What's left of the battalion is out of the line in a village nobody's heard of, being
made up with drafts. The drafts are boys. After March they've started sending them out at
eighteen and a half, and here they are, boots squeaking, hair cropped by the depot barber,
eating anything they can find.

On parade the colonel reads out an order from the Commander-in-Chief. Every position to be held
to the last man. No retirement. Our backs to the wall. He reads it twice, the second time
slower, because the wind took it the first time.

The boys listen with their mouths open. The old hands look at their boots.

[if war.mate3]Pilling's a corporal now, nineteen, with a face like a shut door. He's been given a lad called Tattersall from Darwen, who follows him round like a dog and stands the way he stands.[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.told_pilling_ease] He's stopped volunteering for everything. He says it's because he's got Tattersall to think about.[/if]

choices.text: Take one of the boys on. Show him how to stay alive.
choices.text_after:
His name's Clegg and he's from Rochdale and he's frightened of everything except what he
ought to be frightened of. You show him how to keep his feet dry, how to tell their shells
from ours by the sound, when to run and when to lie still. He writes it down in a notebook
with a pencil he keeps behind his ear.[if war.mate3] Across the billet Pilling's telling
Tattersall the same things in the same order, in the words you used to him in 1915, and
doesn't know you can hear.[/if]

choices.text: Keep away from the boys. Don't learn their names.
choices.text_after:
You don't learn their names. You learn them anyway, the way you learn the looms in a shed
without meaning to: Clegg, Tattersall, the two Hargreaves who aren't brothers.[if war.mate3]
Pilling sees you not looking at them. "You were like that with me," he says. "At first."[/if]

v18_flu.title: Three-day fever
v18_flu.text:
May, and the weather's turned lovely, and the battalion's going down like skittles.
Three-day fever, the MO calls it. The papers from home call it the Spanish flu. A man goes from
right as rain to shaking in an hour, with a head like a cracked slate and his bones aching from
the inside, and three days later he's up again, wobbly on his legs, and the man next to him is
going down.

You feel it coming on at stand-to: a heat behind the eyes, a cold sweat down the back, the
rifle sling too heavy all at once for your shoulder.

choices.text: Go sick. Lie down before you fall down.
choices.text_after:
Three days in a barn on straw with forty other men, sweating and shivering and coughing in
the dark, an orderly coming round with a bucket of tea and a tin of Number Nines. You dream
about the shed, the racket of it, and wake with your teeth chattering in time to the looms.

choices.text: Stay at duty. Everybody's got it.
choices.text_after:
You stand your sentry with your teeth going and the wire swimming in front of you. At dawn
the sergeant takes one look and sends you down anyway, and you cry all the way to the aid
post. It's the fever, you tell yourself. It's only the fever.

v18_yanks.title: Americans
v18_yanks.text:
Americans, at last. A company of them comes up to learn the line, big and well fed, with
cigarettes in packets of twenty with pictures on, and tinned peaches, and they call everybody
buddy, and they want to see a German so badly it hurts to watch.

Duckworth adopts one, a long lad from somewhere called Ohio who has never seen a mill and wants
to hear all about it. So Duckworth tells him. The shed, the noise, the tackler, the weavers
mee-mawing to each other across the looms because you can't hear yourself speak, the knocker-up
rattling the bedroom window at five. The American listens as if it's the Bible.

choices.text: Trade him your spare cap badge for a tin of peaches.
choices.text_after:
He gives you two tins, and a packet of cigarettes, and shakes your hand as if you'd given
him a medal. You and Duckworth eat the peaches in the bottom of the trench off a jack-knife,
turn and turn about, drinking the juice out of the tin, and they're so sweet that neither
of you can talk.

choices.text: Get Duckworth to tell him a tackler's tale.
choices.text_after:
It's the one about the tackler who took his pigeon to the doctor's. It has never once been
funny, not in the shed, not in the drill hall, not at Loos. The American laughs till he has
to sit down on the firestep and wipe his eyes, and Duckworth looks at him like a man who has
found the one person in the world who understands him.

v18_censor.title: The letters
v18_censor.text:
Every night in the dugout, by a candle in a bottle, you read the platoon's letters. It's an
officer's job. You sit with a blue pencil and a pile of envelopes and read their mothers and
their wives and their girls, and strike out the names of places, and pass the rest, and sign
the corner.

You know these men. You know their mothers. You stood in the Co-op queue behind some of them.

[if war.mate1]Shaw's is on top, in the round careful hand he learned out here.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.best_man] "Dear Edith, I am keeping well.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.best_man] "Dear Mother, I am keeping well.[/if][if war.mate1] We have a new officer, you know who. He is all right. He still has his tea out of the dixie with us when he thinks nobody is looking."[/if][if war.mate3] Pilling's is half a page of nothing, I am well, hope you are well, and at the bottom, crossed out, but you can read it: Mam I am that tired.[/if][if !war.mate1 && !war.mate3]A boy from Bacup has written to his mother that the new officer is a mill lad himself, and the men don't know yet whether to like it.[/if]

choices.text: Pass them all as they are. Sign the corners.
choices.text_after:
You sign them and seal them and they go down the line in the sack with the rest. You don't
strike a word. Let somebody at home know where we are, you think. Let somebody know.

choices.text: Do it by the book. Strike out the places.
choices.text_after:
Blue pencil through every village and every wood. That's the rule, and men have died for
less than a careless letter.[if war.mate3] You leave Pilling's crossed-out line alone.
It isn't a place.[/if]

v18_moving_up.title: Keep your mouth shut
v18_moving_up.text:
July. They move you at night, only at night, and in the day you lie up in woods and barns out
of sight of the aeroplanes. Somebody has pasted a notice inside the cover of every pay book:
KEEP YOUR MOUTH SHUT. The roads at night are packed with guns, limbers, lorries, and tanks under
tarpaulins, all going one way with no lights, the drivers swearing in whispers. The air's thick
with petrol and horse dung and the dust off the road, and it never settles.

Something big. Nobody says it.

The post comes up with the rations, and there's one from your mother.

"Dear Son, just a few lines. Our Jack has had his papers, he went Tuesday to the camp at Prees
Heath. Your father walked him to the station and came home and went straight down the yard and
stopped there. Jack keeps asking me what it is like out there and I said ask your brother. So
he will be writing to you. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write to Jack and tell him what it's like.
choices.text_after:
You write it in a barn by a candle stuck in a bully tin, and it takes two nights. You can't
tell him the worst of it. You tell him enough. Keep your feet dry. Keep your head down. Don't
volunteer. Don't believe a word they tell you at the depot. Write to Mother every week, even
if it's only a field card, because she stands at the door for the post.

choices.text: Write to Jack that it's not so bad.
choices.text_after:
You tell him the grub's all right and the lads are a good crowd and he'll be fine if he keeps
his nose clean. It's all true, near enough. You write it fast so you won't put anything
else, and seal it before you can read it back.

v18_old_ground.title: The old ground
v18_old_ground.text:
The end of August, and you're going forward. Forward, every day. You come over a rise one
morning and you know it before you know why: the slope of the land, the line of a road, a
stump of a tree. It's the old ground. The first of July.

There's our old front line, the trench you went over from, fallen in and grassed over. The wire
in front of it is still there, rusted the colour of a cart axle, with grass growing up through
it. Out in the middle the craters have gone soft and green, with poppies in them, and there are
little crosses everywhere, leaning, dozens of them, and in the long grass the bits of things: a
water bottle, a boot, a helmet with a hole in it, a tin of something with the label gone.

It smells of hay. You'd forgotten how short a walk it was.

choices.text: Walk out to where you think it was.
choices.text_after: You can't find it. Everything's where it was and nothing is. [if flag.brought_discs]You stand where you think you crawled out for the discs, that night, and there's only grass, and a lark going up.[else]You stand in the long grass where you think it was, and a lark goes up, and keeps going up, singing, till you lose it in the sun.[/if]

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the man in front. Keep walking.
choices.text_after:
You keep walking. The column goes down the road into the next valley and the old ground
falls behind, and you don't look back, and you know exactly where it is behind you all day,
the way you know where the fire is in a dark room.

v18_shaw_photo.title: Walking
v18_shaw_photo.text:
Shaw's had a new photograph from home: the lad, stood up, holding on to a chair, in a little
frock, with his hair done in a curl on top. Albert Shaw, a year old and a bit.

"He's walking," Shaw says. "Edith says he's walking. He was walking in June and I never knew
till now."

He keeps it in the oilskin pouch with the old one of Edith from the studio on Market Street,
and on sentry you see him take it out and hold it up to the light of the flares, and put it
back, and take it out again.

choices.text: Tell him you'll get him home to see it.
choices.text_after:
"You will," Shaw says, flat, as if you'd told him the time. He puts the photograph away. Then,
not looking at you: "You'd better."

choices.text: Ask to see it properly.
choices.text_after:
He hands it over as if it's an egg. The lad's got Shaw's ears, sticking out, and Edith's
mouth. On the back, in pencil, in Edith's hand: For his Dad.[if flag.wet_babys_head] "He's
had his rum ration already," Shaw says. "Off the section. He'll be a sergeant."[/if]

b_spring_1.title: The twenty-first of March
b_spring_1.text:
You wake because the ground is moving. It's a little before five and dark, and the whole of
the east is lit up from underneath, end to end, flickering, like the sky over the foundry on a
casting night. Then the noise reaches you, and it isn't guns any more. There are no gaps in it
to count.

Gas with it. The sneezing kind first, that gets in behind the mask and makes you want to tear
it off, then the other kind. Through the eyepieces everything's green and running, and the
rubber stinks, and your own breath roars in your ears.

When it gets light, it doesn't get light. Fog. Thick as a wet blanket on a line. You can't see
the next post, forty yards off. You can hear it.

[if flag.p18_reported]The officer had you all stood to since four. He'd listened.[/if][if flag.p18_reported && flag.dug_deep] [/if][if flag.dug_deep]The dugout you dug in January holds. The timbers groan and drop chalk down your neck, but they hold.[/if][if flag.french_stove]The French stove goes over in the first minute and you stamp out the coals in the dark with your mask on, and the post fills with the stink of hot iron and scorched wool.[/if][if flag.sweep_21 && war.mate2] Duckworth gets his mouth right up against your ear in the din. "You've won," he shouts. "You jammy beggar. You've won the sweep."[/if]

[if war.path == rifleman]Beside you {mate} is counting the shells under his breath, and gives up.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section is spread over two posts you can't see from each other. You have to choose which one you're in.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's on the parapet under a groundsheet, the drums stacked in the recess, and there's nothing in the fog to fire at.[/if][if war.path == signals]The buried cable goes in the first ten minutes. A lamp's no use in fog. You've two pigeons in a basket, and a runner, and the runner's gone.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You've two boxes of Mills bombs and a fog you can't see ten yards into.[/if][if war.path == snipe]A sniper in fog is a man with a rifle. You wrap the telescope in a sock and put it in your pack.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You're with the tunnellers in the battle zone, behind, with charges laid under the bridges and the dumps, and orders to blow them when the infantry are back through.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]Your platoon is in four posts and you can see none of them. The last order from company, an hour old, was to hold the forward zone at all costs. You've a revolver, a whistle and a map of a country you can't see.[/if]

Then, somewhere about twenty to ten, the noise changes. The shells go over, further back. Out in
the fog, something is coming.

choices.text: Get up on the firestep, mask on, and face the fog. ({risk_push})
Go along the post getting the masks on the new lads. ({risk_help})
Get down the dugout steps till it lifts. ({risk_ground})

b_spring_2.title: Out of the fog
b_spring_2.text:
They don't come at the front. They come round. The first you see of them is a man on the
parados, behind you, in a coal-scuttle helmet, throwing something. Then they're everywhere,
little groups of them, quick, with light machine guns and flame-throwers, slipping between
the posts in the fog and leaving the posts for the men behind them.

The post on your left goes quiet. Then the one past it. You hear them go out, one at a time, by
the sound: the rifles, a bomb, shouting, then nothing.

Down the trench a whole platoon comes up out of a deep dugout with their hands up, one man at a
time, blinking in the fog, because a German at the top of the steps has a bomb in his hand and
there's only one way out.[if flag.dug_deep] Twenty steps. You dug every one.[/if]

[if war.path == lewis]The gun fires at shapes. You change drums by feel.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]A runner gets through to you with an order from company to fall back on the redoubt. He's the third they sent.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your men. You keep getting a different number.[/if]

choices.text: Fire at the shapes, front and back. ({risk_push})
Get the post back to the redoubt together, wounded and all. ({risk_help})
Stay down in the bottom of the trench and let it go over. ({risk_ground})

b_spring_3.title: Back
b_spring_3.text:
After that it's back. Five days, six, you lose count. March by night, dig in by day, and they're
on you again by the afternoon. Men go to sleep walking and walk into the man in front. A
quartermaster pours a whole dump of rum into a ditch so the Germans won't get it, and men lie
down in the ditch to drink it.

Behind you the dumps burn. Bully beef, biscuits, a canteen store with tins of pineapple bursting
in the fire, so the whole night smells of burnt sugar and petrol.

And the names on the signposts. You know the names. You're going back over the old Somme ground,
the ground that took a summer and a half to win, and you're giving it up in a day.[if start == pit] Somewhere out there on your left is the great crater at La Boisselle.[/if][if flag.brought_discs]
Somewhere out there is where you crawled for the discs.[/if]

[if war.path == tunnel]Your charge is under a bridge over a canal. You wait in the reeds for the last of the infantry, counting them over. Behind them, the first grey helmets.[/if][if war.path == signals]No wire, no lamps, no pigeons. You carry messages on foot, and half the time the battalion headquarters has moved before you find it.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]You've nineteen men left of thirty-eight, and a map that ran out yesterday.[/if]

choices.text: Stay with the rearguard on the ridge. ({risk_push})
Carry the wounded lad between you, whatever it slows you. ({risk_help})
Lie up in a cellar and let them go by. ({risk_ground})

b_spring_4.title: The embankment
b_spring_4.text:
The end of March, and a railway embankment in front of a town you've never heard of, and
somebody says that's it, no further. You believe it because you can't walk any further.

They've slowed. The word is they stopped at our dumps, and found the white bread and the jam and
the boots and the whisky, and couldn't believe it, and some of them are drunk in the cellars.
They thought we were starving.

New men come up on your right in slouch hats, Australians, who look at you as if you're
something the cat brought in, and give you their water.

At dusk the grey lines come up the slope at you one more time.

[if war.path == lewis]You set the gun up on the rails, on its bipod, between two sleepers, and the barrel's still hot from the morning.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]You walk the embankment behind your men, which is where an officer walks, and the bullets go over the rails with a noise like tearing calico.[/if]

choices.text: Get up on the embankment and fire into them. ({risk_push})
Go along the embankment with ammunition. ({risk_help})
Keep under the embankment and let the guns do it. ({risk_ground})

b_amiens_1.title: The eighth of August
b_amiens_1.text:
Twenty past four in the morning, and fog again. This time it's ours.

There's been no bombardment, no days of it the way there was before the Somme, no warning. The
guns open all at once, every gun at once, and the barrage comes down a couple of hundred yards
in front and starts walking. Out of the fog behind you come the tanks, dozens, more than you
knew there were in France, lurching and roaring, and the air's full of hot oil and petrol and
their exhaust.

The ground's green. That's what you can't get over. Standing corn, uncut, up to your waist, and
poppies in it, and the fog lying on it white.

[if war.path == rifleman]Beside you, {mate} wades through the corn with his rifle held up out of it like a man crossing a river.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section goes forward behind a tank, the way they've practised, in little worms of men, and you've never seen it work before.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You fire from the hip as you go, the way you were never taught, and the corn in front of you jumps.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go behind the company with a reel on your back, and the wire runs out behind you in the wet corn, and holds.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You've bombs in a bucket, and the men you're going for are behind the tanks, not in front of them.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You're out on the flank looking for their machine guns in the edges of the woods.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You go up behind the infantry to search the dugouts they take for charges set to blow. They've been leaving them, lately, under the stairs.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]You blow your whistle and nobody hears it, and they go anyway, because they know what to do now better than you do.[/if]

[if war.stalled]On the left the fog lifts too soon. A tank's burning by a copse, black smoke rolling off it low over the corn, and a machine gun in the copse has the whole company down.[else]Their front line comes up out of the fog, and it's half empty, and the men in it have their hands up before you get there. Their breakfast is still on the fire.[/if]

choices.text: Keep up with the tanks. ({risk_push})
Keep the section together in the fog. ({risk_help})
Get down in the corn till the fog clears. ({risk_ground})

b_amiens_2.title: The wood
b_amiens_2.text:
A wood, with a road running into it, and machine guns at the edge. The tanks go at it and one
stops with smoke coming out of it, and the crew climb out and lie under it.

Most of them give up. They come out of the dugouts in crowds, with their hands up and their kit
packed, as if they'd been waiting. An officer asks you in English for a receipt for his field
glasses. But the machine-gunners at the edge of the wood are the other sort, the old sort, and
they fight till they're dead.

choices.text: Go in at the guns from the side. ({risk_push})
Get the tank crew back out of the open. ({risk_help})
Get down behind the bank and fire at the wood's edge. ({risk_ground})

b_amiens_3.title: Open country
b_amiens_3.text:
By the afternoon you're further than anybody has been since 1914. Seven miles, somebody says.
There are no trenches here. There are fields and hedges and a farmhouse with the washing still
on the line, and cavalry go past you at a trot, real cavalry, through the oats.

Their field guns are firing over open sights from behind a hedge, at the tanks, and at you.
You dig in at dusk in a field of oats, scraping a hole with your entrenching tool, and the
earth's soft and brown and smells of rain. Like the allotment.

choices.text: Go for the guns behind the hedge. ({risk_push})
Dig the hole for two. Bring the wounded man in. ({risk_help})
Dig in deep and keep down. ({risk_ground})

b_oct_1.title: The river
b_oct_1.text:
A river, in October, in the dark. The sappers have been out all night putting footbridges over
it, planks on floats, and you go over in single file with the water black and quick under the
boards and the smell of it cold and green, like [if start == pit]the burn below the pit heap[/if][if start != pit]the canal under the mill[/if] in winter.

Gas in the valley, lying in the low places. Fog over it.

[if war.path == rifleman]Behind you, {mate} has hold of your pack strap. On the bridge his boot goes through between two planks and you haul him up by the collar.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your section onto the bridge, and off.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's on your shoulder. If you go in, you'll go straight to the bottom with it.[/if][if war.path == signals]The wire goes over the river with you, pegged to the floats.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You go over with the bombs in a sandbag held up against your chest.[/if][if war.path == snipe]On the far bank, the railway embankment. You know they're on it. You look for the glint.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You're on the bridges themselves, up to your waist in it, lashing the floats while they cross.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]Your platoon's first over. You go first on the bridge, which is what they pay you for.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The far bank opens up before half of you are over. A bridge goes, men and all, and the river takes them.[else]On the far bank there's an embankment, and a hedge, and the barrage coming down on both.[/if]

choices.text: Get over and up the embankment. ({risk_push})
Stop on the bank and pull men out of the water. ({risk_help})
Get down under the near bank. ({risk_ground})

b_oct_2.title: The village
b_oct_2.text:
A village, still standing, with roofs on, and people in it.

They come up out of the cellars when the firing's moved on: old men, women, children with faces
the colour of candles. Four years they've been behind the German lines. An old woman in a black
shawl kisses you on both cheeks and smells of onions and cellars, and pushes a cup into your
hands. It's coffee made of roasted barley, and it's the best thing you've ever tasted.

There's a machine gun in the church tower. It's firing down the street.

choices.text: Go for the church through the gardens. ({risk_push})
Get the people back down into the cellars. ({risk_help})
Get into a doorway and fire at the tower. ({risk_ground})

b_oct_3.title: The last of it
b_oct_3.text:
They come back once more, at evening, out of an orchard, and it's half-hearted, and it's still
enough to kill men. Apples on the ground everywhere, gone soft, and wasps in them, and the smell
of cider in the dusk.

After that, quiet. Just the guns, further off every day.

There's a rumour, the way there's always a rumour. Only this time the officers are saying it too.

choices.text: Go out into the orchard after them. ({risk_push})
Get the wounded in out of the orchard. ({risk_help})
Keep down behind the wall. ({risk_ground})

e_armistice_mill.title: The Armistice
e_armistice_mill.text:
{ending_line}

It comes up in the morning with the rations, on a message form, in the adjutant's hand.
Hostilities will cease at 1100 hours today. Nobody believes it. Then everybody does, all at
once, and nobody knows what to do with their hands.

The guns go on to the last minute. A battery behind you fires off everything it has, as if it's
somebody's birthday, and at a minute to eleven a German machine gun across the valley fires a
whole belt into the sky. Then a man stands up beside it, takes his helmet off, bows, and walks
away.

Then eleven. It goes so quiet you can hear a wood pigeon, and a cart a long way off, and the man
next to you breathing.

[if war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Shaw sits down in the road and gets the photograph out, and doesn't put it away again all day.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.promised_shaw] "Well," he says. "You got me home, then." It isn't true yet. You let him have it.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.promised_shaw]You told Shaw you'd get him home to see the lad walk. You think of Edith, and the little fist round your finger.[/if][if war.mate2] Duckworth starts to tell a joke and can't get to the end of it.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.tackler_tale] "There's a lad in Ohio," he says, "telling the one about the pigeon. That's what I did in the war."[/if][if !war.mate2 && flag.gave_fags] You light a Woodbine and think of Duckworth, who owed you one, and paid up.[/if][if war.mate3] Pilling stands in the road and doesn't know what to do, and in the end he takes his tin hat off and throws it as far as he can into a field of turnips.[/if][if !war.mate3] You think of Walter Pilling, sixteen at Loos, who'd have been twenty in March.[/if]

You don't get home till the spring. The letters come. The influenza's in the street, the bad
sort this time; Mrs Ormerod's two girls; the schools shut. On the day, your mother says, every
mill buzzer in the town went off at eleven, all at once, and the chapel bells after, and your
father stood in the yard and wouldn't come in for an hour.[if flag.had_the_flu] You've had it,
out here, and got up again. You read that part twice.[/if]

[if flag.told_jack_truth]Our Jack never went out. He was at Prees Heath when it finished. He writes that he read your letter till it fell to bits, and he's glad, and he's sorry, and he doesn't know which.[/if][if flag.told_jack_easy]Our Jack never went out. He was at Prees Heath when it finished, and he writes that he's fed up, he's missed it, it isn't fair. You put the letter in the stove.[/if][if !flag.told_jack_truth && !flag.told_jack_easy]Our Jack never went out. He was at the camp when it finished. Your mother says it three times in one letter, as if she's counting.[/if][if flag.walked_old_ground] Some nights you're back in the long grass on the old ground, looking for the place.[/if][if flag.peaches] You can't look at a tin of peaches.[/if][if flag.took_a_lad] Clegg writes from Rochdale, once, to say he's back at the dye works and thank you.[/if]

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}, and you went out of the shed a boy.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

v18p_ashington.title: The new posts
v18p_ashington.text:
January, and the battalion's moved south into a quiet stretch the French have handed over.
The new idea is posts, little islands of men in the chalk a hundred yards apart, with
nothing between them but frost.

And new men. A Tyneside battalion has been broken up, there aren't enough men to go round any
more, and sixty of them come into the company in one night. Pitmen, most of them, from
Ashington and Bedlington and Choppington, with the same blue marks on their foreheads as you,
and they stand in the snow with their kit at their feet and won't look at anybody, because
their battalion's gone, and their pals with it.

The ground in the posts is frozen. The officer wants them deepened.

choices.text: Get the Ashington men on the picks with you. Dig the post deep.
choices.text_after:
You put them on the picks beside the Blackhaugh lads and by the end of the first shift
they're talking, about seams, about managers, about whose pit has the worst roof. By
February there's a dugout under the post, twenty steps down, timbered the way you'd timber
at home, and the Ashington men did half of it.

choices.text: Leave them be. Let them grieve their own battalion.
choices.text_after:
You leave them be. They keep to themselves in the next post, and sing at night, low, their
own songs, and after a week one of them comes over for a light and stays an hour.

v18p_bell_corporal.title: Lance-Corporal Bell
v18p_bell_corporal.text:
They've given Bell a stripe. Jim Bell, who argued with every sergeant in France, who read the
Herald in the beer vat, who drank to the Russians. A lance-corporal.

"They've run out of men," he says. "That's all it is. They've run clean out." But he's sewn it
on straight, you notice, and he's the first up at stand-to now, and he goes round the new lads
at night making sure their feet are dry, and he gives them his own socks when theirs are wet.

"Somebody has to look after them," he says, when he sees you watching. "God knows nobody else
will."

choices.text: Call him Corporal, and salute.
choices.text_after:
He tells you exactly where to put your salute, in words the Herald wouldn't print. Then he
laughs, properly, the first time since the spring. "Corporal," he says, trying it. "Me da'll
never live it down."

choices.text: Help him with the new lads. Say nothing about the stripe.
choices.text_after:
You do the feet with him, the two of you going along the posts in the dark with a tin of
whale oil and a sack of dry socks. He talks the whole time, about the war, about the owners,
about after. You let him. Somebody has to listen.

v18p_combout.title: The comb-out
v18p_combout.text:
April, and after March the battalion is half new faces. Some of the faces you know. The army's
combed out the pits for men, the young starred men they kept back as war work, and here they
are in a draft from the depot: lads you went to school with, who stayed at the face when you
went, in khaki now, with new boots.

Joe Todd from the bottom row, who was a shot-firer, comes up to you at the cookhouse. He went
down the pit the same week as you. He stayed. He looks at you the way you'd look at a man who'd
come up out of a fall.

"They said you'd be here," he says. "I didn't think you would be. Still."

choices.text: Show him the ropes. All of it.
choices.text_after:
You show him where to stand, when to duck, how to keep his feet, the sound of the shells
that matter. He listens the way he'd listen to a deputy. At the end of it he says, "You've
changed." You don't know what to say to that, so you say nowt.

choices.text: Leave him to the sergeant. He stayed home.
choices.text_after:
You leave him to it. It isn't fair, and you know it isn't. He didn't choose to be starred any
more than you chose to be eighteen. But you can't make yourself, not yet.

v18p_robson.title: After
v18p_robson.text:
A warm evening behind the line, the two of you sat on a bank with your backs to a hedge,
and swallows going over. Robson's quiet, the way he always is. Then he says the longest thing
you've ever heard him say.

"I'm not going back down. After. If there's an after. I've been under the ground in France
four year one way and another, and I've been under it at home since I was twelve, and I'm not
going back down." He's pulling at the grass. "Me da's got the birds. I'll get a bit of a
smallholding. Hens. Birds. I'll work in the light."

He looks at you. "What about you?"

choices.text: Tell him you're not going back down either.
choices.text_after:
"Good," Robson says. "Good." He goes back to pulling at the grass. After a while: "You'll
have to come and help with the hens, then. You're no use for owt else." It's the nearest
he's ever come to a joke.

choices.text: Tell him you'll go back. It's what you know.
choices.text_after:
He nods. He doesn't argue. "Aye," he says. "Your da did." After a while he says, "I'll keep
you a pair of birds. You can fly them from the pit gates," and that's the end of it.

v18p_charlton.title: The farmer
v18p_charlton.text:
Going forward through villages the Germans have held since 1914, and in one of them an old
farmer standing in his yard with nothing in it. No cow. No pig. No horse. The Germans took the
lot. He's stood looking at the empty stalls.

Charlton's with the transport, coming up the road behind the battalion, and he sees the old
man, and stops. He's got a spare mule, lame in the off fore, that the transport officer's
marked down to be shot.

choices.text: Help Charlton leave the mule in the old man's yard.
choices.text_after:
Charlton leads her in and ties her in an empty stall and shows the old man the bad foot,
in signs, and how to poultice it, and the old man takes hold of Charlton's face in both his
hands and kisses him on the forehead. The transport officer is told she died. Charlton
whistles all the way to the next village.

choices.text: Tell him he'll be on a charge. Keep going.
choices.text_after:
Charlton keeps going. He looks back once at the old man in his empty yard, and the mule
limps along behind the limber, and that night the farrier shoots her, and Charlton doesn't
eat.

v18p_dugouts.title: Dugouts
v18p_dugouts.text:
January, and the mining war's over, near enough. Nobody's digging under anybody's line now.
The company's put to dugouts for headquarters, and subways, and bridges, and once, for a
week, a bath-house for a general.

[if !flag.p17_lost_pascoe]Pascoe says it's the first time in thirty year he's dug a hole that nobody wanted to blow up.[/if][if flag.p17_lost_pascoe]Evans says it's a waste of good miners. He says it every day, the way Pascoe used to say his prayers.[/if] Mott says he'd sooner have the Tube.

And the officer wants the dugout under the forward post sunk deep, in case they come in the
spring.

choices.text: Sink it deep. Twenty steps at least.
choices.text_after:
Twenty steps, timbered like a shaft, the way your father taught you to set a prop. You put
the last frame in on the first of February and stand at the bottom looking up at the square
of grey sky, and think, that'll hold anything.

choices.text: Dig it to the book and no more.
choices.text_after:
To the book, and the book's not bad. You finish a week early and get three days in a barn
with straw and a stove, and Mott teaches the crew a card game from the docks that nobody
else in France has heard of.

v18p_mott.title: Mott
v18p_mott.text:
A shell on the dump at the shaft head, and Mott's in the way of it. Not bad. His leg, below the
knee, a clean one. A Blighty one. He's sat on the duckboards grinning white while you put the
dressing on.

"Blighty," he says. "Blighty, Geordie. I'll be on the Tube by Sunday." Then he stops grinning
and grips your sleeve. "You look after Evans. He's soft, under all that singing."

choices.text: Carry him down to the aid post yourself.
choices.text_after:
Two miles on your back, him talking the whole way, about the Tube, about his mum's pie shop
in Bermondsey, about a girl. At the aid post he shakes your hand like a man at a station.
"Come and see the Tube," he says. "I'll show you every yard of it."

choices.text: Get him onto a stretcher and get back to the shaft.
choices.text_after:
The bearers take him. He waves from the stretcher like a lad on a charabanc. You go back
down, and Evans is at the face on his own, not singing, and you take Mott's place beside
him.

v18p_traps.title: Traps
v18p_traps.text:
Going forward, and the Germans have left their dugouts full of presents. A helmet on a table
with a wire under it. A loose duckboard on the stairs. A stove that will go up when it's lit.
And worse: charges buried under crossroads and bridges with clocks on them, acid eating
through a copper wire, set to go days after the last German has gone.

The infantry won't go into a dugout now till the tunnellers have been through it. So you go
first. Down the steps with a candle, slow, looking at everything, the way you'd go into an old
working that's been shut up for years, feeling for the wire before you see it.

At the bottom of this one there's a gramophone on a box, and a record on it, and the handle
wound.

choices.text: Leave it. Trace the wire first, however long it takes.
choices.text_after:
An hour on your knees with the candle. There's a wire, fine as cotton, from under the
gramophone down into the floor, to enough explosive to bring down the dugout and everybody
in it. You cut it. Then, because nobody's looking, you play the record. It's a waltz, and
it's scratched, and it goes round and round in the dugout under the ground.

choices.text: Get out and call up the officer. It's his decision.
choices.text_after:
The officer comes, and looks, and has the whole dugout blown in with a charge from the top,
gramophone and all. Probably the right thing. You hear the record in your head for a week,
a tune you never heard.

v18p_waiting.title: The ground
v18p_waiting.text:
February. They're coming. Everybody knows it. The deserters say it, the airmen say it.

[if war.transferred]Down in your dugout you lie with your ear to the floor at night, the way you'd listen to a roof, and the ground's alive with it. Not picks: wheels, thousands of them, and hooves, and the deep thud of guns being dug in, miles off, coming through the chalk like through a drum.[/if][if !war.transferred && war.mate1]Robson's on his knees on the floor of the post with his ear to the chalk, the way he was the first night in 1915. He stays there a long time. "Wheels," he says. "Thousands. And guns, being dug in. It's coming through the ground like a drum."[/if][if !war.transferred && !war.mate1]You put your ear to the floor of the post at night, the way Robson did the first night in 1915. Wheels, thousands of them, and the thud of guns being dug in, miles off, coming through the chalk like through a drum.[/if]

choices.text: Tell the officer what the ground's saying.
choices.text_after:
He listens. He writes it down. "Everybody's hearing it," he says. "Everybody knows." He looks
at you. "Still. Thank you. [if flag.pit_reported]You're the one who heard them in 1915, aren't you? Somebody told me.[/if][if !flag.pit_reported]Pitmen hear things.[/if]"

choices.text: Lie and listen. There's nothing anybody can do.
choices.text_after:
You lie and listen till you can't tell it from your own heart. Then you sleep, and dream of
the cage going down, and the roof talking, and your father saying it's only the roof.

v18p_letter.title: A letter from home
v18p_letter.text:
"Dear Son, just a few lines. I am keeping well. Mary is still at the works in Newcastle and
comes home yellow and says the girls call each other canaries and laugh about it. I do not
think it is funny.

They have combed the pit again and took the young starred men. The manager has took women on
at bank, on the screens, where your father was. I went to look. I could not stop.

[if war.transferred]Your money still comes. I have put most of it in the Store. You will want something when you come home, for a start, whatever you do.[/if][if !war.transferred]Mrs Todd says her Joe is with you now, and she is glad of it, she says it is the only thing that lets her sleep.[/if]

I sit in your father's chair now of a night. I could not, at first. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back. Tell her about after.
choices.text_after: You tell her about after: [if flag.p18_not_going_down]that you'll not go back down, that you'll find something in the light, that Tommy Robson's going to keep hens and you'll help[/if][if flag.p18_going_down]that you'll go back down, to the face, your father's seam[/if][if !flag.p18_not_going_down && !flag.p18_going_down]that you don't know yet, that you'll know when you're home, that there'll be time[/if]. You tell her to keep sitting in the chair.

choices.text: Keep it with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket with the rest. Your father's letter's in there too, the one
he never wrote, the one you keep expecting.

v18p_crater.title: The Glory Hole
v18p_crater.text:
The end of August, going forward, and the road goes past La Boisselle. Past the crater.

It's grassed over at the edges now. Poppies on the lip. A hundred yards across, and the white
chalk still showing on the steep sides where nothing will grow, and at the bottom a pool of
green water. There are crosses round the rim, little wooden ones, and some have names you know.

[if war.transferred]You made it. Two years ago, with Evans and Pascoe and Mott, tin by tin, in your socks, in the dark.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_chalked_tin] Somewhere in all this, your name in chalk on a syrup tin.[/if][if !war.transferred]You stood there that morning and watched it go up, higher than the pit heap, higher than anything. You were in it all that afternoon.[/if][if !war.transferred && flag.p16_birds] It's where the bird went up from, round once, round twice, and west.[/if]

choices.text: Fall out for a minute. Walk round the rim.
choices.text_after: The sergeant lets you. You walk round the lip slowly, reading the crosses. [if !war.mate1]You look for Robson's name, and don't know if you want to find it.[/if][if war.mate1]Robson walks round with you, and doesn't say anything, and stops at one cross, and stays there till the sergeant shouts.[/if] At the far side there's a lark going up, and you stand and listen to it, and then you go after the column.

choices.text: Keep marching. Don't look.
choices.text_after:
You keep your eyes on the pack in front. You can feel it there on your left all the way
past, the way you can feel a pit shaft in the dark without seeing it.

e_armistice_pit.title: The Armistice
e_armistice_pit.text:
{ending_line}

It comes up in the morning on a message form. Hostilities will cease at 1100 hours today.
Nobody believes it, and then everybody does.

The guns go on to the last minute. Then eleven. And then a quiet like the quiet at the face
when the cutter stops and the dust settles, a quiet you can hear, and in it, somebody's
laughing, and somebody's crying, and a wood pigeon.

[if war.transferred]Evans sings, in Welsh, and this time nobody tells him to whisper.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p18_carried_mott] Mott's on the Tube by now. He wrote you twice, from Bermondsey, on pie-shop paper.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_saved_pascoe] Pascoe's somewhere behind the line, coughing. He'll go home to Camborne.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_lost_pascoe] You think of Pascoe, who never raised his voice.[/if]

[if war.mate1]Robson sits down at the roadside and takes off his helmet and lifts his face to the sky, and keeps it there.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.p18_not_going_down] "Hens," he says, to nobody. "Birds. In the light."[/if][if !war.mate1]Robson isn't here to hear it. He'd have had his ear to the ground.[/if][if war.mate2] Lance-Corporal Bell gets the section in a ring and makes a speech, about the soldiers and the workmen, about after, about the owners, and for once nobody tells him to shut his mouth.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.p18_ribbed_bell] He still won't let you salute him.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.p18_helped_bell] After, he tells you he'd never have managed the feet on his own, and it's the only time he ever thanks anybody for anything.[/if][if !war.mate2] Jim Bell would have had something to say about it, and it would have taken all afternoon.[/if][if war.mate3] Charlton's down with the transport, and you find him in the horse lines with his face against a mule's neck.[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.p18_gave_mule] "There's a mule in a French farmer's yard," he says, "that's never going to hear a gun again."[/if][if !war.mate3] Somewhere at home there's a black ribbon on a pony's stall.[/if]

[if !war.transferred && flag.p18_showed_todd]Joe Todd from the bottom row finds you in the road and shakes your hand, and doesn't say why, and doesn't need to.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p18_traced_wire]Some nights for years you'll hear a scratched waltz going round under the ground.[/if][if flag.p18_walked_crater] Some nights you're on the rim of the crater again, reading the crosses.[/if]

You don't get home till the spring. When you do, the heap's still burning on the skyline, and at
eleven on the day, your mother says, the pit buzzer went and didn't stop, five minutes of it, and
the whole village came out into the rows, and nobody knew what to do, so they went to chapel.

Your father's chair is by the fire. Your mother sits in it now.[if flag.p18_wrote_after] Your letter about after is on the mantel, behind the tea caddy, where his pay notes used to go.[/if]

[if flag.p18_not_going_down]You don't go back down. You told Robson you wouldn't, and you don't. You stand at the pit gates on the first Monday, and watch the cage go, and walk away up the road in the light.[/if][if flag.p18_going_down]On the first Monday you go back down, to your father's seam. The cage drops and the dark comes up round you, still dark, the dark that doesn't move, and you're surprised how glad you are of it.[/if][if !flag.p18_not_going_down && !flag.p18_going_down]On the first Monday you walk to the pit gates and stand there. The cage is winding. You don't know yet. You stand there a long time.[/if]

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

x_fallen_webb.title: Arthur Webb
x_fallen_webb.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Webb's beside you, and then he's sitting in the bottom of the trench with his back against the wall, upright, the way he sat at his desk, and his hand goes to his inside pocket, to the notebook, and stays there.

"Put it down," he says. "The time. Somebody put the time down." And then he doesn't say anything else.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Arthur Webb. Killed {fallen_where}.

You sat next to him for three years. You knew the sound of his pen. You'd know it anywhere.[/if][if flag.city_diary_warned] You told him diaries were forbidden. You hope somebody of ours finds the notebook first.[/if][if flag.city_diary_kept] Somewhere there's a little black notebook with every shell in it, and the totals.[/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Webb yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
You write it in your best office hand. You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know.
You put that he kept the books to the end, which is true.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_fenton.title: Percy Fenton
x_fallen_fenton.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Fenton's running, the way he always runs, as if there's a ball in front of him, and then he goes down, sliding, the way a centre-forward goes down in a tackle on a wet pitch, and lies there, and you wait for him to get up, because he always gets up.

He doesn't get up.[else]Somebody tells you at the water cart. Percy Fenton. Killed {fallen_where}.

You think of him on the wing at Walthamstow on a Saturday, in the mud, with the whole office shouting.[/if][if flag.city_played] You played behind him once, against the pitmen, in a stubble field in France.[/if]

choices.text: Write to his father. Tell him about the match.
choices.text_after:
You tell him about the stubble field and the rifles for goalposts, and both goals. He never
missed a Saturday. He'll want every kick.

choices.text: Leave it. You'd never get him right.

x_fallen_marsh.title: Leonard Marsh
x_fallen_marsh.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Marsh goes down on his hands and knees, and his spectacles come off, and he feels about in the mud for them, quite calm, the way he'd feel for them on the bedside table in the morning.

You find them and put them in his hand. He holds them. He doesn't put them on. "It's all right," he says. "I can see."[else]You hear it from a stretcher-bearer who knew him from chapel. Leonard Marsh. Killed {fallen_where}.

He learned the eye chart by heart, the night before the recruiting office, the whole thing, so they'd let him come.[/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Marsh yourself.
choices.text_after:
You tell her he taught the section the books of the Bible, in order, on sentry, to keep awake.
You tell her he was never frightened of anything except being sent home.

choices.text: Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

x_fallen_cottle.title: Will Cottle
x_fallen_cottle.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Cottle goes down on one knee, slow, the way he'd kneel to look at a ewe's foot, and then he's on his side in the grass.

"Fly," he says. Just that. The dog's name. And then he's looking past you up at the sky, the way he'd look for weather from the top of the moor, and he doesn't stop looking.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Will Cottle. Killed {fallen_where}.

You stand there with the bread under your arm. You knew him before you could walk. You learned to whistle a dog from his father.[/if]

At home there's a black and white dog lying by a gate, looking up the lane.

choices.text: Write to old Mr Cottle yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know. You put that the last thing he said was
the dog's name. His father will want that.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_pearce.title: Dan Pearce
x_fallen_pearce.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Pearce was always quick. He's quick now: up and then down, all at once, flat in the grass with his face turned to you, surprised, as if somebody had come on him with a gun when he'd thought the keeper was miles off.

"Well," he says. "They've had me, then." And that's Dan Pearce.[else]Somebody tells you at the water cart. Dan Pearce. Killed {fallen_where}.

You think of him going through the long grass the first night like water. Nobody ever caught Dan Pearce. Fifteen years the keeper tried.[/if][if flag.farm_shared_pearce] Fourteen days on the wheel together, side by side, and he never once stopped talking.[/if]

choices.text: Write to his mother. Tell her about the hare in the wire.
choices.text_after:
You tell her about the hare in the wire the first night, and the partridges, and the wheel.
You tell her he was the best man in the battalion at being where he wasn't supposed to be.
She'll laugh. Then she won't.

choices.text: Leave it. You'd never get him right.

x_fallen_yeo.title: Bert Yeo
x_fallen_yeo.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Bert's beside you, and then he's sat down, and he's holding his hands in front of him, curled, the way they curled round the sally of the tenor bell, as if he's waiting for the rope to come down to him.

You hold on to him. He says something you can't hear for the noise. You think it might be a hymn.[else]You hear it from a stretcher-bearer who knew him. Bert Yeo. Killed {fallen_where}.

He was eighteen. He'd rung the tenor at Dunsworthy since he was twelve.[/if][if flag.farm_bert_stopped] He was going to ring the whole peal, after. When you got home.[/if][if flag.farm_bert_rang] He rang one bell in France, once, and you took the blame for it.[/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Yeo. Tell her about the bell.
choices.text_after:
You tell her about the French church with half a roof, and Bert with the rope in his hands.
You don't know if it's the right thing to tell a mother. It's the true thing.

choices.text: Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

x_fallen_shaw.title: Albert Shaw
x_fallen_shaw.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}, three yards from you. Shaw sits down the way a man sits on a step at the end of a shift, and puts his hand flat on his chest, and looks at it.

"Oh, hell," he says. "Oh, me mam."

You get to him. You get your field dressing out with your teeth. There's nowhere to put it that would be any use. He's looking past you at something, and then he isn't looking at anything.

Somebody pulls you off him. You've got him to the elbows and it's going cold already, sticky, and it smells like the back of the butcher's on Bury Road.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Shaw. Killed {fallen_where}. The man who tells you says it quickly, to get it said, and goes.

You sit on the firestep with the bread under your arm.[if flag.wrote_for_shaw] His mother's last letter from him was in your handwriting. The next one will be in an officer's, and she'll know the difference.[/if][/if]

His mother lives two doors up from yours.

choices.text: Write to Mrs Shaw yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
It takes you till stand-to. You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know. You put
that he talked about her, which is true.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_duckworth.title: Harry Duckworth
x_fallen_duckworth.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Duckworth's halfway through a joke, the one about the tackler and the parson's wife, and then he isn't. There's no sound to it that you can pick out from all the other noise. He's just down, face first, with his rifle under him, and when you turn him over the joke's still on his face.

You stay with him longer than you should. Somebody has to kick your boot.[else]Somebody tells you at the water cart. Duckworth. Killed {fallen_where}.

"He wouldn't have known a thing," they say. You hope it's true. You hope it hard, like a prayer, standing there with the water tins.[/if]

choices.text: Write to his mam and dad yourself.
choices.text_after:
You tell them about the Woodbines on the first night, and the jokes, all of them, even the
one about the parson's wife, because his dad will laugh at that one and his mam will pretend
she didn't hear.

choices.text: Leave it. You wouldn't know what to put.

x_fallen_pilling.title: Walter Pilling
x_fallen_pilling.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Pilling's next to you and then he's in the bottom of the trench, curled up small, calling for his mam in a voice you've not heard out of him since he was nine and fell off the canal wall.

You hold his hand. It's all there is. His grip goes tight, tighter, like a child's at the fair when the crowd closes in, and then it doesn't.[else]The post comes up and there's a letter for Pilling, from his mam, in her careful round hand. The corporal gives it to you because you're from the same street. Pilling was killed {fallen_where} two days since.

You don't open it. You put it inside your tunic, and you can feel it there all night, square and stiff against your chest.[/if]

[if war.stage == 1]He was sixteen. He'd have been seventeen in March.[else]He was eighteen. He'd been telling everybody since March.[/if][if flag.told_on_pilling] You tried, you tell yourself. You tried.[/if][if flag.told_pilling_ease] You told him to ease off. He told you somebody was counting.[/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Pilling. Tell her about the birthday cakes.
Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

x_wound_light.title: Hit
x_wound_light.text:
Hit {wound_where}.

It's like a cricket bat across the shoulder, hard, and you're sat down in the muck before you
know why. Then the heat comes, and the wet. There's a hole in your sleeve you could put your
thumb in.

"You lucky sod," somebody says, crouching over you. "That's not even a Blighty one."

The stretcher-bearers have worse to carry. You walk, down the communication trench with your
arm held against you like a parcel, to the aid post in a cellar. It smells of iodine and
paraffin and blood gone cold. The doctor looks for four seconds. Iodine that makes you shout,
a dressing, a label tied to your tunic button. A week behind the lines, maybe two. Then back.

choices.text: Go down the line.

x_wound_severe.title: A Blighty one
x_wound_severe.text:
Hit {wound_where}.

You don't remember the first part. You remember a stretcher, the bearers swearing at the mud,
the sky going past in strips between the trench walls. Morphia at the aid post, warm and heavy,
like falling asleep in front of the fire. A tent at the clearing station, a long row of you,
chloroform and wet canvas. A train with the windows painted over. A boat. The Channel's rough
and the man in the cot above you is sick all the way across, and you don't care, because
somebody said Southampton.

A hospital in England. Clean sheets that crackle. A nurse from Leeds who calls everybody "my
lad" and smells of soap. Your mother comes on the train with a cake in a tin and sits by the
bed for two hours not knowing what to say, and it's the best two hours of the war.

In a couple of months the wound will close, and they'll send you back.

choices.text: Get well. Then go back.

x_fallen.title: {fallen_name}
x_fallen.text:
{fallen_name} is killed {fallen_where}.

[if war.fallen_present]You're near enough to see it, and far enough that there's nothing to do. Afterwards you can never get the order right in your head: the noise, or him going down, or the noise again.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark, from a man who says it quickly to get it said.[/if]

You knew him before any of this. You knew his mother's kitchen.

choices.text: Go on.

x_fallen_robson.title: Tommy Robson
x_fallen_robson.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Robson's beside you and then he's on his knees, and then he's sat back on his heels, the way he'd sit at the face to eat his bait, looking at his hands.

He doesn't say anything. He never did. He looks at you as if he's going to, and then he puts his head down on his chest as if he's tired, and that's all.

You kneel with him till somebody pulls you up. His hands are black with the earth, the way they always were, and you can't stop looking at them.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion. Robson. Killed {fallen_where}.[/if][if !war.transferred]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Robson. Killed {fallen_where}.[/if]

You were marras at the face two years. You knew where he'd be in the dark by the sound of his pick. [if !war.transferred]You stand there with the bread under your arm and listen for it.[/if][if war.transferred]You'll listen for it underground tonight, and every night.[/if][/if]

At the end of the rows his da will be out at the cree in the morning, letting the birds go.

choices.text: Write to his da yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know. You put what he said about the army's
pigeons, that they were nowt special, because his da will know it's true.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_bell.title: Jim Bell
x_fallen_bell.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Bell's talking, he's always talking, telling you what the owners will be making out of this one, and then he stops in the middle of a word, and sits down hard, surprised, with his mouth open on the rest of it.

"Hang on," he says. "Hang on, man." And that's the last thing Jim Bell ever says, and he'd have hated it, that it was nothing.[else][if war.transferred]A battalion runner tells you, not stopping. Jim Bell. Killed {fallen_where}.[/if][if !war.transferred]Somebody tells you at the water cart. Jim Bell. Killed {fallen_where}.[/if]

[if !war.transferred]It's quiet in the bay without him. You never knew how much of the noise was his.[/if][if war.transferred]You'd gone under. You weren't there to hear the last of what he had to say.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_told_evans] Evans says he'll still buy him that pint, wherever he's gone. He says it in Welsh first, and then in English.[/if][/if][if flag.told_bell_shut] You told him not here, not now. He asked you when, and you hadn't an answer.[/if][if flag.stood_with_bell] You think of him in the beer vat with the Herald held up out of the water, grinning.[/if]

choices.text: Write to his father at the lodge.
choices.text_after:
You tell his father that Jim argued with everybody, sergeants and officers and the Germans
across the wire, and that he was right more often than they liked. His father will read
that out at the Miners' Hall. You know he will.

choices.text: Leave it. You'd never get it right.

x_fallen_charlton.title: George Charlton
x_fallen_charlton.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Charlton goes down and curls up small on his side, and calls out, not for his mam, for the pony, for Captain, the way he'd call him in the dark of the stables to come up.

You hold on to him. He's not frightened, that's the strange thing. He's talking to the pony, low, steady, the way he talked to the mules, and he's still doing it when he goes.[/if][if !war.fallen_present && flag.pit_helped_charlton && !war.transferred]The transport sergeant comes up himself to tell you, which nobody expected. George Charlton, killed {fallen_where}. The sergeant stands there turning his cap in his hands. "Best lad with a horse I ever had," he says. "Best I ever had."[/if][if !war.fallen_present && war.transferred]Evans finds you with a face on him. A battalion runner told him. George Charlton, killed {fallen_where}. You stand there thinking of the pony stables.[/if][if !war.fallen_present && !flag.pit_helped_charlton && !war.transferred]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. George Charlton, killed {fallen_where}. The man who tells you says it quickly, to get it said, and goes, and you stand there thinking of the pony stables.[/if]

He was the gentlest of all of you. He used to carry his pony's bait down the shaft in his own pocket.

choices.text: Write to Mrs Charlton. Tell her about the mules.
choices.text_after:
You tell her about the mule that leaned on him in the dark like Captain used to, and how he
saved his crusts. You tell her he wasn't frightened, which is the only thing you know for
certain.

choices.text: Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

s_raid_1.title: The raid
s_raid_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0][if war.vol]You put your name down.[else]The sergeant picked you.[/if] Burnt cork on your face and hands, cap badge off, pay
book left with the quartermaster. A cosh made of an entrenching-tool handle with a nut bolted on
the end. The officer goes through it again in a whisper in the sap: out through our wire, across,
in at the place where their parapet's been knocked about, a prisoner if we can, back in twenty
minutes.

Out in front the grass is wet and it's dark as a coal hole, and the dark smells of turned earth and cordite.
Behind you is {mate}. You can hear him breathing.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Raid night. The burnt cork, the cosh, and an officer younger than you who keeps
looking at his wristwatch as if it might tell him something. There's a thin moon. He says it'll be
behind cloud by midnight. He's wrong.

The sap smells of wet sandbags and of the cork, which smells like a blown-out candle. Behind you is
{mate}, chewing on nothing.[/if]

choices.text: Go fast and upright to the gap. Time matters more than cover. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run bent double across the grass, every step loud as a door slamming, and nobody fires.

choices.text: Crawl it the way you practised, one arm at a time. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Elbows and knees, face in the wet grass, a yard at a time. It takes an age.

choices.text: Go wide round the shell holes, slow, freezing at every flare. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lose the others twice in the dark and find them again by the smell of the cork.

choices.text: Tell the officer your rifle's jammed, and go back in. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: He looks at you in the dark for a moment and says nothing at all.

s_raid_2.title: The raid
s_raid_2.text:
Their wire. Close up it's not a fence, it's a thicket, rusty, taller than you, with tins hung in
it to rattle. The gap the guns made is narrower than the officer said. Somebody's cutting with
the long-handled cutters, each snip like a gunshot in your head.

Ten yards beyond it, their parapet. You can hear a man coughing on the other side, and smell
pipe tobacco, and something frying.

choices.text: Through the gap and straight over their parapet. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The wire takes a strip out of your sleeve and your arm with it, and then you're over, and dropping.

choices.text: Wait for the cutters, then go through in turn. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Snip. Snip. Your turn. You go through on your belly with the barbs catching your back.

choices.text: Hold back at the wire and cover the others in. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lie at the wire with your rifle on their parapet, and the others go in without you.

s_raid_3.title: The raid
s_raid_3.text:
In their trench. It's cleaner than ours, and deeper, and for one second it's empty. Then a man
comes round the traverse with a mess tin in each hand and stops dead, and looks at you, and
opens his mouth.

There's a dugout entrance two yards on, steps going down, a blanket over the door, light under it.

choices.text: Grab the man with the mess tins. He's your prisoner. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: He doesn't fight. He drops the tins and puts his hands up, and the stew goes all over your boots, and it's still hot.

choices.text: Bomb the dugout and get out the way you came. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Pin, throw, down. The blanket blows out flat. You don't wait to see.

choices.text: Shout the others back now, before their trench wakes up. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You're back over their parapet before the first flare goes up.

x_raid_done.title: After the raid
x_raid_done.text: [if war.result == ok]You come back in through our wire with the dawn starting, and a prisoner, or near enough: a pay book, a shoulder strap, something the intelligence officer can read. The colonel sends down a rum ration for the raiders. The cork won't come off your face for two days. You keep finding it in your ears.[/if][if war.result == failed]It goes wrong somewhere between the wire and the way back. Their machine gun wakes up early. Two of the party don't come in. You lie in the sap afterwards, shaking so hard your teeth click, and somebody puts a lit cigarette in your mouth without a word.[/if][if war.result == turned]The raid goes over without you. You hear it from the firestep: the bombs, the shouting, their flares going up one after another. When they come back in, nobody looks at you.[/if]

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_patrol_1.title: Patrol
s_patrol_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Three of you, a corporal and {mate} and you, out through the gap in our wire at eleven. The job is
to find out whether they've put new wire out by the old sunken road, and come back and say.

No man's land at night isn't empty and isn't quiet. Rats. A tin rolling in the wind. Somewhere
out to the left a wounded man from last week, or a cat, or the wind in the wire.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The sunken road again, a corporal and {mate} and you, to see what they've done to their wire since.
Fog tonight, [if start == mill]thick as the shed on a damp morning[/if][if start == pit]thick as the reek off the pit heap on a wet night[/if][if start == city || start == farm]thick as wet wool[/if], so you can't see the man in front,
only hear the creak of his webbing and his breath going in and out.

The fog tastes of coal smoke from somewhere far off, which makes no sense out here.[/if]

choices.text: Go straight for the sunken road. Get there and get back. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You go quickly, crouched, and get there in ten minutes, with your heart going like a shuttle.

choices.text: Bound from shell hole to shell hole, the way you were taught. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Hole to hole. Down, listen, count twenty, up. The mud gets into everything.

choices.text: Lie still a while first and listen to their trench. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lie with your face in the wet and listen to them talking, and someone over there laughs, and it's like a knife.

choices.text: Tell the corporal you've heard something, and you should go back. ({risk_back})
