choices.text_after: He knows you've heard nothing. He takes you back anyway.

s_patrol_2.title: Patrol
s_patrol_2.text:
The sunken road. And there's somebody in it.

A German patrol, six or seven, lying up along the bank thirty yards from you, the same as you, in
the dark, listening. You can see a helmet against the sky. You can hear one of them breathing
through his mouth. A hand closes on your arm: {mate}.

choices.text: Bomb them, now, while they don't know you're there. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: Two bombs, and the dark goes white and loud, and somebody over there screams in German, and you're running.

choices.text: Lie flat and count them. That's what you're out here for. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Seven. One has a machine pistol. One is smoking under his coat, the fool. You count them twice.

choices.text: Ease back out of the road, an inch at a time. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: It takes you twenty minutes to go thirty yards backwards on your belly.

choices.text: Get out of there and go back in, quick and low. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You go back too fast and a sentry nearly shoots you at our wire.

s_patrol_3.title: Patrol
s_patrol_3.text:
Coming back is the dangerous bit, everybody says, and everybody's right. Our own sentries are
jumpy. The password this week is Blackpool. The gap in our wire is somewhere ahead, and in the
dark one stretch of wire looks like every other.

choices.text: Stand up at the wire and call the password. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: "Blackpool!" A rifle bolt, a pause, and a voice from home: "Come on then, you daft beggar."

choices.text: Feel along the wire for the gap with your hands. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You find the gap by the strip of white tape somebody tied to the picket. You could kiss him.

choices.text: Wait in a shell hole till the flares die, then crawl in. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get in just before stand-to with the cold right through you.

x_patrol_done.title: After the patrol
x_patrol_done.text: [if war.result == ok]You report to the company officer in his dugout, standing with the mud drying on you, and he writes down what you say about the sunken road and the patrol in it and the new wire. He gives you his own tin of cigarettes. Two days later, our guns shell the sunken road all night.[/if][if war.result == failed]You come back with nothing anybody can use. The corporal tells the officer it was too dark, and it was. You lie awake till stand-to, seeing that helmet against the sky.[/if][if war.result == turned]The corporal reports you came back because you'd heard something. He doesn't say what. He doesn't look at you while he says it.[/if]

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_wiring_1.title: Wiring
s_wiring_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Out in front with a coil of barbed wire on a stick across two men's shoulders, and screw pickets,
and mallets with sacking tied round the heads. The barbs catch your gloves, your puttees, your
face. Every few minutes a flare goes up from their side, and the whole party freezes where it
stands like children playing statues.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Pickets and a coil tonight, and two knife rests, wooden frames already strung with wire, carried out
between two men to drop across the worst gaps. They catch on everything. The wire sings
when it brushes against itself, a thin high note, and you'd swear the whole German army can hear it.[/if]

choices.text: Work fast. Get the pickets in before the moon's up. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You get six pickets screwed in, your hands raw, before the corporal tells you to slow down.

choices.text: Work with the others, a picket at a time. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Screw, turn, turn, turn. The picket bites into the clay and holds.

choices.text: Do the work close to our own wire, where there's cover. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You do the easy end. Nobody says anything. Somebody has to do the far end.

s_wiring_2.title: Wiring
s_wiring_2.text:
A flare goes up right over you. It hangs, and hangs, and you're stood in the open with a coil of
wire in your arms and every bit of you lit up white, and you can see your own shadow on the
ground going round slowly as the flare swings.

choices.text: Keep working. Moving men are harder to see than you'd think. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You keep unrolling the wire, slowly, steadily, and the flare dies, and nobody fires.

choices.text: Freeze. Don't move a finger till it dies. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You don't breathe. The flare comes down somewhere behind you, fizzing in the grass.

choices.text: Drop flat into the nearest shell hole. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You're down in the water before you know you've moved, and the wire's somewhere on top of you.

s_wiring_3.title: Wiring
s_wiring_3.text:
One more length and it's done, the corporal says. It's nearly light. You can see the shape of
their parapet now, which means they can see the shape of you.

choices.text: Finish the length. Whatever it takes. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run the last coil out and stamp it down and you're in through our wire as the light comes up grey.

choices.text: Finish what you can and come in with the party. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You get most of it in, and come back in with the others, and the corporal says it'll do.

choices.text: Come in now and leave the last of it. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You leave the last coil lying in no man's land. Someone will have to go out for it.

choices.text: Tell the corporal you're done in, and go back first. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You go back in on your own, and leave them to it.

x_wiring_done.title: After wiring
x_wiring_done.text: [if war.result == ok]In the morning you look over the parapet with a periscope and there it is, your wire, a new belt of it, grey and nasty in the daylight. You put that there. It's a strange thing to be proud of.[/if][if war.result == failed]In daylight the new belt is a mess, half of it lying flat, a gap at one end you could drive a cart through. The officer looks at it through the periscope and says nothing, and you'll be out there again tonight.[/if][if war.result == turned]The others come in after it's light, with the wire done. The corporal hands you a cup of tea and doesn't say a word.[/if]

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_listening_1.title: Listening post
s_listening_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]A hole in the ground out past our wire, two men in it, a string running back to the trench. One
tug for all right, two for something moving, three for them coming. You've a rifle, four bombs
and a flask of cold tea, and three hours to lie here.

In the hole with you is {mate}. His knee is pressed against yours. You can feel it trembling, or
it's yours.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The Coffin, they call this post, because of its shape and for the other reason. Two hours in it with
rain on your back the whole time, running down your neck, filling your boots. The string runs back
into the dark and you keep your hand on it like a rosary.

In the post with you is {mate}, so close you can smell the tea on his breath.[/if]

choices.text: Crawl out ahead of the post to see better. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You lie out in front of the post in the grass, ten yards nearer them, with your ear on the ground.

choices.text: Settle in the hole and listen, the way you were told. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You settle in, and the cold comes up out of the ground into you, and you listen.

choices.text: Keep down below the lip of the hole. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You keep your head down below the lip, and the night goes on over you.

s_listening_2.title: Listening post
s_listening_2.text:
A sound. Out in front, to the right, the wire rattling, or a rat at it. Then nothing. Then again:
a click, metal on metal, and a whisper you can't make out. It might be a German patrol. It might
be a loose picket in the wind. It's two in the morning and every sound is a man.

choices.text: Throw a bomb at the sound. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The bomb goes off in the wire, and somebody over there yells, and their whole trench opens up on the dark.

choices.text: Two tugs on the string. Let the trench know. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Two tugs. The string comes back once. They've got it.

choices.text: Lie still. Wait to be sure. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait. The sound doesn't come again. You'll never know.

s_listening_3.title: Listening post
s_listening_3.text:
The relief's late. The sky's going grey in the east. If they don't come soon you'll have to get
back across in daylight, and their snipers will be up.

choices.text: Go back now, before it's any lighter. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run for our wire in the grey, and dive through the gap, and land on somebody's breakfast.

choices.text: Wait for the relief. That's the order. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: They come at last, swearing about the communication trench, and you crawl back in.

choices.text: Stay in the hole all day if you have to. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lie in the hole all day with the flies, and come in after dark, stiff as a board.

x_listening_done.title: After the listening post
x_listening_done.text: [if war.result == ok]Two nights later a German raid comes over on exactly that stretch, and walks into rifles that are waiting for it. The company sergeant major makes a point of saying who heard them coming.[/if][if war.result == failed]Nobody comes, that you know of. The night was full of sounds and you can't swear to any of them. You come in with your ears ringing from listening.[/if][if war.result == turned]You came in early. Nobody saw anything on that stretch all night, so it doesn't matter, except that it does.[/if]

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_carrying_1.title: Carrying party
s_carrying_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The ration dump at the end of the communication trench: boxes of small-arms ammunition, coils of
wire, duckboards, sandbags of bread, a dixie of tea for the front line with the lid tied on with
string. You're to take it all up. Two miles of trench, in the dark, in the wet, under a German
battery that knows the route as well as you do.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Rations and ammunition as usual from the dump, and on top of them tonight trench mortar bombs, the
ones the lads call toffee apples, a ball on a stick, slung on poles between pairs of men. If one goes off, the carrying party goes with it. Nobody
smokes. Nobody even talks about smoking.[/if]

choices.text: Take two loads at once and save a journey. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You set off with an ammunition box on each shoulder, and your shoulders tell you about it every yard.

choices.text: Take your load and go with the party. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You get the dixie of tea, which is the worst job, because if you spill it the front line will kill you.

choices.text: Take the light load: the bread. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You take the bread. It's the lightest load and everybody knows it.

s_carrying_2.title: Carrying party
s_carrying_2.text:
Halfway up, the battery starts. Whizz-bangs, you hear them after they arrive: a crack and a
flash and earth coming down on your helmet like rain on a slate roof. The trench is knee-deep in
places and the duckboards float. Somebody ahead is shouting to keep moving.

choices.text: Keep moving. Get through the shelled stretch fast. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run, bent double, slopping through the water, with the load banging your back.

choices.text: Get down between shells, then move. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Down, count, up, move. Down. You've got the rhythm of it now. That frightens you.

choices.text: Shelter in a dugout entrance till it stops. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You squeeze into a dugout entrance with three others and the load, and wait it out.

s_carrying_3.title: Carrying party
s_carrying_3.text:
The last stretch. There's a man down in the trench in front of you, one of the party, sitting in
the water holding his leg and swearing, quietly, in a steady stream, like a man reading a list.

choices.text: Take his load too, and leave him for the bearers. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You get both loads up to the front line, staggering, and fall asleep on the firestep the minute you put them down.

choices.text: Get him up and walk him in with you. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You get his arm over your shoulder and walk him in, and he swears at you all the way, and thanks you at the end.

choices.text: Stay with him and wait for the stretcher-bearers. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait with him in the water. The bearers come an hour later. The load doesn't get up till morning.

x_carrying_done.title: After the carrying party
x_carrying_done.text: [if war.result == ok]Everything gets up. The front line has its ammunition and its wire and, still warm, its tea. A sergeant you don't know shakes your hand as if you'd brought him a letter from home.[/if][if war.result == failed]Half of it doesn't get up. The tea's spilt and the bread's soaked and an ammunition box is somewhere at the bottom of the trench water. The front line goes without, tonight.[/if][if war.result == turned]You came back without it. Somebody else takes it up.[/if]

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_bomb_1.title: Bombing raid
s_bomb_1.text:
Eight bombers and a sergeant, a sandbag of Mills bombs each, in the sap at one in the morning. The
pins are bent back ready so you won't fumble them. The bombs are cold and heavy and fit your hand
the way a cricket ball does.

choices.text: Lead the way out to their wire. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You go first, and the others follow your shape in the dark.

choices.text: Go out in your place in the party. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You go out fourth, behind the sergeant's boots.

choices.text: Go out last and keep the line back to the sap. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You go last, the safest place, and the job nobody wants to be seen wanting.

choices.text: Tell the sergeant you can't go tonight. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: The sergeant looks at you a long moment and takes your bombs off you himself.

s_bomb_2.title: Bombing raid
s_bomb_2.text:
In their trench. This is the work: along it a bay at a time. Pin, throw over the traverse, count,
down, the bang, then round the corner fast before they can throw back. Their bombs come over
too, the stick ones, turning end over end in the light of the last explosion.

choices.text: Lead round each traverse. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: Three bays. Four. You stop counting. Your arm aches from throwing.

choices.text: Throw for the man in front. Keep him supplied. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You throw, and pass up bombs, and throw, and the trench fills with smoke you can taste.

choices.text: Hold the bay you're in. Block it with sandbags. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You build a block out of their own sandbags, and hold it, and the others go on without you.

s_bomb_3.title: Bombing raid
s_bomb_3.text:
The sergeant blows his whistle. Out. Their machine gun has started from somewhere further along
and the gap in the wire is behind you and getting further away.

choices.text: Bomb the machine gun before you go. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: Your bomb goes over the sandbags at the muzzle flash, and the flash stops.

choices.text: Go back with the party, carrying the wounded. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You go back with a man over your shoulder who keeps apologising.

choices.text: Run for the gap. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You run, and dive, and you're through.

x_bomb_done.title: After the bombing raid
x_bomb_done.text: [if war.result == ok]Their trench is blocked for a hundred yards and there's a dugout that won't be used again. The bombing officer says the brigadier has heard. You can't get the smell of the explosive off your hands, sweet and chemical, like pear drops.[/if][if war.result == failed]It went wrong. Their bombers were waiting. The sergeant's arm is in a sling and two of the eight aren't back.[/if][if war.result == turned]They went without you. The bombing officer has your name in his notebook now, and not in the good column.[/if]

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_lewis_1.title: The gun
s_lewis_1.text:
Getting the gun into position: twenty-eight pounds of it, the drums in their canvas panniers, your
No. 2 behind you with the spares, out along a sap to a shell hole with a view. You've cleaned it
twice since dark. You can feel every grain of grit in it.

choices.text: Set up in the forward hole with the best field of fire. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The forward hole. You can see the whole of their parapet from here, which means it can see you.

choices.text: Set up where you were told. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: The bipod legs bed into the sandbags. The butt goes into your shoulder like it lives there.

choices.text: Set up back in the sap, under cover. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You set up in the sap. You can see half as much from here. You're twice as safe.

s_lewis_2.title: The gun
s_lewis_2.text:
You open up. The gun shakes against your shoulder and the cooling fins go hot and the empty cases
spill out of the side and ring off the sandbags. Forty-seven rounds, and you're changing the drum
by feel. Then it stops. A stoppage. The cocking handle's forward. You know what that is. Your
hands know before you do.

choices.text: Clear it fast and keep firing. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: Pull, pull, a new drum, and it's going again, and the muzzle flash lights up the whole hole.

choices.text: Clear it properly, by the drill. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: First position, second position. Your No. 2 hands you the drum without being asked.

choices.text: Get the gun down out of sight while you clear it. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get it down into the bottom of the hole and work on it blind, and the firing stops for a minute too long.

s_lewis_3.title: The gun
s_lewis_3.text:
It's done. Now the gun has to come back in, and their machine gunners know exactly where it's
been. The first shells are already coming down behind you.

choices.text: Carry the gun back yourself, fast. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run with the gun across your shoulders, and it gets heavier with every yard.

choices.text: Take it back in turns with your No. 2. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Gun, then drums, then gun. The sap's longer than it was.

choices.text: Wait in the hole for the shelling to ease. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait with the gun in your lap like a sleeping child, until it eases.

x_lewis_done.title: After the gun
x_lewis_done.text: [if war.result == ok]The raid came back in under your fire, every man of it, and the raid officer comes along the trench afterwards to find the gunner. You're cleaning the gun. You keep cleaning it while he talks. Your hands won't stop otherwise.[/if][if war.result == failed]The gun was quiet when it was needed. Somebody out there paid for it. Nobody blames you to your face.[/if][if war.result == turned]You didn't take the gun up. Somebody else's team did.[/if]

choices.text: Clean the gun.

s_signals_1.title: The line
s_signals_1.text:
The pliers in your pocket, the reel of cable on your back, the buzzer in its leather case banging
on your hip. Somewhere between here and battalion the line is cut, and battalion is shouting into
a dead telephone.

choices.text: Run along the top of the trench where it's quickest. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run along the top in the dark with the wire running through your fingers.

choices.text: Follow the wire along the trench floor. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You follow it bay by bay, the wire cold and wet in your hand.

choices.text: Wait for the shelling to slacken first. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait. Battalion waits. The colonel's voice, they'll tell you later, went quiet.

s_signals_2.title: The line
s_signals_2.text:
The break, at last, in the worst place: where the communication trench has been blown in, and
the two ends of the wire are fifteen yards apart across open ground that's under fire.

choices.text: Run the new wire across the open in one go. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run, paying out cable, and fall flat at the far end with your heart hammering, and the cable's across.

choices.text: Crawl the wire across. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You crawl it across with the reel on your back and the bullets cracking overhead.

choices.text: Take the long way round, through the next trench. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: It takes three times as much cable and three times as long, and you nearly run out.

s_signals_3.title: The line
s_signals_3.text: You splice it, fingers numb, by feel, the rubber tape in your teeth. Now to test it.

choices.text: Test it there, in the open. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You clip on the buzzer. Dot dash. Battalion answers.

choices.text: Get back into cover, then test it. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: In the trench, the buzzer. It answers.

choices.text: Leave it for the next man to test. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get back in and tell them it's done, and hope it is.

x_signals_done.title: After the line
x_signals_done.text: [if war.result == ok]The line holds till morning. The colonel gets his company commander, and the company gets its guns when it needs them. The signals sergeant gives you a slice of his wife's cake, which is the highest honour in the signals.[/if][if war.result == failed]The line goes again within the hour. They send a runner, in the end, and he doesn't come back.[/if][if war.result == turned]You didn't go. Another signaller did.[/if]

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_snipe_1.title: The hide
s_snipe_1.text:
Before dawn you crawl into the hide: a hollow in the parapet behind a steel plate with a slit in
it, a sack over the slit, your observer beside you with the telescope and the notebook. You stay
till dark. Fourteen hours. You've a bottle to piss in and a tin of bully.

choices.text: Take the forward hide, the one with the better view. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The forward hide. You can see their trench from here, and the ruined house behind it, and everything in between.

choices.text: Take your usual hide. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Your hide. You know every lump in its sandbags.

choices.text: Take the deep hide, with the narrow slit. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: The deep hide. You can see a slice of their parapet the width of your hand.

s_snipe_2.title: The hide
s_snipe_2.text:
Mid-morning. Your observer touches your arm. At a loophole in their parapet, a piece of mirror,
and behind it a man shaving, his braces down, the lather white on his face. He puts you in mind
of your father at the scullery sink. He has no idea.

choices.text: Take the shot. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The rifle kicks. The mirror's gone. Your observer writes something in the notebook and doesn't look at you.

choices.text: Watch the loophole and wait for a better target. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You wait. He finishes shaving. At noon a man with an officer's cap comes to the same loophole.

choices.text: Let him shave. Mark the loophole and keep still. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You watch him rinse his razor, and wipe his face, and go.

choices.text: Pack it in for the day. Something's wrong out there. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You've a feeling a plate's been moved over there. You trust it, and get out.

s_snipe_3.title: The hide
s_snipe_3.text:
Afternoon. A rifle bullet hits your steel plate with a sound like a bell, and the whole hide
rings. They've found you. Their sniper is out there somewhere, and he's looking at your slit.

choices.text: Find him. He fired; he's shown himself. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You find the flash, a dark place in a heap of bricks. You wait. You fire.

choices.text: Close the slit and wait for dark. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You close the slit and lie in the dark with the plate between you and him, and the hours go slow.

choices.text: Crawl out the back of the hide, now. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You go out the back on your belly, and leave the hide to him.

x_snipe_done.title: After the hide
x_snipe_done.text: [if war.result == ok]The observer's notebook goes back to the sniping officer with two entries in it, and a sketch of the loophole. Nobody shaves at that mirror again. You eat your bully beef in the dark afterwards and it tastes of the inside of the tin.[/if][if war.result == failed]A day in the hide with nothing in the notebook but times and weather. Their side was careful today. So were you.[/if][if war.result == turned]You came out early. The notebook's blank.[/if]

choices.text: Clean the rifle.

s_tunnel_1.title: The gallery
s_tunnel_1.text:
Down the shaft on the ladder, sixty feet, the air getting thicker and warmer. Along the gallery on
your back on the trolley, to the face. The candle goes small and blue. Clay, wet, the smell of it
and of men's sweat and of the bags of spoil going back hand to hand.

choices.text: Work the face, kicking the clay out fast. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You lie on the cross and kick at the clay with the grafting tool, and the spoil goes back down the line.

choices.text: Work it quietly, the way you were taught. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Quiet as you can, the clay coming away in lumps, each one handed back without a word.

choices.text: Shore it up first, frame by frame. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get the timbers in before you dig another foot. The roof creaks, and holds.

s_tunnel_2.title: The gallery
s_tunnel_2.text:
You put your ear to the listening stick against the clay. You can hear them. The Germans, digging
their own gallery, close: the scrape, the thud, a voice. Then the digging stops. They're
listening too.

choices.text: Keep digging, quietly. Get to them first. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You keep digging, slow, silent, and your own heartbeat is the loudest thing in the gallery.

choices.text: Stop and listen. Count how long they're quiet. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You lie still with your ear to the clay for an hour. They start again. You breathe.

choices.text: Pull back down the gallery and report it. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You crawl back down the gallery on your belly and tell the officer, in a whisper, though you're a hundred yards off.

choices.text: Get everybody out of the gallery. Now. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You get everyone out, and up the shaft, and nothing happens, and then you have to go back down.

s_tunnel_3.title: The gallery
s_tunnel_3.text:
The officer decides: a camouflet, a small charge, to blow in their gallery before they blow in
yours. The ammonal comes down the line in bags. Somebody has to tamp it and lay the leads.

choices.text: Lay the charge yourself. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You lay it with your hands steady, which surprises you, and you're up the shaft when it goes. The ground jumps.

choices.text: Tamp and pass up the bags, with the others. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You tamp the charge with sandbags, bag after bag, till the gallery's sealed.

choices.text: Work the windlass at the top of the shaft. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wind, and wind, and the men come up out of the dark one by one, grey with clay.

x_tunnel_done.title: After the gallery
x_tunnel_done.text: [if war.result == ok]Their gallery is gone. The listening officer says there's been no digging since. You sleep twelve hours in the tunnellers' dugout and dream of nothing, which is the best kind.[/if][if war.result == failed]It went off too soon, or too late. Our gallery came in at the end. Two men are still down there, and you know their names, and the officer has started a new shaft.[/if][if war.result == turned]You came up. Somebody else went down.[/if]

choices.text: Wash the clay off, if you can.

w_step.title: Out there
w_step.text: [if war.step == 1]You go out.[/if][if war.step == 2]Halfway. The worst of it is now.[/if][if war.step == 3]Nearly done. Getting back is its own job.[/if]

choices.text: Push it. Get it done fast. ({risk_bold})
Steady. Do it the way you were taught. ({risk_steady})
Careful. Keep low and take your time. ({risk_careful})
Turn back. ({risk_back})

x_sortie.title: Back in
x_sortie.text: [if war.result == ok]It went the way it was meant to. The sergeant nods at you, which from him is a speech.[/if][if war.result == failed]It went wrong, the way these things do, and nobody can say quite where.[/if][if war.result == turned]You came back without doing it. Nobody says anything. Everybody knows.[/if]

choices.text: Get your head down while you can.

c_enlist_mill.title: The drill hall
c_enlist_mill.text:
The queue starts at the drill hall door and goes back past the Co-op and round into Bury Road.
Somebody has chalked GOD SAVE THE KING on the wall, and under it somebody else has put AND OUR
ALBERT, and Albert Shaw is stood right in front of it pretending he can't read.

It's warm for September. The street smells of the mill on a hundred men at once: machine oil,
cotton fluff in their hair, the sour sweat of the weaving shed. Without the looms going your
ears feel hollow, the way they do on a Sunday.

The recruiting sergeant doesn't shout. He's like a good tackler: he doesn't need to.

"Age?"

"Just turned {age_words}, sir."

Behind you Walter Pilling is going to say nineteen. Walter Pilling was born the same winter as
your sister, and everybody in the queue knows it, and nobody says a word.
[break]
What you take with you from the shed is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: The knack you have with a loom, and legs for a ten-hour day.
The knack you have with a loom, and the voice that leads the chapel choir.
Legs for a ten-hour day, and the voice that leads the chapel choir.

c_enlist_pit.title: The Miners' Hall
c_enlist_pit.text:
The queue comes out of the Miners' Hall door and goes down past the Store and the Primitive
Methodist chapel nearly to the pit gates, and behind it the winding wheel's still turning,
because the fore shift isn't up yet. When they do come up they come straight over, black to the
eyes, bait tins under their arms, and join the end of it, and nobody tells them to go home and
wash first.

The colliery band played the first lot to the station in August. They're not playing today.
They're in the queue.

The street smells of the pit on a hundred men: coal dust and wet pit clothes and sweat, and
over it all the sulphur off the heap that's been burning since before you were born. There's a
blue mark on every forehead and every set of knuckles, where the coal got into a cut and healed
in.

The manager came down this morning in his good coat and said coal was war work too. Jim Bell
asked him if coal would pay the widows, and the manager went red and went home.

"Age?"

"Just gone {age_words}, sir."

Tommy Robson's in front of you, your marra at the face these two years, saying nothing, which
is how Tommy says most things. George Charlton's behind you, still smelling of the stables,
because he went down the pit last night to tell his pony he was going.
[break]
What you bring from underground is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: Digging and timbering, and a back for a long shift.
Digging and timbering, and a hand with the engines and the pumps.
A back for a long shift, and a hand with the engines and the pumps.

c_enlist_city.title: Guildhall
c_enlist_city.text:
The queue goes out of the Guildhall yard and down Gresham Street and round into Basinghall
Street, four deep, and every man in it is wearing a bowler hat. Clerks. From the insurance
offices and the banks and the shipping firms, from every desk in the City, come out at dinner
time with their sandwiches in their pockets and stood in the queue instead.

It's warm for September. The street smells of horse dung and hot stone and the river, and of
the City on a hundred men: ink, brilliantine, the starch in a hundred stiff collars. A man in
front of you is still holding a ledger.

The manager came round the office at eleven and shook every man's hand and said the Gresham
and Lombard would make up their salaries for as long as it lasted. Arthur Webb, from the next
desk, wrote it down. Percy Fenton was out of the door before the manager finished. Leonard Marsh
sat up half the night with a card from the optician's, learning the letters.

The sergeant writes your name. "Age?"

"Just turned {age_words}, sir."
[break]
What you bring from the office is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: A clerk's head for reading and figures, and a bowler's arm from Saturday cricket.
A clerk's head for reading and figures, and the St John Ambulance certificate.
A bowler's arm from Saturday cricket, and the St John Ambulance certificate.

c_enlist_farm.title: Harvest home
c_enlist_farm.text:
The harvest's in, and the harvest supper's in the big barn at Court Farm, the way it is every
year: trestle tables, a ham, cider from the squire's own press, the fiddler from Brendon, and
the barn still smelling of the corn it held all summer. Only this year the squire stands up at
the end with a paper in his hand, and there's a recruiting sergeant beside him in a red sash,
and nobody's dancing.

The squire's son, young Mr Venn, is taking a commission. He'll have a platoon, the squire says,
and he'd like it to be Dunsworthy men.

Will Cottle puts his tankard down and stands up first, because his father's looking at him and
he can't bear it. Dan Pearce stands up because Will has, and because it's further from the
keeper. Bert Yeo, who rang the bells for the harvest thanksgiving that morning, stands up
because everybody else is.

The sergeant writes your name. "Age?"

"Just gone {age_words}, sir."
[break]
What you bring from the land is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: A shotgun and a poacher's eye, and the legs to walk the moor all day.
A shotgun and a poacher's eye, and a hand with the threshing engine.
The legs to walk the moor all day, and a hand with the threshing engine.

c_general.title: The last night
c_general.text:
Your mother has sewn your name into everything you own. The kitchen smells of hot iron and the
starch she's put in your collars, which the army will take off you in a week. She's not
talking much. She keeps finding things to fold.

There's one more thing you've got that the army didn't give you.

choices.text: First aid. The ambulance class at the works, certificate in a frame.
A throwing arm. Second eleven, and you can hit a stump from the boundary.
A voice. When you start a hymn, men join in.

c_training.title: Training
c_training.text:
Eight months of it. Huts with floors that never dry. Drill in your own clothes till Christmas,
then in blue serge, then at last in khaki that smells of the store and makes your neck raw.
Route marches in the rain until your feet are one blister and then they harden and you stop
noticing. Digging practice trenches in a field and filling them in again. Bayonet drill on
sacks of straw, the corporal yelling at you to scream, and you feel daft screaming, and then
one day you don't.

You learn to sleep anywhere. You learn to eat anything. You learn the men from home all over
again, the way you never knew them [if start == mill]in the shed[/if][if start == pit]at the face[/if][if start == city]across the office[/if][if start == farm]in the fields[/if]: who snores, who cries, who shares.

In May the orders come. France.

{section_line}

choices.text: Go aboard.

w_tour.title: In the line
w_tour.text: [if war.month == 1 && war.take == 0]January. The ground's iron and the bully beef comes up frozen in the tin. You rub whale oil into your feet every morning, under the eye of a corporal, because trench foot is a crime now, and the oil stinks of fish and the cold gets in anyway.[/if][if war.month == 1 && war.take == 1]January. Frost on the wire in the morning, every barb furred white. The braziers fill the dugouts with coke fumes that give you a headache like a hammer, and you sit in them anyway, because outside your breath freezes on your scarf.[/if][if war.month == 2 && war.take == 0]February, and the thaw. The trench walls go soft and slide in, a bay at a time, and you dig them out and they slide in again. The rats are fat from the winter. One runs over your face in the night and you've stopped waking up for it.[/if][if war.month == 2 && war.take == 1]February. Wet, and then wetter. The duckboards float. Everything you own is damp, your blanket, your socks, your bread, and the whole line smells of wet wool and wet earth and the latrine.[/if][if war.month == 3 && war.take == 0]March. Rain on the wind, and the wind straight off the German line, so it smells of them: their cooking, their tobacco, their latrines. The pumps go all night and the water comes back in all day.[/if][if war.month == 3 && war.take == 1]March. A raw grey month. The sky sits on the trench like a lid. You don't feel your feet from one end of the tour to the other.[/if][if war.month == 4 && war.take == 0]April. Green coming through the churned ground in no man's land, thin and bright, as if nobody had told the grass. At night the frogs croak in the shell holes, a whole chapel choir of them.[/if][if war.month == 4 && war.take == 1]April. Showers and sun, both in an hour. Behind the lines there's blossom on the orchard trees by the billets, and you stand under it with your mess tin and can't take it in.[/if][if war.month == 5 && war.take == 0]May. Warm enough to take your tunic off in the support line. The flies are starting, and the smell from no man's land is starting with them.[/if][if war.month == 5 && war.take == 1]May. The hawthorn's out along the roads behind the lines, white as washing, and the smell of it comes up the communication trench at dusk, sweet, and then the other smell, underneath.[/if][if war.month == 6 && war.take == 0]June. The nights are so short that stand-to is at three in the morning, and the sky's going grey before you've got your boots dry. The water comes up in petrol tins and tastes of petrol and chloride.[/if][if war.month == 6 && war.take == 1]June. Dust, and flies, and the long light evenings. You can read a letter on the firestep at ten at night, and you do, over and over.[/if][if war.month == 7 && war.take == 0]July. Heat. The flies are on everything: the jam, the bread, your mouth if you leave it open. Thirst all day. The sandbags are hot to the touch at noon.[/if][if war.month == 7 && war.take == 1]July. The trench bakes. Men sleep in the afternoon in whatever shade the parapet gives, faces covered with their caps against the flies.[/if][if war.month == 8 && war.take == 0]August. Thunderstorms in the night that you mistake for guns, and guns you mistake for thunder. Behind the lines the French women are getting the harvest in by hand, and they don't look up at the columns going past.[/if][if war.month == 8 && war.take == 1]August. Wasps at the jam tins and the heavy smell of hay from the fields behind the lines, and a storm every few nights that fills the trench to your knees.[/if][if war.month == 9 && war.take == 0]September. Mist in the mornings, low on the ground, so that at stand-to the German line isn't there and then is. Blackberries in the hedges behind the billets; you eat them till your fingers are purple.[/if][if war.month == 9 && war.take == 1]September. The nights drawing in. The air smells of turned earth and the first fires of the year in the farmhouses behind the lines.[/if][if war.month == 10 && war.take == 0]October. Rain, and the mud comes back like an old enemy. Greatcoats again. The leaves are coming down off the last trees in the wood behind the support line, what's left of the trees.[/if][if war.month == 10 && war.take == 1]October. A wet, rotten month. Your puttees never dry. The rum ration starts again and you've never been so glad of anything.[/if][if war.month == 11 && war.take == 0]November. Fog. Dark by half past four. You stand on the firestep in a world the width of your own arm, and every sound in it is close.[/if][if war.month == 11 && war.take == 1]November. Cold rain that turns to sleet at night. The rum comes round at stand-to in the morning and you hold it in your mouth as long as you can, for the warmth.[/if][if war.month == 12 && war.take == 0]December. Frost again, and the parcels start coming up from home: plum puddings in tins, mufflers, socks, a cake from the Co-op in greaseproof paper. The post corporal is the most popular man in the battalion.[/if][if war.month == 12 && war.take == 1]December. The short days. You're in the dark at both ends of every working party. Somebody in the next bay is singing a carol under his breath, badly, and nobody stops him.[/if][if war.back_from_leave] The railhead smells of horse dung and wet canvas and coal smoke. Home is a day and a half behind you and already it doesn't seem real.[/if][if war.back_from_wound && !war.transferred] You're back with the battalion, the wound pulling every time you lift your arm, and the lads look at you as if you'd been somewhere they'd rather be.[/if][if war.back_from_wound && war.transferred] You're back with the company, the wound pulling every time you lift your arm, and the crew make you a brew without being asked.[/if][if war.lost_last == 1 && !war.transferred] {lost_last_name}'s place on the firestep has somebody from the draft in it, a lad who doesn't know where to put his feet.[/if][if war.lost_last >= 2 && !war.transferred] There are gaps in the section now. You keep looking for faces that aren't there.[/if][if war.lost_last >= 1 && war.transferred && war.take == 0] Word comes over from the battalion of men from home gone since. You hear it, and go down the shaft.[/if][if war.lost_last >= 1 && war.transferred && war.take == 1] A battalion man at the water point tells you who's gone from home since. You don't ask him to say it twice.[/if][if war.promoted_last] The new stripe is sewn on crooked. Men who were your mates last week say '[if war.rank <= 2]Corporal[/if][if war.rank >= 3]Sarge[/if]' in a voice that isn't quite their own.[/if][if war.award_last] The {award_last_name} is in battalion orders. Nobody says a word about it to your face, and everybody talks about it behind your back.[/if][if war.detailed_last == wiring] Last tour the sergeant put you on a wiring party.[/if][if war.detailed_last == patrol] Last tour you were sent out on a patrol.[/if][if war.detailed_last == raid] Last tour they put you on a raid, whether you liked it or not.[/if][if war.detailed_last == listening] Last tour you did a stint in a listening post.[/if][if war.detailed_last == carrying] Last tour you were on a carrying party, two miles of trench each way.[/if][if war.detailed_last == bomb || war.detailed_last == lewis || war.detailed_last == snipe || war.detailed_last == signals || war.detailed_last == tunnel] Last tour they sent you out on your own work, though you'd said you weren't fit.[/if][if war.detailed_last != none && war.detailed_ok] It went all right.[/if][if war.detailed_last != none && !war.detailed_ok] It went wrong, the way these things do.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.take == 0]Go on.[/if][if war.take == 1]Another tour.[/if]

w_duty.title: A front-line tour
w_duty.text:
The sergeant wants men for {duty_name} tonight. {friend_line}

[if war.duty == raid]A raid: blackened faces, cap badges off, no pay books, coshes and bombs, and a run across in the dark to drag a prisoner back. The ones who come back from raids don't sleep for a day after.[/if][if war.duty == patrol]A patrol means lying in no man's land for hours, cold right through, listening to them talk in their trench and trying not to breathe.[/if][if war.duty == wiring]Wiring means out in front with mallets wrapped in sacking and coils of wire that bite through your gloves, freezing every time a flare goes up.[/if][if war.duty == listening]A listening post is a hole in the ground out past the wire, two men and a string back to the trench, and every sound in the dark is somebody coming.[/if][if war.duty == carrying]A carrying party: up the communication trench and back with ammunition boxes and duckboards and coils of wire, all night, in the wet, shelled by guns that know the route as well as you do.[/if]

choices.text: Volunteer. ({duty_risk}, {duty_cost})
Keep your head down and let him choose.

w_mission.title: Your own work
w_mission.text:
[if war.path == lewis && war.take == 0]A raid is going over at two in the morning and the gun's to cover it. You set up in a sap head out past the wire with your No. 2 and four drums. The barrel shroud is so cold it burns your fingers through the mittens. When the raiders go, you fire short bursts over their heads at the German parapet, and every burst lights you up like a lamp in a window, and every German on that stretch can see exactly where you are.[/if][if war.path == lewis && war.take == 1]A German two-seater comes over low in the evening, slow and fat and close enough to see the observer's goggles. The officer wants the gun up on its post for it. You'll be standing in the open with the gun pointing at the sky and your back to their line, firing up at it while it fires down at you.[/if][if war.path == signals && war.take == 0]The line to battalion's gone again. Somewhere in the half mile of communication trench behind you a shell has cut it, and the colonel wants the company commander and can't have him. You take the pliers, a reel of D3 cable and the buzzer, and go along it in the dark, running the wire through your fingers, feeling for the break.[/if][if war.path == signals && war.take == 1]A message has to go to battalion, and the wires are all down, and the lamp can't be seen through the smoke. Somebody has to run it. Four hundred yards of open ground they've been shelling since dawn, with the message in your breast pocket in case they find you.[/if][if war.path == bomb]A bombing raid tonight: eight of you, faces blacked with burnt cork, no cap badges, no pay books, a sandbag each of Mills bombs. Into their trench, along it a bay at a time, a prisoner if you can get one, and back before their machine guns wake up.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Before dawn you crawl into the hide in the parapet, a steel plate with a slit, a sack over the slit, your observer beside you with the telescope and the notebook. You stay till dark. They have snipers looking for this plate. Some mornings you see a man over there shaving in a bit of mirror, his braces down, and he puts you in mind of your father at the scullery sink.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Down the shaft, along the gallery on your back on the trolley, to the face. Candle, the smell of wet clay and your own sweat. You lie with the listening stick against the clay and listen for them. If you can hear them digging, they're far enough off. If they stop, they're listening for you. If it goes quiet for a day, they've laid a charge.[/if]

The work's yours now. You can say you're not fit for it. You'll usually be sent anyway.

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Take the gun up.[/if][if war.path == signals]Go.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Black your face and go.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Go out to the hide.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Go down.[/if] ({mission_risk})
Say you're not fit for it tonight.

w_sick.title: Rest
w_sick.text:
[if war.take == 0]Out at rest, in a barn behind the lines. Somebody's got a mouth organ going and somebody else is
frying bread in a mess tin, and the smell of it should make you hungry. You hold your mug of
tea in both hands so the others won't see it shake. It shakes anyway. The tea goes cold and you
don't drink it.[else]Out at rest. You've slept twelve hours and you're more tired than when you lay down. Every time a door
bangs in the farmyard you're flat on the straw before you know you've moved, and the others
pretend they haven't noticed, which is kind of them, and you hate it.[/if]

The medical officer holds a sick parade every morning at seven. He's a busy man, and a tired
one, and he's seen everything.

choices.text: Report sick. The medical officer may give you a tour out of the line.
Say nothing and carry on.

w_course.title: A course
w_course.text:
The company sergeant major stops you at the water cart. There's a place going on a course,
two weeks behind the lines, and he's put your name down unless you'd rather he didn't.

[if war.course == lewis]The Lewis gun: twenty-eight pounds of it, a drum of forty-seven rounds on top like a gramophone record, and a temper. When it jams it jams in the worst place. The gun team are out of the attacks till they're needed and then they're needed more than anybody, and every German gunner looks for them first.[/if][if war.course == signals]Signals: flags, lamps, the buzzer, the field telephone and its miles of wire. When the wire's cut, and it's always cut, the signaller runs the message himself, across whatever's between him and battalion.[/if][if war.course == bomb]Bombing: the Mills bomb, pin and lever, four seconds. The bombers go first along an enemy trench, a bay at a time, and the men who come back from a bombing course don't joke about it.[/if][if war.course == snipe]Sniping: a rifle with a telescopic sight, a hide in the parapet, a partner with a periscope and a notebook. Hours of nothing. Then a second.[/if][if war.course == lead]An NCO course: map reading, fire orders, how to keep a section together when the corporal's gone. They want men who can take charge.[/if]
[if start == mill && war.course == lewis && war.mate2] Duckworth says his dad could strip one blindfold. "It's only a loom that shoots," he says.[/if]

choices.text: Take it. Two weeks out of the line, and a trade after.
Stay with the section.

w_tunnel.title: The tunnellers
w_tunnel.text:
The Royal Engineers want miners. Six shillings a day against your one, out of the attacks, and
work you know. The tunnellers do not go over the top. They go under it.

choices.text: Go to the tunnellers. You will leave the section.
Stay with the men from home.
Push on. ({risk_push})
Help the man beside you. ({risk_help})
Go to ground. ({risk_ground})

w_leave.title: Home on leave

choices.text: Go back. A stripe is waiting: the battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

e_armistice.title: The Armistice
e_armistice.text:
{ending_line}

Nobody cheers, where you are. The guns stop, and the silence comes down so hard that men look
up at the sky as if something's wrong with it. Somebody starts to laugh and can't stop. A
corporal sits down on an ammunition box and takes his boots off, both of them, right there in
the open, and nobody tells him not to.

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}, and you have been in France since you were a boy. You
can smell the wet and the cordite and the horse lines, and under all of it, for the first time
in years, nothing burning.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_posting.title: Home
e_posting.text:
{ending_line}

The war goes on without you. You read it in the paper over breakfast, like everybody else,
the long columns in small print, and you read every name, every day, and you know some of them.

Some nights you're glad. Some nights you lie awake in a proper bed with clean sheets, listening
to the rain on the slates, and you'd give anything to be in a wet bay with the lads, and you
couldn't say to anybody why.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_captured.title: Taken
e_captured.text:
{ending_line}

A boy in grey with a rifle bigger than he is takes your water bottle and your cigarettes and,
after a moment, gives you one of the cigarettes back. You walk east all day with your hands on
your head, then without, past their guns and their horses and their wounded, who look exactly
like yours.

The rest of your war is behind wire: black bread, turnip soup, work in a salt mine or on a
farm, letters that take months. Your mother gets a card in your handwriting from a camp with a
name she can't say, and she takes it round to every house in the street.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_invalided.title: Wounded out
e_invalided.text:
{ending_line}

Morphia at the dressing station, a label tied to your tunic button, a train with the windows
painted over. The hospital ship smells of carbolic and vomit and the sea. In England a woman
gives you tea with sugar in it and you cry like a child and can't stop and she just holds the
cup for you till you can.

You go home in hospital blue, then in your own clothes that don't fit. [if war.stage >= 2]A silver badge on your
lapel, so that nobody in the street hands you a white feather.[else]In the street a girl you've never seen
pushes a white feather into your buttonhole, because you're young and out of uniform, and you let her.[/if] The wound aches when it rains.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_killed.title: Killed
e_killed.text:
{ending_line}

You don't hear the one that does it. The man nearest you does, and afterwards he'll say you
made a small sound, surprised, as if you'd dropped something.

At home it comes three weeks later in a buff envelope, Army Form B.104-82: "it is my painful
duty to inform you". Your mother reads it on the doorstep with the postman still stood there,
because she knew from his face. He keeps his cap in his hands till she shuts the door.
[if flag.last_letter]

The letter from your pay book comes later, with your things: a razor, a comb, a photograph gone soft at the corners. She reads it at the kitchen table, and then she reads it again.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_broken.title: Shell shock
e_broken.text:
{ending_line}

It's your hands first. You look down and they won't stop, and then it's your legs, and then
you're lying in the bottom of the trench and you can hear somebody making a noise like a
kicked dog and it's you. They carry you down the line on a stretcher, though there's not a
mark on you, and you're ashamed of that the whole way.

The doctors call it neurasthenia. At home a door banging sends you under the table. Your
mother learns to close them quietly. Your father doesn't talk about it, which is how he
talks about it.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_court.title: Court-martial
e_court.text:
{ending_line}

The court sits in a schoolroom behind the lines, three officers at a table with the children's
sums still on the blackboard behind them. Nobody asks how long you'd been in the line. You
don't know how to tell them about the noise. It takes twenty minutes.

Most sentences are commuted. Most men go to prison, or back to the line under a cloud that
follows them into every bay. Your name goes in the paper at home, or it doesn't, and either way
your mother stops going to chapel.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

y_1915.title: France
y_1915.text:
You come off the boat at Boulogne into rain, and march up a cobbled hill past French women who
don't look at you, to a camp of wet tents on a cliff. The sea's grey and the sky's grey and
somewhere inland, so faint you think it's thunder, you can hear the guns.

Nine of you from home in the same section. {section_line}

choices.text: Go up the line.

y_1916.title: The second year
y_1916.text:
A year in France. You know now what you didn't know last spring: which noise to duck for and
which to ignore, how to sleep in four inches of water, how to eat with a dead man in the
parapet a yard from your mess tin.

You're {rank_a} now. {section_line} Everybody says this is the year. The big push. The
end of it by the autumn.

choices.text: Go back up the line.

y_1917.title: The third year
y_1917.text:
Nobody says it'll be over by the autumn any more. Nobody says anything about when.

You're {rank_a} now, and you've been out long enough that the new lads call you an old
sweat and mean it. {section_line} [if war.section <= 5]You don't make friends with the new men the way you did. You learn their names when you have to.[/if]

choices.text: Go back up the line.

y_1918.title: The fourth year
y_1918.text:
The Russians are out of it. The Americans are coming, they say, millions of them, and nobody
has seen one. Everybody knows the Germans have men to spare now, and that they'll come in the
spring.

You're {rank_a}. {section_line} [if start == mill]You can't remember the shed, some days. You can remember the noise of it.[/if][if start == pit]You can't remember the pit, some days. You can remember the dark of it, and the smell of the lamp.[/if][if start == city]You can't remember the office, some days. You can remember the scratch of the pens.[/if][if start == farm]You can't remember the farm, some days. You can remember the smell of the byre on a winter morning.[/if] You can't remember your mother's face without the photograph.

choices.text: Go back up the line.

mill.label: The mill town
mill.summary: Cotton and weaving sheds, the mill whistle at six. Half the men in your street joined the same week.

pit.label: The pit village
pit.summary: The colliery, the chapel and the club. You have worked underground since you were fourteen.

city.label: The city office
city.summary: A clerk's stool in a shipping office, a season ticket on the tram, and a rifle club on Saturdays.

farm.label: The farm village
farm.summary: Horses, hedges and a shotgun for the rooks. The harvest was in when the recruiting sergeant came.
